Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Trump says he is 'going to look at' joining Saudi Arabia in the fight against Iran-backed Houthis after deadly airport strike
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309 others. U.S. military involvement in the fight against the Houthis would stretch resources in the Middle East already committed to fighting Iran, analysts said. President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport, a move that could draw the U.S. further into a second front in the Iran war . "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday when asked if the U.S. would back Saudi Arabian strikes. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision. We move very quickly." Two Saudi Arabian government officials told MS NOW that the kingdom is requesting "urgent defense support" from the U.S. following the attacks. The officials, including a senior member of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did not want to be identified because of the matter's sensitivity. They added that the U.S. needs to intervene "as soon as possible" to help the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen fight the Houthis. The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the country's official Saudi Gazette media outlet reported . Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Houthis, described the attack as a "war crime." "Therefore, the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law," Al-Maliki said in a post on X. It was the second deadly assault on Riyadh's airport in less than a week. Three Saudi nationals, including a pilot , were killed in attacks on the facility by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Thursday. Following Saturday's attack, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using ⁠Saudi ‌airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become ⁠a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in a post on X. Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the Middle East, intervened in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and its internationally recognized government after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014. Last month, the Trump administration approved the potential $24.3 billion sale of nearly 50 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia in what was seen as a major boost for the kingdom as it faces intensifying attacks from the Houthis. The sale is under congressional review. International energy conference still on The Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference will still take place in Riyadh on Sunday, Reuters reported. The five-day WPC Energy Congress ⁠is taking place at a convention center near King Khalid airport. State television told Reuters that more than 70 ministers, ⁠300 company executives and representatives of more than 25 international energy organizations have confirmed their attendance, though it was not clear ⁠whether the participants would attend in person or virtually. Reuters said a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to take place, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors. In addition to attacks on civil aviation, the Houthis have also been trying to choke off oil tanker traffic through the Bab el Mandeb strait, a key entry point to the Red Sea, as Iran has effectively done in the Strait of Hormuz to the north of the Arabian Peninsula. Earlier this month, Yemeni government forces said they reclaimed the strategic port city of Mokha from the Houthis. Energy prices have soared since the start of the Iran war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, putting pressure on consumers globally. The surge in domestic fuel prices has been a key issue for voters ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections. But that support would be expensive militarily. "Potential U.S. involvement in the Saudi-Yemeni government air campaign to degrade Houthi ballistic missile capabilities would mark the first direct U.S. military action against the group since the conclusion of Operation Rough Rider in May 2025," according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.

events.title: AI’s quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight
events.summary: The emerging AI safety debate is putting a small group of third-party evaluators at the center of a multitrillion-dollar industry. Nonprofits like METR and Transluce are being called upon to monitor and evaluate models as the federal government opposes establishing regulatory oversight. "Who is paying for these companies to do their work? How are they going to support them?" said Suresh Venkatasubramanian, a computer science professor at Brown University Two months ago, independent evaluators occupied a relatively sleepy corner of the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence industry. Now they're being asked to come to its rescue. While Anthropic and OpenAI are at the heart of a fierce debate over whether they can safeguard their advanced models and grow their businesses simultaneously, they're seeking support from a handful of small third-party groups like Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), Apollo Research, and Transluce. The evaluators, which mostly operate as nonprofits, are still finding their footing in an industry where capital is flowing at historic levels and new models are rolling out faster than ever. Their primary role has been to assess AI model capabilities and risks and to flag instances where the technology behaves badly. Without a federal push for regulation, evaluators have taken on outsized importance. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pledged to embed independent evaluators in his company last month – a move that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly endorsed . President Donald Trump supported the idea, as did most of the largest U.S. tech companies. But left unanswered are questions about how those third parties should be funded, what level of access they will have and what the reporting structure will ultimately look like. "To a degree, the problem, as always, is money," Suresh Venkatasubramanian, a computer science professor at Brown University, told CNBC in an interview. "Who is paying for these companies to do their work? How are they going to support them? You need an ecosystem, you need a viable business model for this." Right now, Anthropic, OpenAI and the infrastructure partners that are profiting from the AI boom are writing the rules. Critics say that's like asking the biggest banks to protect us from a financial crisis or allowing pharmaceutical companies to put drugs on the market without regulatory clearance. Trump recently lauded AI executives for their "tremendous self-policing," and signaled that he intends to leave companies to their own devices, unwilling to impede the growth of the industry that's driving the economy and stock market. The president encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented in late September. Amodei kicked off the conversation in his viral essay last month, when he called for a "slower pace" in advanced model development after researchers left his company and voiced concerns about the existential threats the technology poses. As AI labs move to put evaluators in place, friction is already emerging. OpenAI fired three employees last week for "violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," according to a spokesperson. Two of those employees, Mikita Balesni and Tomek Korbak, said they believe they were dismissed because of how they communicated with third-party evaluators. "My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe," Balesni wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties. I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors." OpenAI disputed that characterization and said in a post on Friday that it's "actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks." "We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work," OpenAI wrote. An OpenAI spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its upcoming work with evaluators "builds on existing collaboration with independent safety organizations," including METR and Redwood Research. Anthropic didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. 'I've never seen an issue move so fast' The AI evaluator ecosystem consists mostly of small organizations, including METR and Apollo Research, and larger accounting and auditing firms like Accenture . AI labs have worked with evaluators in limited capacities, but Andrew Freedman, CEO of policy nonprofit Fathom, said the field is maturing quickly. "I've worked in politics and policy for the last 20 years of my life, and I've never seen an issue move so fast on so many different political spectrums," Freedman told CNBC in an interview.

events.title: These execs think voice AI hasn’t reached its ChatGPT moment yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The theory of voice being the next big interface has picked up strong momentum, with investors pouring billions of dollars into voice AI startups working on areas ranging from model makers to enterprise customer service providers, and from meeting note-takers to AI-powered dictation. Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one. However, in reality, that might not be the case. Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet. “We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models. The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me on stage at the HumanX conference last month. He also said that AI agents in customer service should not sound robotic and should give callers enough confidence that they can solve problems. “I think the next stage will be slightly different because once the voice is good enough, like, and the customer is willing to engage with them for the first two or three turns, they start to build confidence, and over time, they will feel like I probably don’t have to talk to a human if the agent can solve my problem,” he said. Alex Gay, CMO for meeting notetaker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation. The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings. For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting. “If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it. If you aren’t able to have that with an avatar, then it’s just a q and a chatbot,” Gay noted. Voice AI’s understanding and transparency While voice AI models have improved, AI assistants often don’t understand users, or your meeting notetaker shows the wrong transcript or a summary. Wen thinks that ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition) models often miss important keywords, and that creates an issue in capturing the whole context. Otter’s Gay agreed with this, adding that the company keeps working on improving transcription. He also said that language is one area where voice models need to improve. “For Otter, you know, transcription was never the end point. It was just the layer that we could start to drive some of the productivity gains on the back of. But if your original transcription didn’t have the accuracy that you needed, all the follow-up actions that you have become flawed. And the minute that starts to take action, that is wrong. You lose trust in the platform. It is critical for us to continue to improve that ASR model because all of the downstream impacts are significant,” he said. With the new voice tools, there is also a question of transparency. Tools should declare to customers that they are being recorded or talking to AI. Otter said that it wants to instill trust in people who are in a meeting, so even for a meeting where the bot is not present, it wants to try methods like notifying everyone in the chat that the meeting is being recorded. events.title: Creating a ghost town: Lives in limbo behind Israeli gates and checkpoints
events.summary: Israeli restrictions in Hebron have made life for Palestinians from the city a daily ordeal. Hebron, occupied West Bank – Badr al-Tamimi, 60, lives in Hebron’s Old City, where Israeli checkpoints, iron gates and road closures turn the simplest tasks into a dispiriting daily ordeal for Palestinian residents. The situation goes beyond mere restrictions on movement. Israel has created a ghost town in parts of Hebron, where residents feel they are being driven out. This is most pronounced in an area known as H2, where Israel has complete control and Palestinians are subject to the dictates of the military. list 1 of 3 Why Israel loves skunk water list 2 of 3 Israeli settler attacks target Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank list 3 of 3 A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona A few days ago, Israeli authorities installed three iron gates across a 200-metre (656-foot) stretch of Hebron’s Old City – amounting to just 0.2 dunams (200 square metres) – as part of Israel’s apparent attempts to restrict Palestinians’ freedom to move around the city. Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera that one gate was erected on al-Zahid Road, the only route accessible to vehicles reaching the Old City entrance. A second was placed at the start of al-Shalala Street, which leads to shops connecting to the Bab al-Zawiya area in the city centre. A third towers over another section of al-Shalala Street, a thoroughfare used by pedestrians to access the shopping area. They are part of a wider web of travel restrictions across the occupied West Bank, but Hebron, which has a strong settler presence, has suffered more than most Palestinian cities. Approximately 40 percent of the 89 checkpoints in the West Bank and 11 percent of all 925 movement obstacles are located in the H2 area of Hebron, which is under tight Israeli control, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). About 7,000 Palestinians in an area of Hebron where hundreds of settlers live are affected by the latest travel restrictions. Since October 2023, when the genocidal war on Gaza began, only Palestinians with specific identification numbers could enter this area. Checkpoints at the entrance to this zone are generally only open from 7am to 8pm. Al-Tamimi, who lives in the al-Sheikh neighbourhood adjacent to the city’s famed Ibrahimi Mosque, owns a shop in the Old City. Palestinians can be kept waiting for hours at the checkpoints, and the mood of a soldier manning one can decide the commute time of a Palestinian. Worshippers attempting to enter the Ibrahimi Mosque can be held up for hours by soldiers. “They might allow a limited number of people to enter while others are forced to wait, whereas resident movement comes to a halt during incursions, Jewish holidays, and the associated security measures,” he added. Repeated closures have paralysed economic activity in Hebron, making it increasingly difficult for shops and companies to do business. “Our presence in the Old City is a matter of steadfastness, not the availability of the elements needed for economic life,” al-Tamimi said. Even after Israel’s occupation of the city in 1967, Hebron was once a bustling city with lively shops and markets. Residents could move more freely between neighbourhoods, which helped with economic life in the city. Things changed in 1994, the year of the Ibrahimi Mosque massacre , when a US-born Israeli settler murdered 29 Palestinian worshippers. From that point, the Old City’s geography changed, becoming isolated from its surroundings, al-Tamimi said. He points to Shuhada Street, once a vital artery for transport and commerce in the city before road closures and restrictions transformed the area’s reality. “They committed the crime, yet they continue to punish us for it,” he said. In 1997, the Hebron Protocol was signed between the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) and Israel, dividing the city into two zones: H1, which was under relative Palestinian jurisdiction, and H2 – an area which includes the Old City, the Ibrahimi Mosque, and illegal settlements – remained under Israeli security control. Issa Amro, coordinator of the Youth Against Settlements group, said Israeli prohibitions intensified with the outbreak of the second Intifada in 2000 when Hebron became a centre of the uprising. During this period, vast areas of the city were sealed off, shops were forced to close, and residents often remained confined to their homes or neighbourhoods. Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, the number of checkpoints has risen to 32, while other obstacles impeding Palestinian movement now exceed 130. The “closed zones”, designated by Israeli authorities as areas of military activity with restricted access to Palestinians, have expanded around the Ibrahimi Mosque and the illegal settlements that lie in the heart of the city.

events.title: Before my dad died from dementia, I built him a mock checkout platform to avoid huge purchases
events.summary: Nikki Elbaz (left) and Hanna Miller (right) co-created ShieldCart after Miller's father developed dementia. ShieldCart Hanna Miller and Nikki Elbaz created ShieldCart to aid Miller's father with dementia. ShieldCart uses AI to simulate checkouts, allowing older users to shop without financial harm. Miller and Elbaz aim to expand ShieldCart, helping more families manage dementia-related challenges. Everyone in Hanna Miller's family knew her father as a giving and generous person. But as his dementia progressed , he couldn't recall that he'd already ordered something online just a few hours earlier. Gifts, like toys for the grandkids, piled up so quickly he couldn't easily pay for them. Watching his decline was heartbreaking. Miller's father was a biomathematics Ph.D. who spent his career in pharmaceuticals, living abroad but visiting often, always with suitcases full of presents. Whenever his grandchildren called to ask what he was doing, he would answer, "Sitting and waiting for you." But as the dementia worsened, his online shopping habits became more than an annoyance — he would repeatedly order food, and the expenses began to outweigh his modest Social Security and pension income, which covered only rent and basic living expenses. Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . Miller knew she had to intervene, but wasn't sure how. Her sister had power of attorney as her father's caregiver, so they worked together to cancel his online orders and replace his credit cards with a debit card. This not only upset him and led to repeated conflicts, but forced Miller to grapple with ethical questions about parenting her own father so strictly. She felt she was invading his privacy and stripping away his independence. "I was constantly second-guessing myself, thinking: 'Do I really have the right to decide this for him?'" Miller said. Miller wondered whether AI could help find a middle ground: a way for her father to keep shopping without letting each purchase become a financial crisis . She'd played with ChatGPT for personal use but didn't feel confident enough to build a real product that would prevent unnecessary orders. So Miller teamed up with her friend Nikki Elbaz, who had a marketing background. Miller built a service to redirect users to a fake checkout page at any online store, preventing them from completing a real transaction. They called it ShieldCart . "I told him that there's this new AI-based app that's basically a secure checkout. It makes sure that everything's right and there are no problems," Miller said. Hanna Miller said ShieldCart was helpful for her father in his final months. Hanna Miller But this well-intentioned deception went a step further than canceling sporadic online orders, and Miller was deeply conflicted about moving forward. So she went to her rabbi for guidance. He was supportive, likening the act to performing life-saving surgery on an unconscious patient. Miller describes ShieldCart as the dignified solution to a very demeaning problem. "Even though I had to step in and become the 'parent,' I was able to do it in a way that he couldn't feel it," she said. "He didn't need me stepping in and saying, 'I'm taking over. You can no longer be the parent. I have to be the parent.' He didn't have to deal with that." Miller estimates that the family saved thousands of dollars a month, while letting her father believe he was purchasing all the gifts and goods he wanted to, and avoiding the bitter fights they'd faced previously. "It was beautiful to see that he could be generous again," Elbaz said. "We've given him that freedom back." ShieldCart was built with Claude Code . It works as a Chrome extension installed on the aging parent's computer and as an app for the caregiver to monitor their purchases. The caregiver can also block certain websites — in Miller's case, crypto sites — much like parental controls. The app doesn't collect real credit card information; it only asks for the last four digits of the card to create more realistic confirmation pages. Different modes allow purchases to be blocked completely, paused temporarily, or processed and reviewed afterward. In opening the app to outside users — currently in beta testing by application only — Miller and Elbaz are clear-eyed about the ethical quandaries their product engenders. They encourage users to speak with an elder law attorney or to secure power of attorney before installing software on their loved one's device. Miller said the app probably wouldn't work for every family. If children are not as close to their parents, or if loved ones have a less advanced form of dementia, the app may not work as effectively. Miller's father died last month. His death came as a shock, as he had been in decent health and still had his wits to him. After a period of mourning, Miller decided to carry on with the app, now working to get it out to as many families as possible. The goal now, Elbaz said, is to partner with organizations that help people caring for loved ones with dementia . They've been gearing up to get more users into beta testing, making the app free for the rest of the year. They're also developing mobile capabilities for loved ones who only use phones or tablets. "Knowing that the system we built for him will now help other families navigate these challenges with that same respect and love feels like a true privilege and like a secondary, meaningful legacy beyond what lives on through our nuclear family," Miller said. events.title: AI is automating coding. So why are software developer job postings on the rise?
events.summary: What changed? Indeed says U.S. software development postings rose almost 15% from late February 2025 while overall job postings fell 7%. Who is benefiting? The rebound is concentrated: 71% of a May 2025-May 2026 increase came from senior roles and 37% from AI-titled jobs. What is the risk? Entry-level pressure remains: Stanford reports software developer employment for ages 22 to 25 fell nearly 20% from 2024, while BLS projects 10% growth overall for the profession through 2035. U.S. software development job postings have risen since February 2025, the launch date for Anthropic's Claude Code, even as overall job postings fell, complicating predictions that AI would rapidly erase demand for developers. Concerns about the future of the software development career are well-founded, and intensified as companies adopted AI-powered coding tools, especially as those tools keep getting better. As far back as 2023, Microsoft's software development platform GitHub said that on projects where AI was available, it was close to writing half of all code. Some AI experts claim AI-written code across the entire GitHub platform has now passed the halfway mark . GitHub has not confirmed that, but in October it did report that one in three "pull requests" — the process in which coders that collaborate on development propose code changes for projects — now involve an AI agent. A year ago, GitHub said that number was fewer than one in 10. "If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human," it stated . Labor market researchers say that against this backdrop, the profession is evolving rather than disappearing. Data from Indeed Hiring Lab shows that U.S. software-development job postings have risen nearly 15% since February 2025, bucking both the overall job market and the coding data. Some economic experts are pointing to the rebound in software job postings as confirmation for a glass half-full view of AI and the job market. "It wasn't that long ago that we were reading the headline that there will be no more need for software developers," Eric Kutcher, North America chair at McKinsey, said during a recent interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Instead, he said, as companies are producing more code than ever before, software developers who work with AI remain in high demand. "We're seeing much more growth in the places we thought we were gonna see the biggest displacement," Kutcher said. Recent research on AI and the future of jobs from McKinsey Global Institute notes that the earlier decline in the software developer field was not solely an AI story. While in recent years AI has been automating software-development tasks, the rebound comes after a steep drop from a 2022 hiring peak, when technology companies pulled back after a pandemic-era surge in hiring. But even after the recovery, software-development job postings remain about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level, according to Indeed Hiring Lab data . Importantly, the increase is concentrated in senior-level roles and more experienced AI-oriented positions. Indeed Hiring Lab found that senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software-development postings between May 2025 and May 2026. Job titles that mention AI accounted for 37% of the increase. AI tools may be allowing companies to produce code more quickly than developers could on their own. GitHub leaders have said in the past that as much if not more than 80% of code could eventually be written by AI, especially as developers become more comfortable working with AI tools. But that also could mean the demand for workers is concentrated on those who can evaluate AI-generated code or problems and connect new tools to an organization's broader technology systems. Sneha Puri, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said companies are realizing that even if AI can handle some technical coding tasks, they still need developers to oversee that work, refine products and help clients integrate the technology into their day to day operations. One example, she said, is the growing need for workers who can help businesses apply AI tools beyond simply building them. Early gains in AI era may not last, young workers remain at risk Right now, factors like the ones cited by Puri are helping software developers to be among winners in the earliest stage of the AI transformation of the labor market. A recent analysis of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data from economist Steve Rattner found that software developer was among the career categories that showed positive growth from May 2023 to May 2025, though it was merely in line with growth across all occupation and well below the pace of growth in traditionally blue-collar jobs associated with building AI data centers. Anthropic researchers found that even with automation, humans are still needed to oversee that automation and require user input.

events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Now the countries are mired in a tit-for-tat dispute, with both countries escalating tariffs on each other. events.title: India’s crackdown on youth protesters: What next?
events.summary: India’s Cockroach youth movement and student groups have said protests will continue despite detentions. India’s capital is bracing for a second day of protests after thousands of people, including the leaders of the “cockroach” youth movement and opposition politicians, were detained amid a major crackdown on demonstrators. Abhijeet Dipke, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader, called Prime Minister Narendra Modi a “bully” shortly after he was released on Sunday. Thousands of other protesters, some of whom are members of left-wing student groups, were released on Sunday after the Supreme Court called their detention “illegal”. list 1 of 3 India’s Cockroach Party founder, top leaders detained ahead of protest list 2 of 3 ‘How can you stop these kids?’ Indian capital on lockdown before protests list 3 of 3 India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders released from detention after police crackdown “Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” Dipke said in a post on X. The protesters are demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a revision of voter lists that they say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Modi’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Millions of voters, including Muslims, have been deleted from the rolls in a process marred by technical errors and a perceived lack of transparency. The protests erupted across several Indian cities after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper found that two election commissioners objected to many of Kumar’s decisions. India’s Election Commission is a constitutional body with three members, and decisions are taken by majority. What was the scale of the government crackdown? Ahead of Saturday’s protests, the capital, New Delhi, was turned into a fortress with tens of thousands of police and paramilitary forces deployed, trains and metros suspended, and markets and major roads blocked, to prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar – a designated protest site close to India’s parliament. Jantar Mantar was sealed off. Jantar Mantar was the site of the July protest that led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmesh Pradhan. That protest, also led by the CJP, was triggered by a string of exam paper leaks. Security forces also set ⁠up checkpoints on major roads and entry points across the city of 20 million people, checked buses and inspected vehicles searching for protesters. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes. More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the ⁠city, according to local media, and mobile internet services were suspended across several areas of the capital to stop people from online mobilisation efforts by the CJP and other youth groups. Police detained CJP founder Dipke, as well as his associates, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, from an airplane upon arrival in New Delhi from Mumbai. Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.” In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke said: “This is dictatorship”. Delhi police also detained YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist). Some opposition politicians, as well as former chief ministers – Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala – were also detained, television channels showed. Despite the unprecedented crackdown, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”. But police also ended up quashing these protests and detaining journalists trying to cover the demonstrations. Besides New Delhi, some 600 people were also arrested in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, over the protests, according to the ANI news agency. On Sunday, police officials said all detainees had been released. The CJP leaders were released on the condition that there would be ‘no breach of peace’ for a year. Speaking to reporters at a press conference in New Delhi on Sunday afternoon after their release, Saurav Das, the group’s co-convenor, slammed the police for “arriving like mafia dons” and “abducting” them on their plane. After his release, Rathee said he was “KIDNAPPED.” Several journalists from news outlets, including Scroll.in, Newslaundry and others were detained. They have all since been released, but Newslaundry said some of their reporters’ media equipment was seized during the detention. The Committee to Protect Journalists told Al Jazeera on Saturday that it was deeply concerned by reports of journalists being temporarily detained. “Just as police personnel are doing their jobs, journalists are also doing theirs.

events.title: Silicon Valley's horror shows
events.summary: Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire. Four films hitting theaters this fall put some of Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures in the spotlight: Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elizabeth Holmes. Why it matters: Hollywood's portrayal of Silicon Valley and its leaders is getting darker as negative headlines about the tech industry seep into pop culture. Once portrayed as brilliant but flawed innovators, tech leaders are increasingly being cast as creepy villains whose ambitions may do more harm than good. Zoom in: This fall's tech billionaire films span genres, from documentaries to thrillers. 💻 "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his 2010 hit, "The Social Network," opened Friday with Jeremy Strong portraying a more sinister Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leak . Sorkin takes some cinematic liberties with chronology and other details. 🚀 "Musk," the four-hour documentary ( including a 10-minute intermission) about Elon Musk's rise, is playing in select theaters and opens nationwide on Friday. The roller-coaster rollout of the film, directed by Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney, included critical acclaim at the Venice Film Festival and legal threats from Musk's team. 🩸 "You Can See Everything," out Friday, is an experimental documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that follows ex-Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison. The studio, A24, says an "intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss." ( More on the film .) 🤖 "Artificial," a drama directed by Luca Guadagnino, stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and hits theaters Christmas Day. In the film, "[Garfield] depicts Altman as a manipulative, power-hungry psychopath who lies as easily as he breathes and will use anyone, anytime, anywhere to get what he wants," The Verge reports . The studio, NEON, calls it "the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. ... As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle rages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity." These projects represent a sharp turn away from some earlier movies and documentaries about Silicon Valley, like "Jobs" and "Something Ventured," which celebrated the ingenuity of founders and venture capitalists. "With tech, it was an ardent love affair," says Margaret O'Mara, a University of Washington historian who studies Silicon Valley. "And when you fall out of love, you fall out of love fast." "Our popular understanding of Silicon Valley and the products it makes has changed drastically." Zoom out: Hollywood is reflecting the public's growing disillusionment with the tech industry. Polls show Americans of all ages are quickly souring on AI and think it's moving too fast. Two in three Americans say social media has been bad for democracy, per Pew Research Center polling . "Popular movies hold up a mirror to current social anxieties," says writer and editor-in-chief of Film Quarterly J.M. Tyree. Right now, "people are thinking about power consolidating in the hands of the few at the expense of the many." The intrigue: Tech founders are compelling on-screen villains, Tyree says. They bring together two archetypes: the ruthless businessman who's corrupted by greed, as seen in movies like "Citizen Kane" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," and the mad scientist who's morally ambiguous and employs science and technology recklessly, like in "Metropolis" or "Frankenstein." Plus, their eccentricities make for good entertainment. The bottom line: O'Mara, the Silicon Valley historian, notes: "One thing I have learned from studying the history of rich people is that extreme wealth makes you weird."

events.title: My mom was raising me and caring for her mom with Alzheimer's. Our neighbors became our village.
events.summary: Courtesy of the author My mom moved us from Brooklyn to Michigan after my grandma developed Alzheimer's. I helped care for my grandma while my mom navigated caregiving as a single parent. Our cohousing community became an extended family that supported all of us. I spent the first years of my life on the brownstone-lined streets of Brooklyn, waking up to the sounds of birds chirping mixed with car horns reverberating throughout the city. Little did I know that my childhood would take an unexpected turn. In the middle of first grade, my mom pulled me out of school , packed our suitcases, and moved us across the country to Michigan as my grandma, Lillian, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's and needed extra support. My immediate family is small, just my mom and me, and Michigan felt completely foreign at the time. We moved into a co-housing community My mom always emphasized the importance of building family through community. With that in mind, she moved us to Great Oak Cohousing, a community designed around the concept of independent living with shared amenities: a common house, an expansive garden, and a variety of gathering spaces, all collaboratively managed by residents. I fell in love with Great Oak almost immediately. It unlocked a lifestyle that had been missing in New York : raw nature all around us, the ability to run around independently, and an unmatched sense of community. The author moved from New York to Michigan to help care for her grandmother. Courtesy of the author We welcomed my grandma into our new home with open arms, picking her up from my aunt Heidi's house, where she lived during the week, and bringing her to ours for long weekends. My grandma had visited us in New York when I was a baby, but beyond that, we hadn't spent much time together. Almost immediately after the move, we became rascals together, finding many ways to play and get into trouble. We had a community My mom often tells the story of a time we were at our local grocery store . I was tasked with pushing my grandma in her wheelchair. Soon after we arrived, we disappeared from my mom's view. When she spotted us, I was whisking my grandma up and down the aisles while she stuck her arm out, knocking boxes of cookies off the shelves as we went, the two of us bursting into laughter. We were two peas in a pod. At cohousing, we could sit outside and toss tennis balls around while neighbors strolled by and engaged us in friendly small talk. We could enjoy our dinner at picnic tables on a warm day. Everyone knew my grandma, welcomed her, and met her with patience and kindness. When she had a medical emergency, I called 911 while my mother got the attention of neighbors. Within minutes, three people rushed into our condo to help, while another stood in the street waiting to direct the ambulance. In one of the scariest moments of my childhood, we weren't alone. A story I often think back to is from a time when we were at a community event, watching a girl play the piano. Midway through the song, my grandma began singing along in a shrill voice. Instead of shushing her, the whole community joined in. What could have been an uncomfortable moment turned into one of joy. It truly captured what Great Oak meant to us. My grandma was never treated as a burden or an outsider. She was simply part of the community. It was painful to see my grandmother with Alzheimer's Still, witnessing her Alzheimer's brought challenges that, as a young child, I didn't immediately understand. I helped her get dressed, enduring a fight or two along the way, and even discovered that I had pretty good reflexes when it came to dodging the occasional flying plate of food. Despite those challenging moments, I understood that she couldn't help it. It was painful to watch her lose her sense of self, and I can only imagine how much harder it was for my mother, who had to watch her own mother struggle in this way. I often look back at that time through a different lens now that I'm older, specifically from my mother's perspective. Caring for a parent with Alzheimer's while raising a young child as a single mother was no easy task. I have immense admiration for her and for the strength she displayed through it all. Experiences like these teach you lessons that are difficult to learn anywhere else: patience, unconditional love, sacrifice, and, perhaps most importantly, the power of family. Caring for my grandma not only brought the two of us closer together, I also grew closer to my aunt, someone I look up to tremendously. I witnessed the sacrifices she made, opening a bedroom in her Detroit-area home so my grandma could stay during the week. What could have been a lonely experience became one that was defined by community. Great Oak became an extended family of our small one, showing me that family isn't only who you're born to, but who welcomes you in, stands beside you, and shows up when you need them most. events.title: I’m a psychologist who studies couples: The No. 1 way to end a fight before it escalates—it works ‘almost immediately’
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships Harvard-trained psychologist: 5 'red flag' phrases that signal your relationship is over Psychology and Relationships I'm a psychologist who studies couples—to avoid feeling 'quietly resentful of each other,' make 1 simple change Psychology and Relationships Emotionally intelligent couples ask 1 question every morning: Psychologist Raising Successful Kids Parents who are really good at handling tantrums do 5 things—their kids become more emotionally intelligent, says psychologist How to Talk to People Stop saying 'let me know if you need anything,' says psychologist—how to talk to a friend who's struggling Couples tend to slide off-course when they argue. You might start out talking about something real and specific. Maybe a plan that was altered without a check-in or an impulse purchase that should have been discussed. Then suddenly you've stopped talking about that thing and started talking about each other: "You're being impossible right now." One minute you're trying to solve a problem together, and the next you're each trying to prove you're the more reasonable person in the room. And once an argument becomes about that, it can't really be resolved. Because now, the battlefield and ammunition are endless. As a psychologist who studies couples, I know that, thankfully, there's a practice that can act as a guardrail for disagreements. I call it a partial yield, and it prevents this all-too-familiar detour. A partial yield is a type of phrase you use when you concede the specific piece of the argument you're genuinely responsible for, the moment it comes up, without conceding the rest of your position. It usually sounds very ordinary: "That's fair, I did forget to tell you." "I shouldn't have made that decision without talking to you first." So you're not agreeing that you were wrong about everything. But you are admitting the fault that's actually yours, before your partner has to pry it out of you. In my experience, nothing de-escalates a conflict faster. Why a 'partial yield' works so quickly When your partner confronts you, some part of them is preemptively braced for the effort of convincing you. It's why voices get louder and why examples start piling up. They're not trying to hurt you. They're trying to get you to believe them, and they've assumed it's going to be hard. A partial yield releases the pent-up steam that can otherwise fuel an escalation. The effect is palpable almost immediately, and it rarely feels like a defeat for either person. Your partner gets the acknowledgment they were pushing for, and you get to be honest about your part without signing away the rest. It's also easier on you than a full apology, which matters more than you might think. Most of us don't withhold small admissions because we believe we did nothing wrong. We withhold them because admitting to one thing feels like admitting to all the rest, too, and we'd rather concede nothing than concede everything. What happens when you skip this step I'd pay attention to what happens when you don't use a partial yield phrase. If you never take accountability in the moment, the problem doesn't just go away. Your partner notices and files it away. They might bring it up again three weeks from now in the middle of an unrelated argument. It may look like score-keeping, but more often it's an old grievance that never got heard and owned, finally finding an opening. Couples who concede small things routinely don't build up much of that "back-pocket" inventory, so there's nothing to reach for at a moment's notice. Their arguments tend to stay roughly within the context of whatever caused them. How to use the 'partial yield' effectively A few steps differentiate a real partial yield from a fake one: Be specific about what you're claiming. "You're right, I shouldn't have said it like that in front of your mom," works. A vague "Okay, fine, I was wrong!" reads as surrender under protest, and your partner will hear it that way. Don't attach a "but." "You're right, that part's on me, but you also…" cancels the whole thing. If you have a counterpoint, it will survive the next 90 seconds. Let the concession stand alone first. Do it early. The yield loses most of its power once someone has already started listing their old grievances. The ideal moment is the first time you notice you're technically in the wrong about something small, which is usually much earlier than we like to admit. Say it even when you're mostly right. Especially then. Being mostly right is the most common reason people refuse to concede anything at all. In my experience, genuine partial yields are the difference between couples who argue about — and solve — problems and couples who get stuck arguing about each other. Mark Travers , Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder.

events.title: My favorite hidden gem in California has incredible food and wine — and it's more affordable than Napa Valley
events.summary: Paso Robles is my favorite hidden gem in California. Courtesy of JUSTIN Winery My favorite hidden gem in California is Paso Robles, a central coast town filled with wineries. Paso Robles has much cheaper tastings than Napa. The average cost is $27, while it's $79 in Napa. There's also a range of great restaurants, from Michelin-starred dinners to handmade pastas. Where should you go in California for delicious food, sprawling vineyards, and the satisfying sound of a freshly uncorked wine bottle? Let me guess, you're thinking of Napa . But what if I told you there's a hidden gem on the central coast where you can get all of the above with fewer crowds, lower prices, and cooler tasting experiences? Welcome to Paso Robles . A wine for everyone You'll find the stunning Justin vineyards and winery in Paso Robles. Courtesy of JUSTIN Winery Growing up in the Bay Area , Napa Valley quickly became a special place for my family. With no relatives living in the US, my Greek parents took us there every Christmas to make the holidays feel special. I've visited Napa over 20 times, but over the past few years, Paso Robles has stolen my heart. Paso Robles is almost exactly in the middle of Los Angeles and San Francisco, about 200 miles each way. Parallel to the mountains and the sea, the region has a unique terroir due to big temperature swings. The topography's distinctive microclimates are perfect for growing a variety of grapes, helping Paso distinguish itself in a crowded California wine market . "The diversity of this area really separates itself from the monoculture that Napa has become," Andrew Jones, the owner of Field Recordings Winery, told me. Adding to that diversity is the low barrier to entry in the Paso Robles wine industry. Most of the wineries are small and family-owned, and the winemakers are often on-site to guide you. This refreshingly laid-back approach makes tastings feel intimate and approachable, and they're at a far more accessible price point than Napa, where the high cost of winemaking has trickled down to tourists. Silicon Valley Bank's 2026 direct-to-consumer wine report found that the average tasting fee in Napa is $79, while it's $27 in Paso Robles. "Napa has a taller order; they have to live up to a brand that's worldwide," said Neeta Mittal, one of the first Indian women to open a winery in the US. "Where we thrive in Paso is we're able to etch our own identity, and that's a great nimbleness that we're allowed." Tasting experiences with a twist My wine-and-spice pairing at LXV Wine. Anneta Konstantinides/Insider Mittal and her husband, Kunal, own LXV Wine , which offers the only wine-and-spice pairing in the US. I visited LXV on my first trip to Paso Robles and was delighted that my tasting included cheeses covered in various spices. I learned how ginger and black truffle salt can bring out the flavors of Cabernet and why Szechuan peppers and Nebbiolo pair so well. I also love the tastings at Field Recordings , which prides itself on making wines that "are all about the flavor — with none of the pretension," as its website reads. Jones specializes in small-batch, single-vineyard wines. They're fun and funky, decorated with colorful labels and names like "Kitties" or "Super Gnario." Tin City is one of my favorite parts of Paso Robles. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Field Recordings is in Tin City , my favorite part of Paso Robles. The converted industrial hub features over 20 wineries, all within walking distance of each other, where tastings typically cost between $20 and $30. It's perfect for a wine crawl, but there's also a brewery and the very fun Tin City Distillery if you're craving cocktails instead. Where you can wine and dine Another reason I keep going back to Paso Robles is the fantastic restaurant scene. I never skip a dinner at The Alchemists' Garden , which has a fun cocktail list and some of the best fries. My parents still rave about the meal we had at Il Cortile Ristorante . Its pappardelle is handmade and paired with a rich, luscious Bolognese , and the branzino is light, bright, and cooked to perfection. But the star is the risotto covered in white truffles, a holiday splurge I've never forgotten. My first meal at The Alchemist's Garden, featuring the incredible french fries. Anneta Konstantinides/Insider The Restaurant at Justin , which earned its first Michelin star in 2022, bested any fine-dining experience I've had in Napa. I still have pictures saved from that dinner, where my fiancé and I feasted on maple-leaf duck breast, prime filet, and various veggies picked from their 26-acre farmstead. And no visit to Paso is complete without a stop at  Brown Butter Cookie Company , which has mastered the salty-sweet combo in a little treat. The hand-rolled cookies are made locally and available in a variety of flavors. On my last visit, I grabbed a dozen bags for my family, friends, and myself, of course. A destination for any season The "Field of Light" is a popular tourist spot in Paso Robles. Jeff Amlotte/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Blessed with California sunshine, Paso Robles is a great vacation year-round. I've gone in the fall, summer, and winter — where it's festively decorated for the holidays — and have always been charmed by the small-town vibes and friendly locals. (Don't miss karaoke nights at the Pine Street Saloon.) The winemaking world is slowly starting to learn about Paso Robles, but the town itself remains a hidden gem . For now, at least, this is California's best-kept secret. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: We live on a 'family compound' with my parents and siblings. It's made raising our daughter much easier.
events.summary: We have our own house, but my husband and I live on the same property as my parents and siblings. Taylor Bunting My husband and I live in a separate house on the same property where my immediate family lives. In total, nine family members and three dogs live in the two houses on our "family compound." We love spending time with my close-knit family , and it's been great for our daughter, too. There's a popular saying that it takes a village to raise a child. I'd always understood the saying as a metaphor. But when my husband and I decided to build a house on the same property where my parents, younger siblings, and my brother's fiancé live, that adage became a lot more literal. Now, we're raising our daughter on our "family compound," with our village right next door. A compound wasn't the initial plan, but living here has been an incredible experience My parents built their house first. Taylor Bunting Although my family had jokingly talked about building houses next door to each other since I was a child, we never thought we could make that a reality. However, the arrangement started to materialize in 2024. At the time, my husband and I were living about 15 minutes from my childhood home, which was bursting at the seams with my three siblings, my brother's fiancé, both my parents, and their two adorable golden retrievers. My parents had been searching for a larger home for years, but eventually decided to purchase a piece of land in our Massachusetts hometown. Here, they built a house big enough for all six of them to live together comfortably, and realized there was enough room left on the property for my husband and me to build our own house if we wanted to. They began construction on their home that same year, and not long after, my husband and I decided to sell our existing home and break ground on a new place on the property. In total, nine family members and three dogs live in the two houses, which are just a short walk away from each other. I love that our house is just a quick walk away from my parents' home. Taylor Bunting We've now been living here for six months and couldn't ask for a better living arrangement . I love being able to see my siblings off for their first day of school or prom night, having game nights with my family, and enjoying slow, cozy days watching football together. Not only are my husband and I fortunate enough to have our built-in best friends only a short walk away, but we also get to watch our daughter grow up with direct access to her grandparents, aunts, and uncles. It's nice that we never have to worry about finding a sitter we trust, as my family members love to keep an eye on her for any reason, from a date night to me squeezing in a workout while my husband is out. Even having one of my younger siblings pop over and play with our daughter while we get chores done around the house makes a huge difference. My siblings love spending time with their niece. Taylor Bunting Childcare is expensive , especially in Massachusetts, and we are forever grateful that we don't have to take on that financial burden. And although my family spends a lot of time together, and have some shared spaces (like a pool and a detached garage), we never feel like we're on top of each other. We have a shared pool and detached garage. Taylor Bunting In fact, there are plenty of days I don't even see my family members because of busy school and work schedules. Plus, we're all very respectful of boundaries. If we borrow each other's clothes, we wash and return them. If we want to take a snack from someone else's pantry, we ask first. The living arrangement feels like a continuation of our close-knit relationship My family loves spending time together. Taylor Bunting I'm frequently asked why my siblings and I would want to live in such close proximity to each other and to my parents. To me, though, it just felt like a continuation of something that my parents had already created. They were incredibly intentional about keeping our family close while we were growing up, so as adults, we naturally want to spend time together. Plus, my parents never weighed the success of their parenting on whether we got into fancy colleges, established huge careers, or moved away to be "independent." They believe their parenting will have been successful if their kids want to spend their time with them and each other. Their goal was to raise us to want to be each other's best friends. The next question I'm typically asked is how my husband feels about the arrangement. Honestly, he was just as excited as I was to build a house next to my parents. Now, he loves playing basketball outside with my brother, and luckily, his side of the family lives just 10 minutes away — so, we spend lots of time with them, too. Unfortunately, our current property isn't large enough to accommodate additional houses, so as our family continues to change and expand, we've already begun looking for a bigger piece of land down south that can accommodate each sibling, should they someday want houses of their own. Our current setup is perfect for this stage in our lives, but we want to make sure there is always room for all of us if we want to continue living together on the same property. events.title: Sweet protein brazzein shows promise in reducing blood sugar spikes: Study
events.summary: Study shows that the sweet protein Brazzein could help reduce blood sugar spikes caused by eating ice cream. A new study has shown how the sweet protein brazzein could help reduce blood sugar spikes, the Science Alert news outlet reported. Brazzein is a natural protein originally found in the West African oubli plant, but now largely produced through a fermentation process. It is known for its intense sweetness and has long been eyed as a potential sugar alternative. list 1 of 3 Global health’s defining test list 2 of 3 ‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season list 3 of 3 Can GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic cause vision loss? What we know about the risk Researchers at Russia’s Federal Research Centre of Nutrition, Biotechnology and Food Safety conducted a test on 101 adults living with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The condition, where fat builds up in the liver, is often associated with diabetes and obesity. The study, published in the Clinical Nutrition ESPEN journal, was a randomised trial that focused on ice cream. Participants ate a 100 gram vanilla ice cream serving on three separate days: one with sugar, one with brazzein, and one day with brazzein and a fibre called inulin. Post-meal blood sugar spikes were lower when participants consumed the brazzein or brazzein and inulin versions, compared with the sugar-sweetened version, the study showed. The reductions in sugar spikes were most notable in participants with type 2 diabetes, according to the study. “Longer-term studies are needed to determine whether repeated substitution of sucrose-containing desserts with brazzein-sweetened alternatives translates into sustained metabolic, hepatic, microbiome, or behavioural benefits,” the researchers wrote. The negative health effects of sugar have been widely researched and debated over the years. The World Health Organization advised in 2023 against the use of non-sugar sweeteners for weight control, and released guidelines warning of “potential undesirable effects” from their long-term use, such as an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

events.title: I thought we'd be at an extended-stay hotel for 2 weeks. We stayed for 3 months while house-hunting.
events.summary: The author and her family stayed in an extended-stay hotel for nearly three months while looking for a rental. Courtesy of Tonya Russell We wanted to find a rental to live in while building a new house. It took nearly three months, and we stayed in an extended-stay hotel during our search. I felt cramped at times, but I missed some things about it when we moved. After eight years in the same home, my family needed a change. We planned to rent while we built a new house , imagining a brief transition between the two. Instead, the rental market had other plans. Apparently, it was a very popular time to be looking for a new place to live. With multiple families vying for each house, landlords could be choosy. Being self-employed with dogs put us near the bottom of the list. In the meantime, we were living in an extended-stay hotel . Still, I wasn't discouraged because…well, how long could it take to find a match? What I thought would be a two-week hotel stay stretched into nearly three months. During that time, my husband, our 1-year-old daughter, Talia, two dogs, and our cat learned what it meant to live with little space . More surprisingly, hotel living changed how I parented — and eventually, my views on home. We took what we needed, and the rest went in storage We moved everything we owned into two storage units, and I packed for a short stay. We took what fit in our SUV: a large suitcase, a bag for my daughter, stuffed with pajamas and outfits, a few toys and books, a box of diapers, a litter box, the travel stroller we kept in our car, and a travel wagon that would become a lifeline. By the second week, I was making weekly trips to storage to rotate my daughter's toys. Living in a hotel can make toddlers bored fast. I also started feeling boxed in. I missed my home, hated walking the dogs at all hours, and dreaded the slow elevators that occasionally got stuck. Some days, I'd climb four flights of stairs or take my high-energy dog for runs. Talia and I frequented the supermarket just to keep from going crazy. The author's daughter enjoyed playing in the hotel. Courtesy of Tonya Russell I rethought how I parent I also had to rethink some parenting rules . At home, I was against both junk food and screen time. But the hotel breakfast buffet had limited vegetarian options. When Talia pointed at the plain donuts, I let her have one. She usually took one bite. She also asked for my husband's vegan sausages, so she had one with him most mornings. Screen time became another compromise. I still needed to work, and concentrating while sharing a hotel room with a toddler was nearly impossible. Fifteen minutes of Miss Rachel or Gracie's Corner gave me enough time to put on my noise-canceling headphones and dump a thought onto the page before I forgot it. When a storm ruined our beach plans, a friend suggested we use the hotel's conference room for a change of pace. It became part of our routine, with Talia playing peekaboo around the tables with the sales manager. I enjoyed getting to know our 'neighbors' Not everyone in an extended-stay hotel is a long-term guest. There were vacationers, business travelers , military members waiting for traditional housing, truck drivers, and people whose employers maintained corporate accounts. Then there were families who simply had nowhere to go. I met veterans and families navigating the housing system. Agencies sometimes place families in hotels until they find housing. Extended-stay hotels can accommodate entire families — including the dogs and cats that can make rental searching even harder. I also bonded with the staff. One woman spoke only Spanish, yet somehow, I started picking up on what she was saying, which allowed me to help translate for other guests. I chatted with second-shift front-desk workers, who shared their aspirations with me and looked the other way when I snuck into the kitchen for cornflakes. Talia earned the nickname "spicy water baby" because she and I shared seltzer from the bar. We've found a rental, and I was surprised to miss the hotel I spent weeks worrying about what she was missing by not being home and what bad habits would stick. Now that we've moved, she still asks for "Pad," but only needs a few minutes before wandering off to color or read. And every day feels like 15 minutes of Christmas as she rediscovers another toy from storage. When we finally left the hotel, I expected relief. Instead, I felt a strange tug of homesickness. In those nearly three months, my daughter had gone from saying a random word or two to speaking full-on toddler gibberish. She stopped face-planting in the hallways and learned to run. Talia was living her life, enjoying playing in the conference room, splashing in the pool, and making friends with the people who knew her name. Maybe that was what I hadn't understood when we checked in with one carload of belongings and a two-week plan: Home is wherever your family is. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Kenya’s Eliud Kipchoge wins his first marathon in three years in Melbourne
events.summary: Kipchoge is attempting ⁠⁠to run a marathon on all seven ​continents over two years as part of his ‘World Tour’ campaign. Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge has won his first marathon in three years, with the Kenyan great cruising to victory in Melbourne, Australia. The most decorated marathoner in history crossed the finish line in 2 hours, 9 minutes and 10 seconds, two seconds under the race record, on Sunday. list 1 of 3 Flares and fury: How Liverpool fans plan to ‘welcome’ Man City at Anfield list 2 of 3 Vinicius apologises for hair-pull red card but could miss El Clasico list 3 of 3 Ronaldo suspended by Portugal FA after leaving camp and criticising coach It was his first victory over the distance since Berlin in 2023 and part of his “World Tour” to raise funds for causes he believes in. The 41-year-old former world record-holder announced in 2025 that he planned to complete marathons on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years. Melbourne was the third stop after South Africa and Brazil. He broke away inside the last 10km on a course that partly used the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG). “On the course, it was really wonderful; I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name,” Kipchoge said, looking fresh at the finish. Kipchoge would have gone faster, but he slowed down at the MCG, waving to fans. “It was actually different – running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground,” he added. “I believe that my body is still peaking – still able to compete with the next generation. “The oldest athlete ⁠⁠is still competing, but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs. I [increased] the pace after 30km to ⁠⁠see whether I can run well and beat the [race record]. My ⁠⁠plan went well.” Australian Thomas ⁠⁠Do Canto finished second behind Kipchoge at 2:10:35, while compatriot Reece Edwards was third at 2:14:33. New Zealand’s Camille French ‌‌won the women’s race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver at 2:28:49 and Nichola Sheridan ‌‌of ‌‌Ireland at 2:29:13.

events.title: I'm having my third child at 39. It's a different experience from when I was pregnant with my other 2 boys.
events.summary: The author is pregnant for the third time at 39. Courtesy of Bethaney Phillips I'm 39 and pregnant with my third boy. I had my other two at 29 and 31. It's different this time around. I'm experiencing more nausea and fatigue, but my boys help me out. I'm having my third child at 39. It's a different experience from when I was pregnant with my other 2 boys. My 40th birthday is in April, and my third son is due just two months before my milestone age . It's a fact that came as a bigger surprise to me than anyone else. A few days after a missed period and continual cramping, I asked my husband to go buy a test. It lit up with double lines so quickly that, in my shock, I wondered if there were multiple babies. Later, I learned I was hosting just one new babe. Things are different this time The pregnancy was unexpected , but not unwelcome. After several miscarriages, likely due to my bicornuate (or heart-shaped) uterus, I thought our days of having babies were over. However, this one found a viable spot to hold onto, and he's now over half-grown, having just completed his anatomy scan with nonstop movement. Unlike my earlier pregnancies , this one is taking a greater toll. At five months pregnant, I'm more tired and nauseous, and my belly has gotten bigger faster. That meant earlier acid reflux, more bathroom breaks, more months of waddling, and all the difficulties that come with pregnancy: it's a process to stand up, hard to bend over, and I'm just plain slow. Every day, the words, "And that's Uncle Joe, he's a moving kinda slow" from Petticoat Junction play in my head. Not unlike Uncle Joe, I'm moving very slowly at all times. And that's with extra sleep — after getting my sons (7 and 9) to sleep each night, I'm in bed right behind them, usually crashed out by 8:30 or 9. This body is doing a lot of growing, and it's exhausted. Much to my husband's chagrin, there was no "fun period" of this pregnancy. I went straight from constant nausea to feeling uncomfortable. This is likely due to it being a third advanced pregnancy. Despite only gaining 15 pounds thus far, I'm short with a short torso, so when the baby grows, I grow along with him. One thing that has made life easier this go-around is that my children are older now. Now, I have two helpers who can pick things up, fetch drinks, or take out the trash. At home, they do most of my bending and gathering and are happy to help; it's a far cry from the early days of having two under 2. I have a clean bill of health, though we'll be doing more frequent monitoring My doctor noted that 35-39 is a "gray area" for the advanced maternal age protocol. Though chromosomal and gene variant blood tests are recommended after 35, my insurance disagreed, opting not to cover the recommended prenatal blood tests due to my heritage. Thankfully, we weren't on the hook for the entire $12,154 bill due to the company's income requirement guidelines — families up to 400% of the federal poverty level are eligible for heavy discounts — but my insurance rant is beside the point. The tests were done, and all came back with good news. Considering the annual increase in risk to pregnancies in one's 30s, it came as a huge relief. There will be a point where my doctor visits increase — to date, I've been seen once a month, but after 32 weeks, that jumps to once a week for fetal monitoring and blood pressure checks. Medically, this is the only change from my previous pregnancies I've seen so far, thanks to an otherwise clean bill of health. Hopefully that continues to be the case, but there's no denying this pregnancy is taking a toll on my body. Pregnancy is a young person's game, but thankfully, I'm over halfway through. In the meantime, I'll continue to sleep and rest, helping us both through a healthy pregnancy. Read the original article on Business Insider
