events.title: Yemen fighting expands as Houthis attack Saudi airport: What to know
events.summary: Saudi coalition blames Houthi group for the missile strike that struck King Khalid international airport in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has said it will “firmly” retaliate against an attack on Riyadh’s international airport, in which at least 12 people were killed, with United States President Donald Trump calling the attack “terrible”. The Saudi-led military coalition on Sunday blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group for Saturday’s attack on King Khalid international airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime”. The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the latest strike. list 1 of 3 Saudi Arabia says 12 killed, 300 wounded in Houthi attack on Riyadh airport list 2 of 3 Saudi-led coalition says it’s carrying out operation in Yemen list 3 of 3 Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’? However, on Sunday, the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God), renewed ⁠⁠⁠⁠their warning to ⁠⁠⁠⁠airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using ‌‌‌‌Saudi airports, saying the warning should be taken seriously ⁠⁠⁠⁠and that the ⁠⁠⁠⁠kingdom “bore responsibility for failed interceptions”. The attack comes amid escalating fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces following the collapse of a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely in place since 2022. The fighting has raised fears of a wider regional confrontation, with Trump suggesting the US could join Saudi military operations against the Houthis. Dania Thafer, executive director at the Gulf International Forum, said Saudi Arabia will likely hit back at the Houthis “pretty hard”. “I still think that the Saudis probably want de-escalation. They don’t want long-term escalation, but the Houthis are making it very difficult by not only being a threat to Saudi national security but also a threat to international maritime security,” Thafer said. “So this battle is much bigger than just a tit-for-tat.” According to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA), a missile struck King Khalid airport in Riyadh on Saturday. It killed 12 people and wounded 309 others, some of them critically. The dead included four Saudi nationals, two Bangladeshis and one citizen each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. It was the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade. “The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia … which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X. The Houthis, who have yet to take responsibility for the attack, said on Sunday they “renew their warning to all aviation companies, experts, employees, workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, because they are exposed to targeting and are a theatre of operations by our forces”. “They urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions,” military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X. Airport operations were suspended, with flights cancelled or diverted. Schools across Riyadh were ordered to switch to remote learning for a week following the attack. The attacks have disrupted international flights, with several airlines suspending services to Saudi destinations. Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd international airport in Dammam in the country’s east. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, said the Iran-backed group was retaliating by attacking what it called Saudi Arabia’s “most precious assets”, which are Aramco oil facilities and the airport in Riyadh. “Although Saudi Arabia has said it will retaliate, let’s not forget that it’s carried out many air strikes across Yemen, and the Yemeni group is still able to launch ballistic missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia,” he added. What other areas have the Houthis targeted? The Iran-aligned Houthis have launched a series of missile and drone attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, including areas near the border with Yemen. On Monday, attacks on King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in the southwestern city of Jizan and Najran international airport wounded three people and caused material damage, according to the GACA. On Tuesday, attacks on Abha airport and Riyadh airport killed three people and wounded 36 others, according to Saudi authorities. The Houthis also claimed to have targeted an Aramco oil refinery in Rabigh, on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, with missiles and drones, saying the attack caused a fire. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claim. The Houthis imposed a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia in July following the outbreak of the latest round of fighting.

events.title: Modi is in trouble
events.summary: The CJP protests sweeping through the country have exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy. It is said that if you pluck a chicken one feather at a time, nobody notices. That is how some people deceive themselves into believing that small wrongs will never catch up with them. The trouble with this method is that, one fine day, the truth stands bare, impossible to ignore. This October, Indian democracy resembles a plucked chicken, stripped of its plumage, as protesters who ironically call themselves “cockroaches” swarm our streets. list 1 of 4 India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders released from detention after police crackdown list 2 of 4 Photos: Thousands detained in police crackdown on India’s youth protest list 3 of 4 Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi detained over election chief protest list 4 of 4 ‘Cockroach stir stripped Modi’s carefully confected image’: Arundhati Roy A lot of feather-plucking went on for 12 years before Prime Minister Narendra Modi found himself cornered, retreating behind barricades, facing the wrath of students for whom the slow erosion of democracy has left little to lose and even less to fear. Confronted with a major protest on October 10 demanding the reversal of a purge of the voter rolls, he went on a self-incrimination spree. His government imposed measures reminiscent of the emergency era: no trains to New Delhi, paramilitary forces deployed at protest sites, the internet disrupted. Ahead of the demonstration, leading figures linked to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest movement – Ratna Singh, Abhijeet Dipke, Dhruv Rathee – were detained. Many other known activists, including Mahatma Gandhi’s great-grandson Tushar Gandhi, were also detained. Regardless, demonstrators poured into the streets of New Delhi, trying to reach designated protest sites, in a scene that repeated in city after city across India. Through the day, the police played an endless game of whack-a-mole with the protesters, who kept resurfacing across the capital city, reassembling in one corner after another, driven from the designated protest sites but unwilling to disappear. By the evening, at least 2,500 protesters and 15 journalists were detained across the city and taken to detention centres set up in various locations. Many have since been released. These acts further erode the tenuous position Modi is in, prompting more rebuke from critics who now question his fitness to occupy the office of the prime minister. On Friday, the opposition parties, led by Rahul Gandhi, met President Draupadi Murmu and submitted to her that the government had subverted India’s democratic framework. Under Modi’s watch, problems have accumulated like barnacles on the side of the ship. Every time he has been challenged, he has gone farther away from the democratic principles on which this nation was founded. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls – the last feather he plucked – was an exercise in bureaucratic fascism. There is simply no other way to frame an event that strips 130 million Indians of their right to vote. The fact that this process helped sway elections is no longer up for debate. That the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw SIR, is not resigning – out of shame – is astonishing. Even more so now that a corruption case from 2006 against him has resurfaced. The chaotic, angry, defiant tableaux in the streets of New Delhi and beyond represent a reckoning that has been long in the making. The young, diverse protesters are a stark contrast to Modi and his cabinet – old, humourless men, who have bet on a strategy of demonisation and exclusion to succeed. His cabinet is filled with men full of self-importance, who had, mistakenly, wagered that crimes of elected officials should be tolerated and that a country can be governed indefinitely by creating fissures and manufacturing enemies. We have now seen what happens when breakers of the law become makers of law. Criminal behaviour has been the organising principle of the party, and together, the values of these people have defined the years that Modi has ruled India. In the process, he has presided over the shredding of the Constitution of India. Now that all this has come back to haunt him – in the form of “cockroaches” he is unable to exterminate – Modi has turned New Delhi into a fortress and unleashed all the power he has at his disposal on unarmed protesters. This is consistent with his policy of pretending to aspire to peace but unerringly generating conflict throughout his tenure: with neighbouring nations as well as among neighbours within cities. October 10 is just an opening salvo. Over the next few weeks, Modi’s troubles will likely deepen. The CJP has announced protests will continue. Opposition parties have said they will protest on Monday. The “cockroaches” seem to have resolved any remaining questions regarding Modi’s utter ineptitude as prime minister.

events.title: The invisible hand needs a conscience
events.summary: On Sept. 30, Citadel founder Ken Griffin pledged more than $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, the largest individual gift in the history of higher education. Much of it will build a new CMU campus in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, which is expected to enroll its first students in 2028, pending regulatory approval. Griffin described the challenge facing universities as how to “reignite both the belief and the realization of the possibility of the American dream.” Griffin’s gift is an extraordinary act of philanthropy. It also raises a question philanthropy alone can’t answer. Must stewardship wait until a fortune is given away, or should conscience be part of how the fortune is made? Griffin’s gift undoubtedly deserves admiration. The larger question is whether stewardship should begin only after wealth has been created, or whether it should also help guide the way wealth is created in the first place. I believe it should. I also believe we rarely ask that question because we have come to expect too much of the invisible hand. We are asking an economic mechanism to perform a moral function it was never designed to perform: to supply a conscience. I first met the invisible hand in an undergraduate class taught by Dr. Michael Smith. The idea is that individuals pursuing their own interests in a free market can, without intending it, advance the interests of society as a whole. It has stayed with me for a lifetime. But Adam Smith was a moral philosopher before he was an economist. Seventeen years before  The Wealth of Nations , he published  The Theory of Moral Sentiments , a book about sympathy, virtue and our obligations to one another. Its central figure is the “impartial spectator,” the imagined observer within each of us who judges our conduct as a fair-minded stranger would. That is as good a definition of conscience as I know. Smith understood that markets don’t operate in a moral vacuum. They depend on trust, on restraint, and on people who measure themselves by more than what the market will let them take. The invisible hand helps explain how self-interest can create prosperity. It cannot tell us when enough is enough, or what we owe the people who helped make our success possible. I believe strongly in capitalism. It rewards ingenuity, hard work, risk and ambition, and it has created extraordinary prosperity. But implicit in our defense of economic self-interest has always been a bargain: if individuals are free to prosper, society prospers too. There are reasons to wonder whether that bargain is under strain. Federal Reserve data from the second quarter of 2026 show that the wealthiest 10% of U.S. households hold roughly 69% of household wealth, while the bottom half hold just over 2%. And in a 2025 Gallup survey, only 15% of Americans said they had a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in big business. No one builds a fortune alone. Every great business rests on a foundation it did not create: schools that educated its employees and customers, courts that enforced its contracts, and roads and networks that carried its goods and ideas. We inherit that foundation; we don’t create it from scratch. Many successful people have earned what they have. The harder question is whether benefiting so greatly from that foundation creates some responsibility to leave it stronger for whoever comes next. Philanthropy usually arrives near the end of the story, once the fortune has been made. Conscience belongs earlier. It shows up in how a business owner treats employees, how widely opportunity is shared, what an investor chooses to back, how a company treats the environment it draws from, and what values a family passes along with its money. Some companies have tried to build that idea into the way they do business. Costco reported an average U.S. hourly wage of about $32 for hourly employees in 2025—about $46 when benefits are included—even as the company earned $8.1 billion in net income. Publix took a different route: founder George Jenkins believed employees should have an ownership stake in the company they helped build, and today Publix remains the largest employee-owned company in the United States. Neither company is a charity. Both are successful businesses. The point is that sharing prosperity need not be the enemy of creating it. For those fortunate enough to accumulate far more than they will ever need, some questions have no answer on a financial statement. What did I build? Whom did I help prosper? What did I return to the society that made my success possible? What did I leave stronger than I found it? Those questions take wealth seriously. They recognize how much power it gives a person to improve the lives of others. Government cannot supply that conscience, and neither can the market. It has to come from within, which is exactly where Smith placed his impartial spectator. So…I would ask every executive, founder and investor to add one question to the financial questions they already ask:  If this decision succeeds, who besides us will be better off?  Ask it when setting compensation, allocating capital, choosing investments and deciding how employees will share in the value they help create. Not every decision will benefit everyone equally. But the question itself belongs at the table. Capitalism does not need to apologize for producing winners. But those who benefit most from it might ask more of themselves than capitalism asks of them. The invisible hand can help create extraordinary wealth. It cannot tell us what we owe one another. For that, it needs a conscience. Ours. events.title: Marco Bezzecchi wins in Indonesia as Martin takes MotoGP lead
events.summary: Bezzecchi’s win, the 300th victory for an Italian in MotoGP, also kept his faint championship ​hopes alive. Marco Bezzecchi has stormed to victory in the Indonesian Grand Prix while Jorge Martin finished third to reclaim the overall season lead in the MotoGP world championship. The Italian Bezzecchi, riding an Aprilia, made his move on pole-sitter Raul Fernandez in the final third of a captivating Grand Prix at a sweltering Mandalika International Circuit on Sunday. list 1 of 3 Flares and fury: How Liverpool fans plan to ‘welcome’ Man City at Anfield list 2 of 3 What are the top five clashes between Liverpool and Manchester City? list 3 of 3 Vinicius apologises for hair-pull red card but could miss El Clasico Spain’s Fernandez came home second and compatriot Martin third, also on Aprilia bikes. Ducati’s reigning seven-time world champion Marc Marquez finished sixth. That meant Martin retook the lead in the championship from Marquez by two points, with five more race weekends remaining. Martin leads with 355 points, with Marquez on his tail on 353. Bezzecchi is still alive in the championship title hunt, in third position with 309 points. “It’s amazing, I’m very, very happy,” said Bezzecchi, who last won a race in May. “It was a nice battle with Raul and I think me and all my team deserve a result like this. They have been through tough times with me.” Martin, who will head to Australia in a fortnight with the most slender of leads, said he had done all he could. “I did the maximum,” said Martin, who started alongside title rival Marquez on the second row of the grid. “I did my best. At the start I lost a lot of positions but tried to be calm and was overtaking riders step by step. “We are still in the fight and still in the lead,” he added. Fernandez, having to improvise to brake after fracturing two fingers in Saturday’s sprint, got away cleanly from his first-ever pole. He and Bezzecchi, who started alongside him on the grid, had clashed and crashed out in the sprint. The sprint was won by Marquez to grab the championship lead for the first time from compatriot Martin. After a third of the 27 laps in the Grand Prix, Fernandez kept the fellow Aprilia of Bezzecchi at bay despite his injury. Former world champion Martin was running third, with Marquez looming in fifth without ever really threatening. Fernandez, who had two previous victories, kept his cool under tremendous pressure from Bezzecchi until lap 19, when the Italian made his move to grasp the lead. Bezzecchi streaked away from there to win by 4.26 seconds as Fernandez gamely hung on for second.

events.title: Fujairah shows why resilience is the Gulf’s greatest energy asset
events.summary: For a city sometimes unfairly described as “sleepy”, Fujairah is keeping the global energy industry awake these days. The Indian Ocean port has emerged as a crucial hub for the world economy, sustaining the UAE ’s energy exports despite the Hormuz crisis. Last week, Fujairah’s importance was highlighted when Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, and chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc), attended the UAE Energy Markets Forum in the city. This continued a hectic run of conferences as the global energy industry emerges from a sticky summer and tries to find a way through conflict and disruption. The biennial WPC Energy Congress takes place in Riyadh this week, its first time in the kingdom and only the second time it has taken place in the Middle East , after Doha in 2011. The event has gone ahead despite the fatal attacks on the Saudi capital’s airport . Then, at the start of next month, executives take on the final boss, at Adipec, the world’s biggest energy event. Probably the most popular word in Fujairah last week was “resilience”. The UAE has managed to sustain, and possibly even increase, its oil exports through the conflict, as well as maintaining its essential imports. The Indian Ocean ports of Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and the others have been crucial. Rather than hasty workarounds, this rapid shift builds on years of preparation. The Habshan-Fujairah oil pipeline, with capacity up to 1.8 million barrels per day, was opened in 2012. Preparation for a second line had begun before the war, with the announcement in May and planned completion next year. Massive oil storage in caverns hewn out of Fujairah’s rugged brown mountains began construction in 2018. Adnoc Logistics and Services has amassed a large fleet of tankers and other ships, which has proved essential for moving oil. Supertankers are now in desperately short supply – it costs more to hire one, $80 million, than to launch SpaceX, a bargain at $74 million. Work on the impressive, modern new railway to Fujairah started in early 2020. The Barakah Nuclear Power Plant, an important part of assuring electricity even when gas facilities came under attack, began splitting atoms in August of that year. Regional preparedness Beyond the UAE, we could highlight similar regional examples of preparedness, such as the Gulf Co-operation Council electricity grid, Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline , and the new port, refinery and oil storage facility at Duqm on Oman’s south-east coast. Like Adnoc, Saudi Arabia – with Bahri – Kuwait and Qatar have their own sizeable tanker fleets. Physical assets are only one part of resilience. Adnoc has over several years built a strong trading capability. That was profitable in the years of peace. In months of war, it has been even more important by salvaging supply to customers, and seizing attractive commercial opportunities. These assets were not accumulated with precise foreknowledge of the current conflict. Of course, blockade of Hormuz, or general trouble in the Gulf, has been a known risk since the Tanker War of the 1980s, if not before. In general, though, having a broad set of deployable national assets, whether in one company or several, whether in state or private hands, enables a country to cope with crises of all kinds. That could be regional political unrest as in 2011, a price crash such as that of 2014, a pandemic such as 2020, or a far-off war as in 2022. We do not know what the next challenge may be: a natural disaster, a big climatic upset, an energy technology breakthrough, an international market meltdown over AI or government debt. But combining physical, institutional and human capabilities with a flexible and proactive mindset is the best way to come through such storms. Resilience alone, though, is not enough. When the bombers thundered through the sky on February 28, politicians and observers alike thought it would be a short war. It has now ground on for more than seven months, though most direct strikes on Gulf and Iranian territory have stopped. Other theatres – Yemen, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq – have become entwined. Every regional country, even the non-involved such as Turkey, Egypt and Cyprus, have seen some unwelcome visitor land on their soil, and have suffered disruption to their airspace and trade routes. On Friday, US President Donald Trump announced proudly that Russia’s Vladimir Putin had promised to provide some diesel to ease the growing global fuel crisis, a product of the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine. Handling future crises The Gulf energy industry must build on the resilience established so far, establish new options to respond to future crises, and accelerate creating value. Of course, that is not easy to do while the spectre of renewed violence hovers over the region, and while shipping routes are still not functioning freely. The regional countries were, overall, investing heavily and sensibly in their energy industries before this year. They were solidifying their oil upstream, making the downstream more sophisticated, accessing gas for the domestic economy and for export, generating more value from commercial ingenuity, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, electrifying their economies and seizing on transformational new technology in the AI space. Those remain excellent aims, even if specific projects have to be reprioritised for the new regional reality. Regional energy companies can do more. Becoming true international players fills a capital gap, builds their capabilities and somewhat reduces their near-total reliance on the Gulf. They can do more in inventing and deploying truly game-changing hard technologies. These often struggle in the rest of the world because of lack of visionary capital, overregulation and difficulty in co-ordinating diverse interests. Regional energy companies can work together more. Huge gains are possible from networking physical infrastructure – pipelines, ports, electricity grids and data cables. Greater achievements can come from soft integration, such as commercial joint ventures, cross-border investments and technology partnerships. The energy industry, one of the first truly globalised businesses, needs more than most to reimagine or construct institutions that govern its world by laws and not by the missile. The power to convene the world’s leading energy doers and thinkers, as at Adipec in Abu Dhabi, brings positive influence. Finally, at recent events elsewhere, the energy business has sometimes given the impression of being relieved the issue of climate change has been dethroned by that of war. That is a mistake. Conflicts will, by some smart application of strength and diplomacy, be resolved. Climate change, bad or worse, will be with us for the rest of the century and beyond. It will reshape everything we do in energy and itself can inflame war.

events.title: Labour has got the message – developing nations suffer most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart
events.summary: Labour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoil Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries Developing nations face triple shock, UN warns F rom Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless. Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere. Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans. That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency. Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south , and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future. There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state , and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa. The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis. However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran. Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing. The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.” He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries . As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support. “There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference. Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues. Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.

events.title: Your AI agent wants your money back — and that could mean trouble for these companies
events.summary: Personal AI agents are helping consumers claw back cash — and threatening companies that profit from consumer inertia. Cheng Xin/Getty Images Insurance companies have long profited from customers who don't shop around or challenge prices. Personal AI agents could upend that business model by comparing prices and haggling. "It would certainly be disruptive," one insurance analyst told Business Insider. Personal AI agents are coming for one of companies' most profitable customer behaviors: doing nothing. As personal AI agents make their way into people's financial lives, early users are using them to lower internet bills, recover airline credits, find cheaper insurance, chase refunds, and unearth money they had forgotten was theirs. Noah Shinn, the CEO of Instinct, one such personal AI agent, touted their saving benefits on an episode of "Invest Like the Best" released last week, saying they can scan users' bank transactions, identify forgotten subscriptions , and cancel them. "It just sends back the number of what it saved you," Shinn said. Meta has marketed its new agent , Muse, in a similar way. That could come at a cost to insurers, airlines, banks, broadband providers, and subscription businesses — industries that have for decades benefited, at least in part, from consumer inertia: the millions of people who do not compare the renewal price, dispute the fee , call about the credit, or brave the cancellation maze. Wall Street has already seemingly begun trading on that thesis. In the two weeks after Muse launched, the share prices of Airbnb and Booking.com dropped 12% and 10%, respectively. Planet Fitness shares dropped 17% over the same period. No insurer or consumer experts Business Insider spoke to could put a reliable dollar figure on the potential impact. But Tony Soloman, director of insurance intelligence at J.D. Power, said personal AI agents "would certainly be disruptive" for insurers. "Right now, to actually purchase a policy or make a change, you still need to contact someone, but if AI replaces that, then the carriers lose control over the consumer journey," he said. Let the bots do the haggling Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Some early users have already leveraged personal AI agents to make significant savings . AJ Stuyvenberg, an engineer at Datadog, asked ChatGPT to negotiate with Verizon after Comcast offered him faster fiber internet for $50 a month. After a little over an hour in Verizon’s live chat, the agent secured a lower monthly bill — $69.99, down from $94.99 — plus a $47.50 loyalty credit. Stuyvenberg said the deal saved him $347.50 over a year. "It’s nice to use AI to remove some of the sludge from my life," Stuyvenberg told Business Insider. David Pawlan, who works in growth at Merit Systems, used Instinct to track the price of his United flights , then AgentCash’s StablePhone tool through Claude Code to request travel credits after fares fell. He said he recovered $73 across three flights in about five minutes each. "The future of personal assistants will be the ones that can do the painful and proactive tasks for you," Pawlan told Business Insider. The cost of getting customers to act Widespread adoption of personal AI agents could pressure businesses that have long benefited from customers not shopping around, disputing a charge , or tackling a convoluted cancellation process. But the exposure will not be evenly shared. Craig Moffett, a partner and senior analyst at MoffettNathanson, said agents are likely to matter most where prices are hard to compare or suppliers are difficult to identify. "Real estate, insurance, and financial services all fit the model much better," Moffett told Business Insider. Insurance may offer the clearest test. With roughly $560 billion in US auto and homeowners insurance premiums in 2025, if 5% of policyholders used an agent and secured a 10% lower price, about $2.8 billion in annual premiums would be at stake. But that is a scenario, not a forecast. And the disruption would take far more than a small group of early adopters. "I don't think 5% to 10% of customers are going to be enough to meaningfully change" companies' economics, Rhys Williams, chief strategist at Wayve Capital Management, told Business Insider. "If 40% to 50% of customers are using agents, then the effects will be noticeable." Some firms have already paid significant penalties and refunds over such alleged practices, including Amazon, which has issued more than $845 million in refunds as of September under a settlement over allegations that it enrolled consumers to Amazon Prime without consent and made cancellation difficult. Companies, however, are unlikely to sit back and let AI personal agents do all the bargaining. Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the Consumer Federation of America, said firms could make it harder for consumers and their agents to get through in the first place. "The companies are always a step ahead in making those processes harder," Winters told Business Insider, pointing to Amazon’s move to block Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on its site for users. The result could even be an AI-versus-AI battle for customers. events.title: Gen Z is defying trends and betting on California—even as older Americans flee to the Sun Belt
events.summary: California has been shrinking for the past half-decade. The state’s population fell 0.5% between April 2020 and July 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . It also posted the largest net loss of one-way U-Haul customers of any state for the sixth straight year in the company’s 2025 Growth Index . Yet the country’s youngest adults keep packing up and heading for the Golden State. U-Haul’s 2026 Midyear Migration Trends National Report ranks states and metros by their net gain of one-way U-Haul trucks, trailers, and U-Box containers from July 2025 through June 2026. It puts California at No. 2 for Gen Z (born 1997–2012), behind only Texas. As Fortune previously reported , the state didn’t crack the top 10 for boomers or Gen X, whose moves skewed heavily toward the Southeast. San Diego, at No. 9 for Gen X, was the only California metro on either older generation’s list. Millennials ranked California No. 3, behind Florida and Texas. Gen Z hasn’t given up on the Sun Belt. Texas tops its list, and Florida, Nevada, Austin, Charlotte, and Houston all make its top 10. But the generation’s picks look less like a hunt for warm weather and low costs and more like a hunt for people. After Texas and California, Gen Z’s top five states are New York, Illinois, and Colorado. Its top five metros are New York City, Dallas–Fort Worth, Chicago, the San Francisco Bay Area, and Los Angeles. U-Haul said Gen Z is gravitating to densely populated markets with lots of colleges, entry-level jobs, and apartments. That’s a shift from recent trends that saw young workers leave San Francisco for more affordable cities like Nashville and Orlando , and from rankings that name cheaper Midwest and Texas cities as the best places for new grads . The biggest job market in the country California’s scale is hard to compete with. It has been the most populous state since 1962, when it passed New York. Even after five years of decline, it has about 39.4 million residents, roughly 11.5% of the U.S. population. That population supports a huge job market, which matters for a generation just starting its careers. California had 18.2 million nonfarm payroll jobs in August, more than any other state. It also led the nation in monthly job gains, adding 39,400, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . The state’s Employment Development Department said it added 138,500 jobs over the past year. The picture isn’t all rosy. California’s unemployment rate remains among the highest in the country, and the state’s Legislative Analyst’s Office has warned that early-2026 job growth may have been overstated. Still, few states offer early-career workers as many employers in as many industries, from Nvidia, Apple, and Google to Hollywood’s major studios. Expensive, but so is everywhere else California remains one of the country’s priciest places to live. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $734,700, and median gross rent is $2,036, according to Census Bureau data for 2020 to 2024. Gen Z, though, is being squeezed almost everywhere. A record 1 in 3 adults under 35 lived with their parents in 2025 , most of them employed. Because so many young Americans grew up in California, moving home often means moving back to the Golden State. One analysis cited by Fortune found that 20% of working adults in Greater Los Angeles live with their parents , compared with 6% in the Austin metro. Others are getting help from family to stay in expensive cities. A Bank of America study found that 54% of 18- to 27-year-olds pay nothing toward their housing costs . California’s taxes are among the nation’s highest, but the state also offers a broader social safety net than many others, which can cushion young workers between jobs. The lifestyle premium Then there’s the pull that has drawn Americans west for generations. California has beaches, mountains, deserts, and forests, and in parts of the state you can ski in the morning and surf in the afternoon. Much of the coast enjoys a Mediterranean climate that keeps temperatures mild year-round. For many young movers, the high cost of living is a worthwhile premium. U-Haul’s data has limits. Not every mover rents from U-Haul, and not every one-way rental is a permanent change of address. Each move is credited to the generation of whoever signs the contract, and customers must be 18 to rent a truck, so the youngest members of Gen Z aren’t captured. Millennials and Gen X together account for more than 60% of the company’s one-way rentals. Still, the data suggests that California’s scale keeps pulling young Americans in, even as the state loses residents overall: its jobs, its people, and the family ties that bring them home. events.title: I'm a top auto industry analyst. Improv taught me to scare myself in public.
events.summary: Erin Keating took five seasons of improv classes. It taught her about how to really listen to coworkers and family. Erin Keating Erin Keating spoke too fast during her first big presentation. She also felt kinda sweaty. In her mid-40s, she took an improv class to get better onstage. It's taught her lessons about listening to others that have helped at work and at home. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Erin Keating, an executive analyst for Cox Automotive. It has been edited for length and clarity. People should scare themselves. In public. I tested that theory out in my mid-40s by taking five seasons of improv classes at the DC Improv Comedy Club. My goal was not to become a comedian — I wanted to take on a challenge that I could easily fail at. And to add to the pressure, I had to perform in front of my family. I work as an executive analyst in the auto industry at Cox Automotive. I distill data to explain the industry's market dynamics to automakers, dealership groups, lenders, and journalists . The material I cover can quickly get boring if I'm not careful. Some of those conversations happen in small rooms, others happen in high-pressure settings: on stages in front of hundreds or thousands of people, on live television, at product unveilings, in podcasts, you name it. I also consider myself an introvert . I didn't always feel so comfortable in front of people — and I certainly haven't always been the funniest person in the room. Getting on the stage At my first major corporate presentation, I couldn't stop sweating. My colleagues said I was good, but I was talking too fast. Their feedback was basically, "You did fine. Slow down." I improved over time and got less sweaty when talking in front of people. There was still more I could learn. I decided to take the improv classes in 2018 because, honestly, I was a little bit bored. I had just left a marketing communications job and was trying to figure out what to do next. I knew I liked talking: I was hosting a successful podcast about books, but I wanted to be better at having conversations. Loving to talk is definitely not the same as being a good conversationalist. The classes with a cast of characters… So, I joined my first class. I was there with a biology teacher, a German woman who was really funny, an older woman who had done a ton of onstage acting, and a handful of people (like me) who were nervous about participating. The majority of us stuck it out for our five consecutive seasons. At the beginning, I fought against my preconception that I had to be funny. I remember playing a game called "Die, not today," where we had to mime throwing a hammer or a spear at each other. If the object was heading your way, you had to come up with how you'd survive the attack on the spot. Most people just tried to shield themselves, but one woman staged a dramatic scene where a spear nearly struck her nose. She grabbed it at the last second, saving her (improv-ed) life. It was amazing. … And their lessons Improv is really about paying attention to what another person is giving you. You have to build upon the scenario they set up, a principle called "yes, and." You accept the premise someone introduces, and add something to it. You also learn about status. In a scene, you might be the character driving the action. In your next, you could be supporting the other person's arc. Scenes are most interesting when you watch people respond to each other and create together through those statuses. Some of the worst scenes are when two people are just trying to compete to be the funniest. All of that applies to work and your life more than you might realize. Before I speak at big conferences, I talk to people in the audience to understand the energy in the room and what is on their minds. I don't like working from a script. It can get too prescriptive and keep you from responding to the people in front of you. I'm listening for the thought that is begging for a "yes, and." The same goes for one-on-one conversations. When someone talks, improv has taught me to follow the unexpected and respond to what was actually said. Those skills also matter a lot for office politics. Those classes taught me to recognize an awkward moment, assess the reaction, and apologize if I misread it. I am now comfortable saying, "Thank you for receiving that with the intent it was given," when I know I don't express myself well. The final big lesson was authenticity. Near the end of my third improv season, I jumped into a scene and used the New York Jewish-grandmother voice I'd always been able to pull off (do not ask me to do other accents — even when I think I sound like a señorita, I always revert back to that Eastern European drawl.) I'd avoided that voice because I thought, "This is not acting, I'm not supposed to do that." But for that scene, it was exactly what my partner needed. My classmate asked me why I had never done it. That voice was a breakthrough for me. I realized I could bring my whole self to that stage. Onto the next challenges Human skills are becoming more important , especially as AI changes how we work . Sure, technical skills will remain important. But I think people who can listen, relate to others, read a room, and recover gracefully from an uncomfortable moment will have a real advantage. Those are human skills that you can't fake by memorizing a script. So, I suggest doing the thing that scares you: get onstage, take a class, give the speech. You may sweat, and you may talk too fast. But you'll get through it — and learn something about how you show up for the people around you. I plan to keep testing that theory myself. My first stand-up comedy class starts on Tuesday. And I'm terrified. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: As youth sports booms, churches compete for American families' Sundays
events.summary: America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields. Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time. The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures . Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change. As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry , more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago. "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of " Take Back the Game : How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore." By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found. Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play . Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found. State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity , massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams. Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor. How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region. Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships. That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending. Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches. Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found. What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times. "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship." Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender. Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field. Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels. Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said. Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said. The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven. For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.

events.title: Photos: Thousands detained in police crackdown on India’s youth protest
events.summary: Demonstrators intercepted and detained as authorities crack down on ‘cockroach’ movement rally in central New Delhi. Thousands of people were detained across New Delhi on Saturday as Indian authorities mounted a sweeping security operation to stop a protest by the youth-led “cockroach” movement demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief. Police fanned out across India’s capital to block access to Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site, stopping buses and cars at checkpoints, erecting barricades and deploying antiriot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers along key routes. Many demonstrators were intercepted long before they reached central New Delhi, chased away or dragged into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centres. Several movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained en route, effectively halting the rally before it began. Authorities said they had denied permission for the gathering because the request was submitted late and insisted the measures were necessary to maintain order. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, dismissed the protesters as “anarchic elements” staging a “flop show”. Despite the clampdown, some protesters broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and the Election Commission of India (ECI), before being detained. “We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force,” said college student Tanya Negi, who travelled from Mumbai. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?” The movement led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) emerged online in May and gained prominence through protests over exam paper leaks that led to the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July. Its latest campaign targets the ECI’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which opposition parties say has already removed more than 130 million names from voter rolls and disenfranchised supporters. The ECI and the government deny any political bias, but critics say the crackdown highlights shrinking space for dissent as key state polls approach.

events.title: Retail's holiday hiring push is shaping up to be worse than last year's disappointing run
events.summary: Retail is a key step in many workers' career journey, and seasonal roles are how a lot of retail employees got their start. Joe Raedle/Getty Images The retail industry's seasonal hiring push is on track to be the lowest in years. The shift reflects a trend toward earlier hiring and less reliance on seasonal workers. Fewer seasonal jobs could also start to erode a once-common first step on workers' career ladders. The annual stampede of seasonal retail job openings continues to taper off, with hiring expected to be at its lowest level since the Financial Crisis. As mid-October approaches, some major companies have not said if they will bulk up their front lines to a specific target. "It's a little bit of chicken right now with retailers and the economy going, 'Okay, who's going to move first?'" said Trent Cotton , head of talent-acquisition insights at recruiting-software company ICIMS. "It will be interesting to see this at the end of the year." This year's retail industry hiring push is on track to be lower than last year's tally of 461,000, according to career transition firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. A report released last month projects that this year will see around 450,000 seasonal retail jobs, the lowest gain in nearly 20 years. "Almost every hiring announcement we've seen in the last three years is smaller and more surgical than the pre-pandemic playbook. Even if the big names come in at last year's numbers, the total will likely fall well short of the 2019—2021 peaks," chief revenue officer Andy Challenger said in a statement. This year, Spirit Halloween and craft shop Michaels led the charge, saying they intended to hire 52,000 and 10,000 seasonal workers, respectively. Amazon has not yet shared its plans, and Walmart told Business Insider it will take the same approach as last year, which did not have a hiring goal target. "Our stores are well-staffed and ready to serve customers this holiday season," the company said. Target said it will once again rely on its on-demand team of about 43,000 workers and leave further hiring up to local managers. Walmart and Target both said last year they would prioritize assigning additional seasonal hours to existing employees . Cotton also said that these smaller numbers reflect a trend toward earlier hiring and less reliance on seasonal workers. "They're moving it back to over the summer, so that way they're fully staffed by October going into November and December," he said. That point also came up several times during visit Business Insider had with Target's chief stores officer Adrienne Costanzo in August. For some Target stores, the larger hiring push already happened in preparation for the critical back-to-school season , which also enabled managers to train new hires for the holidays. But fewer seasonal jobs could also start to erode a once-common first step on workers' career ladders. Retail workers represent roughly one in ten US workers, and analysis from the Urban Institute estimates that six in 10 workers have held a retail job at some point in their careers . events.title: HPE's networking boss says AI will handle all trouble tickets without humans in two years
events.summary: HPE is extending its AI-powered networking automation across its hybrid cloud portfolio. That news came from Rami Rahim, formerly CEO of Juniper Networks and now president and general manager of HPE's networking business, whom The Register met last week when he visited Australia. Rahim champions what HPE calls "self-driving networks" – AI-assisted monitoring and automated remediation, part of the broader field known as AIOps. The networking boss thinks AIOps will mean human network administrators soon won't need to work on any trouble tickets. "I think we're now at probably around 70 to 80 percent of all tickets don't require human intervention," Rahim said. "Within two to three years, we'll have no issues that require humans." He allows that hardware swaps will be the exception to that rule, but even for that job he thinks skilled network administrators shouldn't be involved. "The technology should, without your knowledge, order a new part. It comes in the mail and you don't need an IT person, just an intern can come and take this thing, attach it to where the failed device is, and everything else just happens automatically." Why you'll trust your career to a machine The Register asked why net admins should trust AIOps, given that following bad advice issued by a machine is unlikely to improve anyone's career prospects. Rahim responded by pointing out that self-driving taxis have quickly become widely accepted in the Bay Area, and that first-time riders draw on their past experience of adopting cars with automatic transmissions, then cars with cruise control, lane assist, and self-driving capabilities. Each successive experience of automation working safely, he suggested, imparts confidence to try new forms of automation. "And so what we do is we give the operators the ability to turn on actions, automated actions, feature by feature, and capability by capability," he said. Simple jobs like allowing AI to reboot a port on a switch is a fine place to start, he suggested. The metrics he uses to measure the success of automation are the number of tickets lodged about poor Wi-Fi performance and the speed with which they are fixed. "I think if you look at the number one trouble ticket that is filed in a typical enterprise environment, it is 'the Wi-Fi sucks.'" "Regardless of what the actual problem is – it could be an application going down, or a WAN issue, or a cloud provider issue – the experience is first felt through Wi-Fi and therefore it's as simple as 'The Wi-Fi sucks.'" Rahim thinks AI will figure out why Wi-Fi isn't at its best quicker than a human can do the job and also use agents to fix it faster. Those agents, he suggested, make automation even more important because they represent a new class of users that are dependent on networks. "We're quickly approaching a realm in which every enterprise has way more agents working than humans working, and they need a reliable network connection to do their work," he said. Organizations can't scale their human teams to a size at which they solve problems fast enough to manage all those connections. And because agents make so much traffic, buyers will need to add more networking hardware, which will further scale networks to a size no human can hope to manage alone. Only AI, Rahim believes, will make it possible to use AI. A 'networking company'? Of course he would say that, given that he claims HPE's networking portfolio and AI capabilities are second to none since it closed the acquisition of Juniper in July 2025. The Register covered that moment with the headline "HPE-Juniper deal closes, integration questions remain." Rahim assured us it's going swimmingly, pointing to the fact that HPE continues to sell Wi-Fi access points that started life as products from Aruba and Juniper – but that users can now drive them with management tools from either vendor. He proudly pointed to that becoming possible within 18 months of the acquisition closing, then made a sharp reference to certain other vendors taking far longer to achieve the same thing. The Register mentioned Cisco and Meraki: Rahim didn't show any signs of disagreement. Asked about HPE CEO Antonio Neri's statement on the company's last earnings call that "we are at the core becoming a networking company," Rahim emphasized networking's importance across workloads. "When you look at the AI datacenter, it's become as much a networking problem as it is a compute problem. So I just believe that networking is becoming more important in general for the industry, and it's certainly becoming more important for HPE as a company," he said. Which is why HPE is now bringing the self-driving network tech that started life at Juniper to the rest of its portfolio. "We've already, for example, integrated our network fabric management capabilities with OpsRamp, which is the observability software for the hybrid cloud stack," Rahim said. "So that would be an example of something that's now done. But more and more pieces will come along the way." ®

events.title: I work 4 p.m. to midnight, and I love my schedule. Here's how I make time for sleep, the gym, and relaxing.
events.summary: Jimmy Kibuswa's work schedule allows him to hit the gym for two hours each weekday. Courtesy of Jimmy Kibuswa Jimmy Kibuswa, who lives in Kenya, works remotely from 4 p.m. to midnight for a US company. He builds his day around reading and staying active and says his unconventional schedule has been life-changing. The recruiter used to have a long commute. Now he asks: "What can I use these extra hours for?" This is an as-told-to essay based on a conversation with Jimmy Kibuswa, 32, who lives in Nairobi, Kenya. He works remotely as a healthcare recruiter for a US company and shares what it's like to work an unconventional shift. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. I work American time from here in Kenya. In Kenya, when it's 4 p.m., it's 8 a.m. in Chicago. I've always been cautious about my health and well-being . When I got this job about three months ago, I thought, "How am I going to structure my day so that I can go to the gym, read, and rest?" My work begins at 4 p.m. and ends around midnight, so I can be online for the US workday. Immediately after midnight, I normally don't do anything else. I just get ready to go to bed. In the first month, I struggled. I would take naps during the afternoon before my shift. Nowadays, I don't feel like I need those naps because I've adapted. I always ensure that I sleep for eight hours because if I don't sleep well at night, I'm not going to function well the next day. I keep a regular schedule I love waking up around 8:30, preparing breakfast, and then maybe reading a chapter or two. I'm a big fan of self-help books. When it gets to 10:30, I go to the gym for two hours. I walk on the treadmill for 30 minutes and then run for 15 minutes. I started working out consistently when I got this job. Before this, when I was working locally in Nairobi, I'd work out for a month , then not pay the gym subscription for the next month. The beauty of getting to the gym at 10:30 is that most people go early in the morning. So, by the time I arrive, it's almost empty, and I've got the full attention of the coaches. After the treadmill, the coach will tell me, "Today, this is what we're going to do." After two hours, I'm done. I get back to my place — it's about 2,000 steps — and I prepare my one big meal of the day, besides breakfast. That's around 2 p.m. or 3 p.m. Then, during work, I have nuts and water. That's all I need. Between about 2 p.m. and 4 p.m., I might strategize. I still consider myself early in my career , and I think, "Where do I want to be in the next five years or maybe the next 10 years?" Maybe I didn't finish something the previous day, so I'll be thinking, "How can I find that talent that I really want for this particular role?" If I don't do those things, I'll relax and listen to music. People need downtime . I grew up in the countryside. That's why I'm such a homebody. I'm lucky because my girlfriend also works the same kind of hours as I do. We only meet on the weekends, and then on Monday when it's time to go back to work, we're all sorted. My friends know the best time to communicate with me. I also communicate with my family between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. My routine makes me feel sharper Today, when I meet people that I used to work with, they're like, "You're getting even younger. What's happening? What's the secret?" In Kenya, it is hard to find a remote job . It's what so many people would wish to find. I thank God I did. I am sharper now because my mind is relaxed. I get sleep, and when I exercise, I feel like my brain absorbs more information. I can solve problems better, and I'm more creative. Before this job, it was all about work. I used to get stressed. Now, when I'm able to incorporate sleeping, reading, working out, and relaxing, I feel like I'm not stressed anymore. I think it all stems from the schedule that I've incorporated. One thing that really surprised me when I started this schedule was how much time I have on my hands. In a previous job, I would work about nine hours and then spend almost two hours on the road. Now, I'm like, "What can I use these extra hours for?" Do you have a story to share about your work schedule? Contact this reporter at tparadis@businessinsider.com . events.title: A nurse was sued by her student-loan company. After losing a chunk of her paycheck, here's how it turned out.
events.summary: Hannah Bates has represented herself for nearly two years in a lawsuit filed against her by her student-loan lender. Nic Antaya, Alyssa Powell/BI It's been over a year since Hannah Bates, 31, was sued by her private student-loan lender — a legal battle she called lengthy, expensive, and confusing. It started in October 2024, when Sallie Mae notified her that she'd made the final payment on her outstanding balance of $55,000. Bates knew that was a mistake. In fact, she was falling behind on her $1,500 monthly payments and had years' worth left. When she tried to clarify with Sallie Mae, she said she received conflicting information on how to avoid default. Six months later, Sallie Mae sued her to collect. When she's not working her 12-hour nursing shifts, Bates has represented herself in the lawsuit, with the help of ChatGPT. She said it's taken a significant emotional and financial toll, and after multiple unsuccessful attempts to reach a payment agreement, the court ordered that her wages be garnished. She lost $884 from her roughly $2,700 paycheck for two pay cycles, prompting her to pick up extra shifts at her hospital. "It's the weight of the world," Bates said. "Some days are better than others, but I didn't think I'd be here." More student-loan borrowers could soon find themselves in Bates' situation. Private student loans comprised only 10% of the $1.85 trillion student-loan market in 2025, according to Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Data. But President Donald Trump's repayment overhaul , which took effect July 1, is expected to drive more borrowers to private lenders like Sallie Mae, which lack substantial federal oversight . Business Insider's previous reporting revealed widespread confusion in lender communication as borrowers moved toward default and litigation — about one in four complaints filed with the CFPB in 2025 were about private student loans. A report from advocacy group Protect Borrowers said that private lenders sued more than 100,000 borrowers between 2012 and 2016. Bates said that her legal process taught her that she's "very much not alone." "At first, I was really embarrassed and ashamed to talk about it," Bates said. "Now I'm absolutely not." This story is part of Business Insider's "Student Debt Spiral" series, which explores how rising student debt is changing the financial futures of millions. Do you have a story to share? Fill out this form , and we'll be in touch. Read more of our student-loan coverage here: They were told their private student loans were paid off. Then they were sued. A 60-year-old took out student loans to help her kids succeed. She's facing retirement with a $156,000 balance. 'A bunch of red tape': Student-loan borrowers can't get clear answers from the companies that manage their debt What came after the lawsuit Before defaulting, Bates was paying what she could afford — around $560 a month — but was unable to make her full $1,500 payments. She tried and failed repeatedly to negotiate a lower monthly bill, and didn't know how to return to good standing after she defaulted. "I didn't hear anything for months," Bates said. "I had contacted them once or twice throughout this process, waiting to hear back, and no one ever had an answer for me." A Sallie Mae spokesperson previously told Business Insider that it could not comment on Bates' account and that the company "proactively and consistently" communicates with its customers, including sending notices when a customer defaults, when that defaulted loan is sold, and informing them of the new owner. After Bates was sued, the judge encouraged her instead to reach a settlement or agree to a payment plan with Sallie Mae. Bates said Sallie Mae offered her a payment plan of around $1,600 a month — higher than the original payments that had led her to default in the first place. "That's not feasible," she said after the hearing. "I am more than willing to pay back what I took, but it needs to be a payment that is manageable, and that's not going to put me on the streets." Ayelet Sheffey covers all things student debt, from the latest Education Department news to stories of borrowers navigating their loans. To stay up to date on her coverage, sign up to get email alerts for her new stories here . She requested a lower payment plan and waited months for Sallie Mae's sign-off. She saw in August that a garnishment notice had been added to her court docket. Weeks later, she lost a chunk of her paycheck. "It's hard going to work knowing that with everything you deal with and go through, you're not getting paid the way that you ultimately deserve," Bates said. At the end of September, a judge signed off on a plan allowing her to make $600 monthly payments toward her balance until it is paid off. It won't be easy, she said, but it's preferable to losing about $1,700 a month to wage garnishment. "Home-wise, with bills and finances, it's not 100% feasible," Bates said. "But it's given me some sort of empowerment because at least I have the ball back in my court, and the money won't just be taken from me." Bates will begin making payments through the court's payment system on November 1. Looking back, she wishes she had better understood how lengthy litigation can be, so she could have better prepared herself for the legal battle ahead. While she still has years of payments to go, she's relieved to close this chapter. "I'm optimistic," Bates said. "I feel a lot better mentally because it's not consuming my life as much as it was." events.title: ‘Never seen anything quite like it’: How rural Pennsylvania’s $165 million data center fight became representative of the bipartisan battle against AI
events.summary: An area of Pennsylvania once known for its anti-immigration crackdown is now resisting data centers, just one example of how the AI buildout has created a unified, bipartisan front in an increasingly splintered America. About 20 years ago, Hazleton passed the controversial Illegal Immigration Relief Act , which withheld permits from businesses employing undocumented immigrants and fined landlords who rented to them. Capitalizing on a time of deindustrialization and demographic changes in a heavily Hispanic city, the law galvanized a base of white, working-class supporters.  Fast forward to today, and Hazle Township, the area where Hazleton sits at the foot of the Poconos, is still making headlines. But this time, it’s the AI infrastructure boom. Data center opponents, diverse in both class and political party, have jumbled what was considered a left-versus-right issue and created a powerful united front pushing politicians to alter their platforms and policies in a consequential election year. Over the summer, residents of Hazle Township received letters from NorthPoint Development, offering the township’s 4,500 residents each a potential $10,000 payday in exchange for permission to build a 1,300-acre data center in the area, part of the developer’s $165 million proposed investment into the township. At the same time, about 30 properties in nearby Sugarloaf Township faced eminent domain threats from the local utilities company over a proposed high-voltage power line that would run through the homes and power that same proposed data center, dubbed Project Hazelnut. Locals formed the group Alliance to Stop the Line and filed 20 formal protests against the utilities company over the health and property-cost risks associated with the power line, while others filed right-to-know requests, demanding transparency on the end user of Project Hazelnut, which emails revealed to be Amazon . An Amazon spokesperson told Fortune it is “evaluating multiple sites across the Commonwealth” but does not have a definitive agreement in place with NorthPoint. What has stuck out to some locals is the demographics of those opposing the data center. Annie Vinatieri, a Sugarloaf Township protester, observed that the data center opponents are a combination of working, middle, and upper classes, mostly white, but definitely nonpartisan, including many who are new to environmental protests. “It’s invigorating, in the sense that you’re meeting people who might not be like-minded on a lot of things, but it feels for so many people like this a righteous cause,” she told Fortune . “We can maybe disagree on the political finer points of things, but we can find this very real camaraderie in the midst of everything.” Why data centers became a bipartisan enemy Data centers have become the common enemy of Democrats and Republicans alike. About 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local areas, according to one Gallup poll , including 75% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans. The backlash is beginning to have material impacts on the tempo of the AI boom. At least 75 data center projects worth more than $130 billion total were delayed or cancelled in the first three months of this year, according to a Data Center Watch report published in June. All the while, active opposition groups grew from 396 to 833 over the same period. One significant reason behind the bipartisan dissent toward data centers is how tech companies have marketed them to the American people, Tatishe Nteta, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of UMass Poll, told Fortune.  “There has been little to no clear communication of the benefits, economic or otherwise, that are associated with data centers for everyday Americans,” he said. “And there has been extremely clear communication regarding the costs, whether those be environmental in terms of increased use of energy…but also the cost that’s associated more largely with artificial intelligence on the economic well-being of Americans.” The universality of data center hate has allowed Democrats to make it a wedge issue, Nteta said.  But AI infrastructure and AI more broadly have also struck chords with ideologies held by both Republicans and Democrats, just in different flavors, according to Ben Green, assistant professor of public policy at the University of Michigan’s Ford School. For example, environmental concerns around data center buildouts are bipartisan. The difference is that Democrats use words like “climate change” to define the issue, but Republicans focus more on the protection of land. “Democrats and Republicans might talk about that differently, but massive corporations coming in and forcing a community to deal with some type of project and not really giving a community any voice and operating in secrecy—no one’s really a fan of that,” Green told Fortune . Pennsylvania’s data center profile Pennsylvania has established itself as a nexus of data center backlash. The commonwealth is home to only 174 data centers out of about 4,767 total projects in the U.S., but its position as a purple state with a governor widely expected to run for president in 2028, makes it a unique case study in the conversation around national data center opposition. Gov. Josh Shapiro announced Project Hazelnut in November 2024 immediately following an executive order fast-tracking permitting for AI infrastructure. In July 2025, he announced a $20 billion investment from Amazon for data center buildout in the commonwealth, the largest capital investment in Pennsylvania’s history. But following public pushback over data center projects in Hazle Township and surrounding areas, Shapiro walked back the permissive AI infrastructure policies. He signed another executive order in August eliminating fast-track permits and gave local agencies power to approve data center projects, rather than the state-level Department of Environmental Protection. “What I was finding after listening to the neighbors about their concerns, and then talking with some of these developers, is those developers who were wreaking havoc on the communities, they actually didn’t have any access to power,” Shapiro told CBS News Philadelphia last month.  The future of data center opposition With Pennsylvania’s gubernatorial election coming up next month, candidates’ stances on data center development could further scramble traditional partisan divides.  According to Vinatieri, Democrats are discouraged by Shapiro’s changing data center stance. Meanwhile, Republican candidate Stacy Garrity has largely not broken from Trump’s pro-data center position. From Vinatieri’s vantage point, there are even enough disgruntled residents that a meaningful number of voters could write in Democratic Sen. Katie Muth, who has sponsored a statewide data center development moratorium . “I’ve never seen anything quite like it before,”
