events.title: ChatGPT for Teens is live. Here's how famed parenting expert Emily Oster says parents should approach it.
events.summary: Emily Oster is an economics professor at Brown University, the founder of data-driven parenting resource ParentData, and the author of the bestselling books "Expecting Better" and "Cribsheet." Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Emily Oster OpenAI launched "ChatGPT for Teens" in August, aimed at users ages 13 to 17. It includes study-help features and content guardrails, with the goal of making AI safer for teens. Emily Oster, founder of ParentData, shared how parents can navigate their teens using AI. OpenAI seems to have solved the problem of adolescents lying about their age: if they type like they're under 18, it automatically assumes that they are — and restricts them to a teen version of ChatGPT. It's one of the main features boasted by OpenAI's "ChatGPT for Teens," which officially launched in August and was the subject of a parent forum in New York City on October 7. But even with those protections, parents face the harder question of how their kids should actually use AI. "If I had to pick a word for how people are feeling about this moment, it's probably confused and anxious, which is not how we want parents to feel," Emily Oster , the founder of ParentData, a data-driven parenting and pregnancy resource, said at the ChatGPT for Teens Parent Forum. OpenAI is trying to address these concerns with ChatGPT for Teens. Besides its age-estimation feature, which analyzes a user's language patterns, the questions they ask, and the time of day they use ChatGPT, ChatGPT for Teens also has a "study mode" to break down math problems into steps or create custom flashcards. An example of "Study Mode" in ChatGPT for Teens. OpenAI It also includes guardrails such as a more neutral tone of voice (to avoid ChatGPT sounding too friendly or romanticized), content restrictions, and notification tools to inform parents with linked accounts if their teens are asking about topics such as self-harm or eating disorders. The goal, according to Allison Mishkin, head of child development at OpenAI, is to create a version of ChatGPT that is not only safer but also more age-appropriate for teens, but that also includes features that will directly benefit teens who need extra homework help or have a genuine interest in using AI tools. So far, the roll-out has had some mixed feedback. A Common Sense Media report published on October 7 that analyzed 4,000 prompts found that the platform failed to alert parents after talks of suicidal ideation, was inconsistent in identifying teen users, and could still be used to provide answers to homework . For many parents, AI feels like an inevitable part of their teens' future, and something that's increasingly difficult to avoid. Oster spoke to Business Insider about three ways they can manage their teens' AI use. You should already be mindful about screen time Oster said parents should be setting boundaries around screen time in general, including AI. Hispanolistic/Getty Images Over the past few years, parents have expressed concerns about their teens' relationships to their screens . AI adds another dimension to the worry: what if it's yet another reason for their kids to remain glued to their devices? Oster told Business Insider that the same advice for navigating a teen's social media use exists for AI: good parenting starts with actually knowing what your teen is doing online and their relationship to these platforms. If it remains a complete mystery, Oster encouraged asking open-ended questions. "I would urge parents to come into that conversation without an aim to come out of it with some rules or controls," she said, which can hopefully get teens to share what they use AI for more freely. Ultimately, she said it's "incredibly important" for parents to think about how all screen use — AI included — fits into their kids' lives. "How do we give kids enough time to do the things that are really important — to do their homework, to sleep enough, to spend time with their families, to be outside?" she said. "I would encourage parents to think about that time displacement regardless of what your kid is doing on their computer." Take advantage of the best tools, like customized tutoring ChatGPT for Teens includes features like custom flashcards. OpenAI One of the biggest controversies around AI is students using it to either outwardly cheat on assignments or do most of the thinking for them. It's a tension, Oster said, that researchers are still exploring. "I do think that the struggle piece is a huge part of learning," she said. "We do see when kids are using AI to answer all their homework questions, then they can't do the tests. So that's not good." At the same time, she said everyone learns differently, and some might benefit from having the material repeated or explained in a different way. One father in California previously told Business Insider that he programmed ChatGPT to quiz his two daughters on their classroom materials until they're confident enough to pass their tests. Oster is also excited about the platform's new college planner feature, announced in October, which she said can "make it easier for kids without access to a good college counselor to access information" about specific schools and admission processes. Just as it is for adults, AI is what you make of it. It's on parents to instill the right values in their kids and encourage them to use it as a helpful tool rather than a cheat code . "If your kid hears 'getting 100 on everything is the most important thing in the world,' that changes how they're going to be interacting with a tool that can help them get 100 on their homework every time," Oster said at the forum. "On the other hand, if you ask, 'really, what is school for?' Well, school is for learning how to learn." Be cautious, but not fearful AI can be a helpful tool if used correctly, Oster said. miniseries/Getty Images Considering all the troubling AI headlines in the news, it's no shock that some parents are wary of the future. "I think there's so much fear, and I really understand that as a parent, I really understand the fear and anxiety, but there's also so much promise," Oster told Business Insider. While navigating teen AI use can feel like a unique, of-the-times conundrum, Oster believes it ties into the constant, "core question" of parenting: "How do I make good decisions under uncertainty?" she said at the forum. She said the best thing a parent can do in any scenario is to do their research, make the decision, and set boundaries they feel are appropriate. " We can never be sure that we made the right decision," she said. "We can never live the other path." Her advice is to take necessary precautions, like talking to your teen, but also to keep an open mind about where AI can be helpful. She shared that her own teenage daughter wanted to build something to connect kids to volunteer opportunities, which she built using AI . events.title: I almost fell for an AI job scam because the usual red flags weren't there. Here's how I caught it.
events.summary: Photo courtesy of Daniel Harnack Daniel Harnack nearly fell for a personalized AI job scam that used stolen LinkedIn information. He said AI tools are enabling scammers to create highly tailored and convincing fake job offers. Harnack advises other job seekers to be wary of scams and avoid sharing financial information. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Daniel Harnack, a data analytics professional. It has been edited for length and clarity. About a month ago, I was almost tricked into falling for an elaborate AI scam . A scammer stole a recruiter's LinkedIn picture, linked to her profile, and created a fake email address for her so they could send me a job listing created with the help of AI. The role was perfectly tailored to my experience, and it sounded like a dream job . Also, the pay was double the reasonable salary for that kind of role. All the person needed was my résumé to submit to the hiring manager. When, instead of taking my résumé and suggesting I apply for the role on their career site, they suggested I meet with a "career consultant" to suggest changes to my résumé, that sealed the deal in my mind that this was definitely going to be a scam where they asked for payment. This is just a reminder to everyone that AI is making these very individualized scams much easier to pull off. The usual red flags weren't there This was such a surprising scam because of how personalized, tailored, and realistic it was. The red flags that I'm used to — vague promises, fake names, fake companies, and fake-sounding job titles — had all been addressed or covered up. Unless someone really pays attention, it would be easy to get caught up in a scam like this. The person used a real recruiter's name, organization, and LinkedIn profile. They put together a job description that matched my experience and looked reasonable, and they responded to my questions without typos or grammar mistakes. People on the job market unintentionally make themselves targets of such scams I really think that the current way job seekers are putting themselves out there — noting they are open to work, applying to large numbers of jobs, and publicly posting about the difficulties of the job search — makes us exposed to these scammers who are seeking out vulnerable and eager people looking for jobs. The unfortunate thing is that I don't think there's a good way to avoid this in the current job market . The fact that the job market requires us to apply for so many roles before finding one that connects means our information is likely out there for scammers to harvest. What you can do to avoid being scammed on the job market Because there is no great method of prevention, the best course of action is awareness and scrutiny over folks reaching out to you. The core of any scam is the scammer's desire to get either your money or your information (so they can exploit that information for money). The best thing we can do is to never send banking information or payment to these people. No recruiter should be asking for payment to find you a job. Recruiters should be paid by organizations to fill positions, not by job seekers for the opportunity to be seen. Services exist to review your résumé and help you draft applications, but those services should be transparent that the service is the résumé review, not the allure of a dream job. My professional background has exposed me to the type of tools these scammers are using My background leading data analysts and scientists helped me identify the scam relatively fast. I reached out to the real person on both LinkedIn and by sending an email to their work email, but she never responded. I took that to mean that the scammer and the real person were definitely not the same. Do you have a job-related scam you fell for or avoided that you'd like to share? events.title: ‘If we wait, will it even be there?’ What I’m hearing from retirees about Social Security
events.summary: Last week I met with a couple I’ll call Jeff and Julie, both age 62. Julie had purchased a Social Security claiming analysis for the two of them, and before we started, I asked: “Why did you decide to do this?” Her answer had almost nothing to do with maximizing benefits. “Ray, I read. And everything I’ve been reading about what’s happening with Social Security makes me nervous. If we wait until we are 70 to file, will it even be there?” Here is my advice: Don’t file at 62 because you’re afraid Social Security will disappear. A frightening headline is not a claiming strategy. I understand why Julie is nervous. I do not agree that claiming now is the answer. Most of my clients are affluent and can afford to wait. Yet nearly every client I have met with this year has expressed anxiety about whether Social Security will be there. Many are considering claiming early, not because the math says to, but because they are afraid to wait. They are trying to protect themselves. My job is to challenge whether the decision actually does that. Start with 2032. If that feels uncomfortably close, that’s because it is. In retirement-planning terms, it is practically next Tuesday. The Social Security Trustees project that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which pays retirement and survivor benefits, will deplete its reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032 under current law. Continuing income would initially cover about 78% of scheduled benefits. That is a financing shortfall, not an expiration date. Payroll taxes would keep coming in. Social Security would not disappear. But a potential 22% shortfall is real money, and for Jeff and Julie it arrives before their first retirement check at 70. Telling them not to worry is not an answer. The administrative news doesn’t help. In a September audit examining fiscal 2023 cases, SSA’s Office of Inspector General found that 46% of the retirement, survivor and disability overpayment notices it reviewed failed to meet agency requirements. Some contained inaccurate amounts. Others omitted information about reconsideration and waiver rights.  If SSA were playing baseball, a .540 batting average would get it into Cooperstown. But these are notices telling people they owe money back. So, being correct 54% of the time is truly abject failure.   Julie concluded, “So, we need to file now and get our money now.” That is where I push back. Being right about the problem does not make you right about the solution. Filing early does not protect your future checks from a funding shortfall. Here is how I explain it: “Julie, you’re worried about the possibility of a 22% cut. But under today’s rules, start your retirement benefit at 62 instead of 67 and you have a 100% chance of a 30% cut to your monthly benefit.”  That 30% is not my forecast. It is SSA’s claiming formula. Congress doesn’t even have to hold a vote. You can arrange this particular cut in your pajamas. You are trying to avoid a possible cut by signing up for a certain one. Before we call that playing it safe, let’s count what you’re buying and what you’re giving up. Claiming at 62 buys five more years of checks than waiting until 67. The price is a monthly benefit that starts 30% smaller. I count those earlier checks, along with the savings spent while waiting. We are comparing retirement income over a lifetime, not just two percentages. The choice has to earn its place in the retirement plan. And here is the part the “get it while you can” argument misses: There is no protection from future cuts attached to an early filing date. Under an across-the-board percentage cut, the early claimant takes another reduction from an already smaller check. The person who waited takes the reduction from a larger one. You collected sooner. You did not make yourself immune. Waiting is not doing nothing. Under today’s rules, someone Jeff and Julie’s age receives 70% of their full-retirement-age benefit by starting at 62, compared with 124% at 70. That is more monthly income for the later years of retirement. I want clients to understand what they are surrendering before they surrender it. Jeff asked, “What do you think Congress will do?”  I let Jeff know that Congress has addressed financing problems before. In 1983, it increased revenue and changed benefit rules, including taxing some benefits and gradually raising full retirement age. That history belongs in the conversation. Predicting the next deal does not belong at the center of their retirement plan. With Jeff and Julie, I have compared claiming at 62, full retirement age and 70. I have calculated lifetime income using their longevity estimates, modeled survivor benefits and shown them how Social Security interacts with their other retirement assets. That is what they hired me to do. They didn’t bring me on to nod sympathetically at the same headlines they have already read. Here is what I recommend: Put your fear into the calculation. Test the claiming strategies with smaller future benefits. Count the earlier checks, the withdrawals from savings and the income left to the surviving spouse. When the numbers say wait, I tell them to wait. Fear does not get a veto over the result. Don’t throw away the stronger strategy because collecting now feels better this morning. Social Security has a financing problem. Among the clients sitting across from me, it has become a trust problem, too. I take both seriously. But I am not asking them to trust Congress. I am telling them not to mistake an early check for protection from Congress. Julie deserves an answer, not an echo of her anxiety. Mine is this: Claim because it strengthens your retirement, not because the news frightened you. Don’t let fear file your application. events.title: This Hispanic Heritage Month, our stallout in the Fortune 500 gives me pause
events.summary: For 20 years, I have been taking the same phone call. A fellow chief executive calls me: more often than not a Latina, and more often than not the first one her organization has ever hired. She was hired to change the place. Everyone she met during the interview process was on board with the plan. Then, somewhere around month nine, something shifts. She realizes the assignment she was handed is one the organization was never built to support. She usually thinks that is a verdict on her competence. It is not. It is a gap in what was built around her. When we hire someone to transform an organization, we tend to hand her the role that was designed for the person who came before: the same budget, the same board meeting cadence, the same outline for a standing agenda. We keep all of it in place and ask her to do something the old design was never built to do. Then, when the change hits a roadblock, we look at the leader. Right now, Hispanic Heritage Month is filling programs across the country with firsts. I want to know what got built around them, because in nine months some of them will be calling me. Here is the number that should give us all pause. A record 55 women are running Fortune 500 companies this year , 11% of the list and the highest share in its 72-year history. Not one of them is a Latina. When Priscilla Almodóvar left Fannie Mae last October, the Fortune 500 lost the only Latina chief executive it had. Now, the Latina executives who call me want the job more than anyone else in the running. In Lean In’s study of Latinas in corporate America , 87% said they want to be promoted, against 81% of women overall, and 44% said advancement had become more important to them over the previous two years, against 36% of women overall. My phone is not going to get quieter, either. Of the 186 chief executive departures Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted in August , government and nonprofit organizations accounted for 62, more than any other sector. The shortfall in support begins with managers, often the first advocate anyone has in their career. Thirty-nine percent of Latinas say their manager shows interest in their career advancement, against 46% of white women, and 47% say their manager makes sure they get credit for their work, against 53%. The loss is felt at the very first rung of the corporate ladder. For every 100 men promoted from entry level to manager, 74 Latinas are promoted . By the C-suite, Latinas are 1% of executives, down from just under 5% at entry level — a drop of 78% across a career, the largest of any group in the study. Thirty years ago, John Kotter spent a decade watching more than a hundred companies try to remake themselves, and he found that most of those efforts fell short. He catalogued eight reasons why. Some of them belong to the leader. Others describe conditions no chief executive can build alone: a coalition of senior people genuinely committed to the change, reporting lines and compensation systems that stop rewarding the old way of working, and a board close enough to the transformation to understand what it requires. We are also not measuring the thing we say we want. In Lean In and McKinsey’s 2024 Women in the Workplace study , 78% of managers said more is expected of them than a few years ago, most often around employee well-being, career development and inclusion. Only 37% of companies evaluate their managers on whether they develop anyone. Expectations went up and accountability never followed. I leave every event with 20 business cards from women asking me to be their mentor. Nobody counts that as infrastructure, but it is what fills in when the institution does not. No board ever sets out to sabotage its own leader. Directors are usually volunteers giving hours to an organization they believe in. Their governance training covers how to hire an executive and how to evaluate one, and then it stops. I have been a chief executive five times, and in the best of those transitions, much of the board’s work began before I walked through the door. The boards that got it right did three things. They built a structure for the first year before anyone needed it. In one of those roles, the chair assembled a formal transition committee that met with me throughout my first six months. It arrived with a detailed plan to introduce me to the people who mattered most to the organization and to hand over the donor relationships, so I was never building every connection from scratch. They made the mandate for change their own, and said so out loud. More than once, a board told its stakeholders early and plainly that I had been hired to redesign the business and that the directors stood behind the changes. One chair went further and advocated for me in rooms I was not in, which mattered most in the months when the work got hard. None of them left me to carry the case for change alone. They treated the top of the organization as a partnership. In one transition, my predecessor stepped back from the day-to-day and made himself available for advice whenever I asked. We agreed at the start that the organization’s success would come before either of our egos, and I can still call him on any issue. One chair put the principle to me simply: a great board chair is a partner, not a hammer. Every one of those steps fit inside the budget the organization already had. What made them possible was a board that treated my first year as a design problem instead of a probation period. For 20 years, the question on those calls has been whether the leader was strong enough. The better question, and the one I want us to ask, is what we built around her. When I got through that door, I took off my chancla and wedged it in the frame. My job was to keep it open for everybody else. events.title: I used Meta's Muse to help my son prep for an astronomy quiz. He aced it.
events.summary: Franco Lopez Franco Lopez asked Meta's Muse AI agent to help his son prepare for an astronomy quiz. Muse made him digital flashcards, a practice quiz, and a podcast for the ride to school. Lopez's son aced the quiz. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Franco Lopez, a 53-year-old from Miami who works in insurance. Business Insider confirmed his son's perfect quiz score. This essay has been edited for length and clarity. I got Muse a couple of weeks ago. I have been hopping on every AI since the very beginning. I talk about it all day, and am completely overwhelmed and excited. I was playing with Grok Bot a lot and loving it. Then I saw Muse, I downloaded it, I tried it, and it felt different. It seemed like a better all-around product, so I ended up canceling my Grok subscription, just like I did with Claude and ChatGPT before that. Now, I'm full-time on Muse and sharing it with everyone I know. I'm a father of four kids, and two of them go to school. Schools email you a lot on a daily basis. I'll get sometimes 30 emails combined between the two schools: homework, events, and payments due. It's a nightmare to keep up with. I have Muse recognizing all of the emails coming in and creating a digest posted into my "Family Operations" Slack channel. I have a daily digest for both of my kids by name, so I know what uniform they have to wear that day, if any homework is due, and I'm on top of it. I shared it with my wife and gave her access to the Slack channel. She loves it as well. When it doesn't work for us, we just make modifications. Sometimes it gets a little too verbose. We say, "Can you trim it down a little bit?" I've done that with the soccer team . I have a Slack channel that all the parents have access to, so we all have one page to review what the coach said, what color shirt to wear on Saturday, how much to bring for the ref fees, all that stuff. I stopped reading emails. I have robots that read emails for me. How Muse helped my son prep for his quiz My wife delegated this one assignment. She said, "I need you to get on this science vocabulary quiz," and handed me this wrinkled-up page. I'm reinforcing something my 10-year-old has already looked at a thousand times. All the fun has already been squeezed out. Lopez's son had to memorize astronomy terms from a crumpled worksheet. Franco Lopez I said to Muse, "What can you do to help him understand this? Can you create some kind of quiz?" I had done this homework experiment with Claude back in the day. I expected something similar: it was very blocky, very straightforward. I got something very different. Muse's was very bubbly and colorful. It had his name on it and an encouraging message. It absorbed that the material was about astronomy, and it added rocket decorations. It was two tabs: the typical flashcard experience, and then a multiple-choice quiz. In the end, it graded him and gave him the opportunity to do it again. The second time, he got an 80 or 90%. He'd done well, and it was getting late anyway, because it was soccer night. Muse made Franco Lopez's son flashcards and a multiple-choice quiz. Franco Lopez The next morning, the day of the quiz, I asked, "What else can we do to reinforce learning?" Muse created a podcast . It was seven minutes, a perfect length, and he was amazed. It caught his attention. It covered all the material with fun and tips to remember it. I finished it, and I prayed that he did well. Mom picked him up that day, and he didn't say anything to me. Later on that day, I heard from mom that he aced it. He got 100. I went up to him and said, "Dude, you didn't tell me you aced it." He goes, "Oh, yeah," like it wasn't a big deal. He had never gotten a 100, not because he can't, but because he hasn't been engaged. I'm feeling confident about AI and education Kids are watching really great content , made by people who are experts at retaining your attention. If that teacher is slightly boring, the kid is going to tune them out. Teachers don't stand a chance unless they build some level of personality. I don't think the classroom piece is going to be successful. I think AI-to-human learning will be cheaper and faster. I see everything changing. I'm in a soccer team with a bunch of parents, and I have conversations with people who have never even opened AI. They're living in a completely different reality. I've tried to break the news, but it's really a subject that only a few of us are handling right now. I don't think there's such a thing as too much AI in parenting . I think there's a wrong use and a right use. My goal is to help him learn how to do it, not give him the answer. I can use it every day and twice on Sunday, as long as I use it to empower him. You don't have to stop doing what you're doing what you're doing as a parent to deal with AI. You can continue to be the parent you need to be. You're just getting some help. You're offloading. You're getting employees. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Korean boffins use oxygen to stop crystals forming in the wrong places, aiming to get tech to commercial sector by 2030 TSMC taps GlobalFoundries to bolster US silicon interposer production in $2B deal 2 days ago Altman-backed Volantis reveals plan to vault the memory wall by baking photonics into AI accelerators 5 days ago America is planning more AI datacenters than its chip supply can fill 11 days ago Marvell pushes GlobalFoundries to light up wafer production 23 days ago ASML and TSMC want bigger masks for smaller chips September 8, 2026 Researchers have demonstrated a way to control where 2D semiconductor crystals begin growing, potentially addressing an obstacle to manufacturing next-generation chips at scale, according to a study published in Nature. The paper, " Spatially deterministic nucleation of 2D semiconductors by etching flux ," was authored by a team including researchers at KAIST and South Korean startup TDS Innovation and published on October 7. The technique uses an etching flux to suppress the formation of new crystals everywhere within each patterned growth region except at its geometric center. Two-dimensional materials are atomically thin rather than literally two-dimensional. Graphene, perhaps the best-known example, is a single layer of carbon atoms, but its lack of an intrinsic band gap makes it unsuitable for conventional switching transistors. Monolayers of some transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), do have a band gap and are being investigated as materials for future transistors and other nanoscale devices. When grown on a wafer, however, 2D semiconductor crystals typically start forming at random points, or "nucleation events occur stochastically at random sites within the growth region," as the paper puts it. This means that multiple crystals form, and as they grow and meet, they create boundaries between them that degrade electrical performance and make devices less uniform. To encourage a single crystal to form in each patterned region, the researchers developed what they call an etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation (EF-SCN) process. Oxygen released from an oxide barrier creates a lateral etching flux that suppresses nucleation except at the pattern's geometric center. The researchers used the process to build working field-effect transistors (FETs), the basic building blocks of modern chips. They reported higher charge-carrier mobility – a measure of how readily charge moves through the material – than previously reported for selectively grown MoS₂ transistors. In a separate test across a two-centimeter substrate, the process produced single crystals at 397 of 400 patterned sites – a yield of 99.3 percent. That is promising for scaling up, although it is not yet a demonstration of commercial chip production. Paper co-author Kibum Kang is co-CEO of TDS Innovation, which develops equipment and materials for 2D semiconductor devices. The firm says stacking 2D semiconductor devices on silicon chips could bring logic and memory closer together, fitting more functions into a given area and reducing the time and energy spent moving data between them. Two-dimensional semiconductor materials are also being investigated for CFETs (complementary field-effect transistors), which stack n-type and p-type transistors vertically rather than placing them side by side. This kind of 3D stacking has been shown off by IBM and Intel . "Building on this ability to control where crystal growth begins, we will form high-quality 2D single crystals uniformly where we want them and develop it into a next-generation semiconductor process that brings logic and memory closer together," Kang states. The paper doesn't say when we can expect to see 2D semiconductors made this way in production chips, TDS's Jony Jung told us: "We are aiming to enable commercial use of 2D semiconductors around 2030.

events.title: Musk vows affordable Starlink in India days before Ambani’s record Jio IPO
events.summary: Elon Musk has previously accused India of stalling Starlink’s entrance into the country’s market. Musk said Starlink will be priced affordably in India to challenge Reliance Jio, as Jio’s parent prepares for India’s biggest-ever IPO. He said competition would help Indian users, while Ambani’s profits would fall. He did not give prices, but noted India’s data costs are already very low. Musk accused Modi’s government and Ambani of delaying Starlink’s entry. India denied bias, saying Starlink and Jio satellite ventures still await final security clearance. BENGALURU, India – Elon Musk said he would price Starlink’s satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani’s low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio’s parent launches India’s largest-ever initial public offering. Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of US$106 billion ( S$135.62 billion ) in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink , Jio’s own satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch. Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio in India, and the one Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle local telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the US. Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about eight cents per gigabyte, among the lowest in the world. “Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,” he said in a post on his social media platform X on Oct 10 . “The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” Musk added. The billionaire’s remarks were the latest in a series of X posts where he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Ambani of stalling Starlink’s entry into one of the world’s biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio . The posts have marked a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi. India’s government has denied any bias in its approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch, including Starlink’s and Jio’s, are all awaiting final security clearance. Late on Oct 9 , Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Reliance has not responded to requests for comment on Musk’s remarks. REUTERS

events.title: Warren Buffett watches YouTube, David Solomon DJs, and this former NFL coach spent 12 years playing Minecraft
events.summary: Most professional coaches and athletes know they only get better with each loss. The purported GOAT of basketball, Michael Jordan, even said so in a famous 1997 Nike commercial: “I’ve failed over and over and over again in my life” and that’s why he’s so successful.  Sports professionals expect some losses, and expect to learn from them. Well, that’s too bad for Mike Tomlin, he’ll never know. During his 19 years at the helm of the Pittsburgh Steelers, he never had a losing season. In fact, he even brought home a Super Bowl trophy. But perhaps the most surprising part of that run, the NFL coach recently revealed, was that he was also building an elaborate city in Minecraft . The 54-year-old, who reportedly earned a $16 million salary in 2025, launched his own YouTube channel last week, showing off the sprawling virtual city. His first episode , titled “ROOFTOPS, PENTHOUSES, AND URBAN LIVING,” has already racked up more than 3.4 million views. In it, Tomlin takes viewers through a virtual metropolis complete with high-rise apartments, a speakeasy, an aquarium, and a baseball stadium. “I really got obsessed with rooftop penthouses,” Tomlin said in the video which spread across social media platforms.  Reactions, however, ranged from pure fascination and respect for his 12-year project to critics questioning whether Tomlin, who parted ways with the Steelers in January of this year, had devoted too much time to his virtual city. The debate highlighted the tricky balance between work and leisure, particularly for people in demanding careers: Hobbies can become distractions, but they can also provide a much-needed break from professional pressures. He holds the NFL record for the longest unbroken winning-season streak. But that doesn’t seem enough for his critics, who argue that’s why the Steelers can’t beat the Patriots. “He’s building worlds, but he ain’t making plays for me,” said former Steelers running back Le’Veon Bell. Tomlin isn’t the only high-profile figure with an unexpected way to unwind. From investor Warren Buffett watching YouTube to Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon DJing, many top leaders have adopted pastimes that let them step away from work—and may even help them perform better when they return. Hobbies like Minecraft can help people recover from work stress, expert says Charles Calderwood , director of the Work Stress and Recovery Lab at Virginia Tech University, told Fortune that engaging in hobbies and other activities outside of work can help people recover from job-related stress, benefiting their overall health and well-being. That recovery can be particularly important for people in demanding jobs with unpredictable schedules, such as NFL coaches.  “As you face more demands and are more stressed out, you need recovery more, but you’re less able to get it,” Calderwood said. “It can create this self-perpetuating cycle over time, where you just become more and more drained, and maybe that leads to burnout or diminished job performance.” Still, not every activity that appears productive or beneficial necessarily helps people recover. Many executives, such as the CEOs of Starbucks and Chipotle for example , tout early-morning work routines as a key to their success. But Calderwood cautioned that such habits can come at a cost if they cut into the time people need to recharge—or even cause injury. For Tomlin’s part, he said he originally became interested in the sandbox game not necessarily as an escape from the competitive football season but because he wanted to connect with his then-teenage sons. “I got interested because I just was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin said earlier this month on Late Night with Seth Meyers. As his sons moved on to high school and college, they spent less time playing, but Tomlin found himself spending more. “I kind of stumbled into the therapeutic component of it,” he added. Tomlin declined Fortune’s request for comment. From Warren Buffett to David Solomon, many top business leaders aren’t afraid to admit they need to escape from business  Tomlin also suggested that his hobby isn’t necessarily unusual. And he has a point: Some of the world’s most successful people have their own ways of unwinding that have little to do with their day jobs. Billionaire investor Warren Buffett , for example, spends his evenings watching YouTube on his television, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. His viewing has little to do with finance, ranging from 1950s commercials to Uzbekistan’s version of America’s Got Talent. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, has long been an avid video game player. The billionaire has logged on to games such as Path of Exile 2 , Diablo IV , and Elden Ring , sometimes livestreaming his sessions. Just this week, he posted about World of Warcraft on X. But Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon has been among the most vocal about his hobby—DJing—and the benefits it brings him both personally and professionally. The banking chief, whose total compensation reached $47 million in 2025, has built an audience of over 250,000 monthly listeners on Spotify . “When I’m doing this, [DJing], I am a 100% present, my mind is 100% clear,” he said in a 2018 interview with PayPal CEO Dan Schulman. “And I actually find that after doing it, the next day, I’ve got room to think about and make decisions about other things.” Solomon stepped back from performing at public events in 2023, citing the media attention surrounding his DJ career became a distraction. He has also spoken about how hobbies can open the door to new connections and experiences beyond the workplace. “One of the great things about passions and hobbies and interests is you wind up doing them or meeting people you know through those endeavors and that enriches your life,” he continued. Tomlin, meanwhile, has already found a community of his own among millions of Minecraft fans, many of whom have praised his commitment to the project. “This is my Super Bowl,” one top commenter wrote on his video. events.title: Saudi Arabia presses on with global energy summit after deadly Riyadh airport attack
events.summary: Saudi Arabia pressed ahead with a major gathering of global energy ministers and industry executives on Sunday, hours after an attack by Yemen's Houthis on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and injured 309. The International Energy Forum's 17th ministerial meeting, hosted by Saudi Arabia and co-hosted by Italy and Nigeria, is being held alongside the WPC Energy Congress, bringing together policymakers and industry leaders. Media access to the ministerial meeting will be restricted, with only journalists invited directly by the IEF permitted to cover the opening remarks, according to a Saudi Energy Ministry spokeswoman. “As you are aware, the ministerial plenary will be held behind closed doors,” she said. No live broadcast pool arrangements were in place, she added. The event is proceeding despite mounting security concerns after repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport , which have forced airlines to cancel flights and complicated travel arrangements for delegates. Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said on Friday that he would participate in the IEF meeting by video link rather than travel to Riyadh. The WPC Energy Congress, which runs from Sunday until Thursday, is also proceeding as scheduled. Organisers have directed delegates to alternative routes into the Saudi capital, including by road from Dammam on the kingdom's east coast. A projectile landed near King Fahd Airport in Dammam on Saturday, a representative for the Saudi coalition said. Saturday's strike was the third on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in a week and the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, which killed four Saudis and eight foreign citizens, including one from the US. Two attacks on the airport this week killed four people and caused extensive damage to a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac. The latest strike caused widespread disruption to aviation, with about 260 flights cancelled and another 219 delayed on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The attacks have heightened security concerns, as Saudi Arabia seeks to maintain its calendar of high-profile international gatherings despite the war's growing regional spillover. Riyadh is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative from October 26 to 29, with organisers saying the event will proceed as planned, with additional security arrangements put in place.

events.title: ‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacular
events.summary: Welcome to Halloweenmas, weeks of themed fun and gifts – from costume parties to decorating trees – without the stress, rules or cost of Christmas The tree is up, the wreath is hanging on the front door and you’ve just opened your advent calendar . All told, it’s beginning to feel a lot like … Halloween . If it sounds like the stuff of nightmares then that’s the point: Britons are increasingly decorating their homes with ghoulish versions of Christmas traditions. Think of it as Halloweenmas. “What was traditionally a single-night celebration has turned into a month-long event mirroring many of Christmas’s traditions, but without the same level of expectation,” said Charlotte Broadbent, the UK general manager for the online wholesale platform Faire. Analysis of thousands of sales transactions on the platform revealed a huge rise in the number of Halloweenmas products available – up more than 500% in the past four years, from 425 in 2021 to 2,632 in 2025. The biggest areas of growth are trees, wreaths and ornaments. According to the budget retailer Wilko, Halloween trees are one of the biggest decorating trends of 2026. It said sales of artificial trees were 200% higher in September than a year ago. “There really aren’t any rules with a Halloween tree,” says Wilko. “You can go all-out or keep it simple with a smaller tree and a few spooky accessories.” The lack of rules is clear from social media, where the looks span student party – black tinsel tree shaped like a witch’s hat – to child-friendly cuteness. The arts and crafts retailer Hobbycraft’s website offers “five ways to decorate a twig tree” that include DIY spiderwebs made out of lolly sticks and felt pumpkins. Libby Ewart, who runs the online partyware and gift retailer The Box Party, has bought 40% more stock this year. “Houses are decorated earlier and with way more thought than before,” she said. “Also, this year it falls on a Saturday, so there has never been a better excuse for a party.” Emily Viberg, a senior retail analyst at the research group Mintel, said Halloween was “no longer just about costumes and sweets, it’s about a full season of engagement, gifting and themed activities”. Mintel’s research shows young Britons, in particular, see it as an opportunity to express themselves and experiment with fashion and makeup, with 16- to 34-year-olds over-indexing in purchases of fancy dress, cosmetics and decorations. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Consumers are increasingly buying into the atmosphere and social moments Halloween creates,” Viberg said. “Younger adults are at the heart of this shift, transforming Halloween from a one-night celebration into a broader season of self-expression and experience-led spending.” Viberg said social media had accelerated this shift, with 40% of Halloween buyers using the platforms to buy products directly. “Viral costume trends, makeup tutorials, home decor inspiration and content tapping into popular culture are shaping consumer spending and helping to extend the season well beyond October,” she said. While some people might complain it is all over the top, Broadbent said: “What we’re seeing is people investing into Halloween as a reason to share quality time together ahead of Christmas, with lots of fun and creativity at its heart and without the need to spend big.”

events.title: Charities and businesses wrestle with diesel cost
events.summary: Cancer charity Daft as a Brush's Scott Jobson said funds raised by donations were being lost at the pump Charities and businesses across the North East have said they are struggling with the rising cost of diesel. The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group . Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide. The North East cancer charity Daft as a Brush said it could no longer afford to upgrade its diesel vehicles to electric as they grappled with filling them up, whilst Teesside Minibus Hire said soaring prices were "not sustainable". Daft as a Brush, which provides cancer patients with transport to their hospital appointments, said it was shelling out £15,000 a month on diesel - £5,000 more than last year. The Newcastle-based charity - which drives 600,000 miles every year in its 30 vans - said it had planned on replacing them with electric vehicles, but now could not afford to because the money was being swallowed up at the pump. Volunteer driver Davey Hall said: "Before the big hikes, we used to maybe fill up and it would take £40-45. "Last week, it was £94 to fill the tank from half full." Head of income generation Scott Jobson said the money was being taken from funds raised by donations, and they were not eligible for any kind of discount. "At the pump, what you see is what we pay," he said. "It stunts our growth and development." In Middlesbrough, Teesside Minibus Hire director Billy Johnson said they often signed contracts with schools and businesses which could span multiple years - and were based on the cost of fuel when they were written. "We're not running at a loss yet, but we're running close it to it not being worthwhile or sustainable," he said. Johnson said they were having to pass the cost on to customers using services such as day hires, but because those customers were struggling with inflation themselves, they were not always prepared to pay the increased price. Instead, people were turning towards cheaper, unlicensed hire services which did not pay the same overheads, he said. Asked whether the business could survive if fuel prices did not drop, he said: "Long term, probably not." In May , the government announced it would extend a fuel duty (tax) freeze until the end of the year. It caps the tax at 5p per litre for petrol and diesel, and was introduced by the previous Conservative government after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine pushed prices up in 2022. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages over the Iran War and has said the country has a "diverse and resilient supply". events.title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
events.summary: Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election. Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week. The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell , but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come . The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills , a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000. Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.” Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party , though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit. Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.” Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England. The party’s U-turn on environmental issues and net zero was contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression. “Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.” While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, which resolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power . Although the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Paul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “The Green party has taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes. “With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.” The battle between the Green party and the Labour party in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds. Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.” At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced a publicly owned body to invest in the energy grid , alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades.

events.title: AI may change the price of your Big Mac and groceries — what this means for shoppers
events.summary: Supermarkets and fast food giants are increasingly using artificial intelligence to digitize their operations. Some have been accused of using so-called "dynamic pricing" to set rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. Experts told CNBC that this could raise the risk of shoppers facing more individualized prices. Fast-food giants and supermarkets are rolling out a range of AI tools that could affect the prices shoppers pay, but experts warn the spread of data-driven tools could make personalized pricing easier to deploy. Just this week, a federal antitrust lawsuit filed against McDonald's alleged the fast food giant uses an AI-powered "pricing engine" to set menu prices across U.S. locations and overcharge customers for Big Macs and fries. McDonald's has denied that it's using AI to determine what individual customers are willing to pay and said it provides its franchisees with "tools, resources, research and recommendations to help them make informed decisions." Even so, food businesses globally are increasingly digitizing operations with AI. Earlier this year, American grocery chain Kroger said it's using an AI platform called FlashFood to mark down perishables nearing the end of their shelf life and marketing them to shoppers via an app. Meanwhile, electronic shelf labels (ESLs), which display the price of items in store on digital screens, are becoming increasingly popular at supermarkets like Kroger, Amazon Fresh, Walmart , and Whole Foods. The technology is also gaining traction among U.K. supermarkets such as Tesco , Morrisons, and Asda. More recently, global financial platform Revolut trialed facial recognition checkout in select coffee shops, allowing customers to pay with just a glance. CNBC reached out to Amazon Fresh, Whole Foods, Tesco, Morrisons, Asda and Revolut for comment on the use of AI but didn't immediately hear back. As AI use becomes normalized among retailers, experts warn that this could lead to more dynamic pricing, which refers to frequent, rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. "Dynamic pricing means changing prices in response to changing market conditions, such as demand, timing, capacity or competitors' prices," Miroslava Marinova, a senior lecturer of commercial law at the University of East London, told CNBC. "It is not new. Airlines, hotels, and ride-hailing services have used it for years." Bank of England economists Clare Lombardelli and Rupal Patel said in April that more sophisticated technology is leading to prices changing more frequently and also becoming more individualized, which could see more firms charging "as close to the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good or service," which they defined as "perfect price discrimination." These conditions could make it harder for statisticians to "measure and interpret" month-to-month inflation data, as the consumer price index is based on a representative sample of prices for shoppers. "That works well when prices mostly move slowly and uniformly. But when prices shift continually – and differently for each shopper – the idea of a 'representative' price becomes strained," the BOE economists added. While dynamic pricing has been in play for a long time, the BOE economists and Marinova noted that AI tools such as ESLs and facial recognition checkout are changing the amount of information that companies can collect on consumers, from transaction histories to browsing behavior, location, and purchasing patterns. On Wednesday, U.K. supermarket chain Sainsbury's released "SmartLists," an AI feature that helps customers create shopping lists and find products just by uploading pictures of what they need or by typing out meal ideas. "This is also why the traditional distinction between dynamic and personalised pricing is becoming less clear in practice," Marinova explained. "Dynamic pricing responds primarily to market conditions, whereas personalised pricing uses information about the consumer to estimate willingness to pay." As companies use both pricing systems, it raises questions around whether customer information is being used to determine the prices consumers see. "As retailers combine market-level information with increasingly detailed consumer data, the boundary between dynamic and personalised pricing becomes thinner," Marinova added. Walmart and Kroger have publicly insisted in recent years that they do not use dynamic or surge pricing to set individualized prices for customers, but have instead used tools to streamline operations. Several U.S. states are moving to curb data-driven pricing. New York requires most businesses using customers’ personal data to set prices to disclose it clearly.

events.title: UAE IPOs and credit markets primed for growth once war ends, Morgan Stanley executive says
events.summary: The UAE is expected to see a rebound in initial public offerings once the US-Iran conflict ends, and the country’s credit market is also set to boom, according to a senior Morgan Stanley executive. While there have been no listings in the UAE so far this year, the investment bank is bullish about the capital market prospects despite the uncertainty caused by the war. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. “I think long term, as the conflicts get resolved or hits some level of stabilisation, you will definitely see a rebound in the IPO marketplace in the UAE,” Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley told The National . “So, we are investing in and have high confidence in that. And we've been so impressed with the leadership on the sort of financial infrastructure in the country all the way around,” he said. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased uncertainty across the Middle East. After the US-Israeli bombing of Iran and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on its Arab neighbours halted in early April, peace in the region has teetered on a fragile ceasefire. A report from the World Bank released last week said Gulf economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. While the International Monetary Fund also anticipates that the Gulf economy will contract this year, the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping, the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said. "I think it [the war] clearly creates a slightly higher and hopefully temporary risk premium in the region, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest," Mr Simkowitz said. The investment bank's commitment to the region is "as strong as it's ever been". "We continue to be thinking about how to invest in growth. Our corporate clients, FDI clients, are still very focused on the demographics in the region, the potential for GDP growth, the diversification that is coming in the marketplace,” he added. There is extreme resilience that has been built in the region, the Morgan Stanley executive said. “There is also real capital strength in the region, and so as they need to either rebuild or redirect energy infrastructure, for example, there is the capability to do so. And … there is international capital ready to help do that,” he explained. Morgan Stanley, which is headquartered in the US and has more than $10 trillion in assets, has been present in the region for the past 20 years. It also opened a new office in Abu Dhabi in 2024. [The war] creates a higher and temporary risk premium, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley The bank currently has well over 100 employees in the region and it plans to expand its operations further. "We're going to stay very committed to growing that. I think wealth and asset management will be a part of that,” Mr Simkowitz said. The company's current pipeline of deals in the region is still active, he said. "Some element is on pause, and I think it would change a little bit in that people will have to re-underwrite maybe some of their resiliency supply chain and diversification. But I would argue most of it that was on is underway." Credit market boom The Morgan Stanley executive is also bullish about growth in credit markets in the UAE and across the region, with global trends also positive. Credit markets cover bonds, government debt, private credit and bank loans. Globally, asset managers and owners, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, are playing a key role in the credit market, he said. “The credit market has become more important because we're entering into a period where high capex manufacturing is back ... and in that context, you need to spend money, and you need to bridge this ‘build to revenue, build to profitability’ gap … and it is not just banks or governments.” Economic tailwinds from the AI buildout and "surprisingly enduring demand" have bolstered credit conditions in many major economies this year, S&P Global Ratings said in a report this month. But the positive momentum of overall credit stability seen over the past few years will become more difficult to sustain, it said. Heading into the fourth quarter, "risks are building amid the sharp rise in benchmark borrowing costs, including yields on government debt, as investors bet that major central banks have a complex challenge in their fight against inflation", the ratings agency said. In the UAE and the Gulf, the credit market “is coming, and I think that's encouraging”, Mr Simkowitz said. Gulf debt capital markets reached $1.2 trillion outstanding at the end of the first half of this year, according to Fitch Ratings. Even in mature markets like the US, the credit market is evolving and building, Mr Simkowitz said, adding that the growth of a fixed income market or a bond market is "incredibly important”. “Over the last several years, the conversations we've had throughout the Gulf with finance ministries, stock exchanges, and other leadership … has been skewing more and more towards bond markets and credit markets, as we've had some great success with ADX [Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange] and with other exchanges in the Gulf around equities, it's a natural progression,” he said. More than $100 billion has been raised in debt markets in the region this year, he said. "That is really important to continue to satisfy the growth, diversification and resiliency ambitions, it can't all be done with equity, and so you need some element of credit and bond markets.” AI, midterms and outlook The big economic theme is AI, which is "incredibly transformational", Mr Simkowitz said. "It's going to require a lot of capital today to drive an immense amount of productivity in the future. "Certainly, the UAE has been at the centre of that. As relative to GDP or even wealth or market cap, the UAE is one of the most important AI players in the world." A recent report by Bain found that the AI industry needs to earn $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed for data centres. events.title: Mary Chia admits disclosure lapses over CPF arrears at four subsidiaries after SGX queries
events.summary: Mary Chia Holdings has admitted that it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries. Mary Chia admitted it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court cases at four subsidiaries. SGX RegCo queried the Sept 11 filing, and the group blamed weak internal checks. The CPF Board revised total arrears to $103,727, down from about $153,000. The company said its chief executive knew of the notices, while independent directors learnt later. Mary Chia is reviewing reporting controls and plans instalment payments for the debts. The disclosure issue comes as it faces loan disputes, weak cash flow, and a planned $1 million share issue. SINGAPORE – Cash-strapped beauty and wellness group Mary Chia Holdings has admitted that it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries, despite its chief executive being aware of the court notices earlier on. The admission came in an Oct 9 response to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo), which questioned why the four subsidiaries and their involvement in court proceedings were not disclosed in the company’s Sept 11 announcement, and when the company first became aware of these matters. Mary Chia’s Sept 11 announcement disclosed $50,208 in outstanding CPF contributions at one subsidiary but omitted arrears and court proceedings involving four others. All five subsidiaries’ cases had already been heard together on Sept 10, and the CEO knew of their court notices. The Catalist-listed company attributed this omission to shortcomings in its internal information consolidation and disclosure assessment processes, saying it failed to sufficiently consolidate information across its human resources, finance and management functions when preparing its Sept 11 announcement. The group said its earlier disclosure assessment had focused primarily on Mary Chia Beauty & Slimming Specialist, whose CPF arrears and court appearance were the subject of SGX RegCo’s initial query. It said it had not undertaken a comprehensive assessment of similar issues involving other group entities, resulting in the omission of four other subsidiaries from the announcement. These were Masego, Organica International Holdings, Spa Menu and Urban Homme Face & Body Studio for Men. Mary Chia also revealed that the outstanding CPF contributions across the five subsidiaries had been revised to $103,727 as at Oct 9, down from approximately $153,000 stated during a court hearing a day earlier. The revised figure was provided by the CPF Board following a reconciliation of outstanding contributions, taking into account payments made by the subsidiaries towards their arrears. The latest filing also shed light on when the group’s management and independent directors became aware of the CPF issues. Mary Chia said its CEO Ho Yow Ping and the group’s human resources manager were aware of the respective notices to attend court upon receiving them. Ho also attended an interview with the CPF Board on July 22 concerning the outstanding contributions of the five subsidiaries. The group’s independent directors, meanwhile, first became aware of CPF contribution discrepancies within the group at an internal audit meeting on May 25. At that meeting, management informed them of the discrepancies uncovered through an internal review, rectification reports submitted to the CPF Board and efforts to settle the arrears. However, the court notices and related proceedings were not brought to their attention. Mary Chia said its two current independent directors, Chay Yiowmin and Foo Say Tun, learnt of the outstanding contributions and court proceedings involving the four other subsidiaries only on Oct 8, when management updated the board following that day’s hearing. The company disclosed that nine separate notices to attend court had been issued by the CPF Board across the five subsidiaries. Although the matters were initially handled separately, the CPF Board requested in August that the court mentions be consolidated. All five companies subsequently appeared together in court on Sept 10 and Oct 8, with their cases adjourned to Nov 12. According to the CPF Board’s updated computation provided on Oct 9, Mary Chia Beauty & Slimming Specialist owed the largest amount, at $52,266, for outstanding contributions covering November 2025 to May. Organica International Holdings owed $25,248 for contributions covering November 2025 to May 2026, while Masego had $11,341 outstanding for the period from November 2025 to April. Urban Homme Face & Body Studio for Men owed $9,847 for contributions covering September 2025 to March, while Spa Menu had $5,025 outstanding for February. The periods refer only to months for which CPF contributions remain unpaid, rather than every month within the stated date ranges. The revised aggregate amount of $103,727 excludes late-payment interest and composition sums.

events.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
events.summary: UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned. Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”. “Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said. Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt. Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East. The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures. But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs. “What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said. “We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.” Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs. De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9%. That is really, really high.” He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring. “For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.” His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs. It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8% since 2019, and wider public spending by 2%. Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.” Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring. Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.” De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action. “We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said. He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields. But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. And that coordinated policy for developing countries cannot just be, ‘you are at the end of the line and we’ll see what happens’.” He declined to say what the specific response should be, but stressed that it should create “time and space” for developing countries to carry out much-needed changes. During the Covid crisis, G20 nations implemented a temporary standstill on debt repayments for developing countries. De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.
