events.title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
events.summary: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference. The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October. Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote. “The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028. “These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.” In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election. Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023. He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits. Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.

events.title: Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported. The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin. Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday. Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation. Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by phone after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan. Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end. The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump. Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call. Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said. The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday. Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports. A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard. The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast. An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged." Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies. Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

events.title: Pokémon card values are soaring. What collectors should know before buying or selling
events.summary: What is driving interest? Pokémon and other trading-card games are drawing strong collector demand, while sources say high sports-card prices are pushing some buyers toward non-sports cards. What determines value? Authenticity, condition, graded population, liquidity and verified transaction history can sharply affect what a card sells for. What is the biggest risk? Counterfeits are rising, especially in Pokémon submissions, making authentication and careful price research critical before buying. In 2022, a rare Topps 1952 Mickey Mantle baseball card — one of sports-card collectors' holiest grails — sold for $12.6 million. Wow, you say, that's a lot of dough for a thin piece of cardboard, slab of bubblegum not included. Well, what do you say about a 1998 Pikachu Illustrator Pokémon card going for $16.5 million earlier this year? If you're pro wrestler and social media influencer Logan Paul, seller of the item, you say, Not a bad return on the $5.3 million (plus a trade) I paid for it in 2021. Those are extreme examples, but a vivid illustration of how TCGs — shorthand for competitive trading card games, led by Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh! — are encroaching on an over-saturated sports-card market as an enticing investment opportunity. Throw in vintage and modern-day non-sports trading cards, depicting historical events and fictional characters ranging from the Civil War to Luke Skywalker, and it's a whole new ballgame. The record $16.5 million Pokémon card sale is drawing fresh attention to a collectibles market where grading, scarcity and authentication can determine whether a card is worth dollars or hundreds of thousands. "It is one of our fastest-growing categories that we've seen and one of the largest contributors to [our] growth over the last number of quarters," said Adam Ireland, vice president and general manager of collectibles at online marketplace eBay , which also provides authentication and price guides for TCGs and non-sports cards. "From an investment point of view, you start with Pokémon," he said. "It was the most searchable term within the eBay collectibles environment through the first half of the year." Heritage Auctions, which deals in art, jewelry, coins and many other collectibles, launched a dedicated TCG department six years ago. "Now it's a $50-million category," said executive vice president Joe Maddalena. "That's just TCGs. I'm not talking about Star Wars and any of that stuff," he said, though he added that non-sports stuff contributed around $10 million to Heritage's overall sales in 2025, which topped $2.1 billion. While buyers can find myriad non-sports cards for less than $10 — almost like investing in penny stocks in hopes of eventually striking gold — Maddalena and Ireland cited some eye-popping sales on their respective platforms. A first-edition Pokémon Charizard card worth $20,000 pre-Covid is now valued by Heritage at $500,000. A Tyler the Great Warrior Yu-Gi-Oh! card shattered records when it was auctioned on eBay for $311,211, while Magic's Black Lotus card has gone for $500,000 on the site. Heritage sold a 1977 Luke Skywalker card for $687,500 in May. Whereas collectability, value and investability of sports cards can rise and fall on the real-world performance of athletes, both trading-card genres share common factors. For instance, rookie cards of superstar athletes are highly coveted; the non-sports counterpart is referred to as first appearance. Especially critical are the authenticity, physical condition, total graded population, liquidity and pricing of specific cards, criteria determined by professional grading services such as PSA and CGC Cards. How cards are graded for monetary value PSA (Professional Sports Authenticator), founded in 1991, is the most recognizable grading service. Its process begins when a trained grader examines a card to verify its originality or genuineness, then assesses the quality and condition of the card using PSA's grading scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most pristine, aka gem mint. There generally are very limited populations of PSA 10s of highly sought-after cards, thus their astronomical values. PSA has been grading non-sports cards since its inception, "but with more people viewing it as a potential asset class or thing they want to potentially invest in or speculate in, you're seeing more demand for grading services in the last seven years," said PSA president Ryan Hoge. Indeed, PSA graded more than 19 million cards in 2025, up from two million in 2020. The company had already graded more than eight million cards as of last May, with output from January through April up 39% year-over-year. Much of that uptick, Hoge said, is attributable to TCGs. "Collectively, TCGs [account for] 50% of our current business, more than all the sports cards combined.

events.title: I work hard to stay close to my friends. A researcher says it’s good for my well-being—and these 3 habits can help
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships Social isolation can inhibit success: ‘You need to make time for people' Psychology and Relationships What we lose when kids can't connect, IRL Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Psychology and Relationships 2 red flags of a big ego and 5 signs someone is truly secure: ‘It’s easy to get hoodwinked,’ says psychologist How to Talk to People I've studied friendship for 10 years: 4 questions to move beyond small talk Not to brag, but without realizing it, I've become a model friend — someone my loved ones admire for how well I maintain my relationships . At least, so they tell me. Last month, my closest friend asked me for pointers on how to stay connected to her community while balancing work, well-being and everything else in her life. It's no easy feat. Loneliness levels in the U.S. are high, and instead of turning to each other, many people reach for their tech devices , found an American Psychiatric Association poll published on May 12. Eight percent of Americans report having zero close friends, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey of about 5,000 U.S. adults. Some businesses now offer to facilitate the friendship process, offering summer camps for adults or guidance from friendship coaches that can sometimes cost thousands of dollars. And when you do form friendships, you could grow apart for a number of reasons, says Jessica D. Ayers , an assistant professor of psychological science at Boise State University: classic ones like moving to a different state for a new job or being in different stages of life, or newer ones like trying to keep up with each other on social media and forgetting to keep in touch outside of your smartphones. Especially if your friends have busy lives or don't often reach out to make plans, putting in the work to stay in touch may seem like a fundamentally selfless gesture. In fact, making the effort to maintain friendships can benefit you too, says Ayers, who researches the science of friendship and how to maintain connections. Staying in touch with friends can improve well-being , lower levels of depression and loneliness , decrease anxiety, and even "increase our chances of survival after things like major surgery ," she says. The benefit is mutual for both parties, Ayers says, especially in "long-lasting and sustained relationships." And a high degree of social fitness contributes to a longer, healthier and more fulfilled life , according to an ongoing 88-year-old Harvard University happiness study. Put simply, your friendships can help you succeed. Staying in touch can require a lot of hard work, at least on paper. I didn't fully realize this until I considered just how many strategies I have for keeping in contact with my community. I set up multiple one-on-one hangouts per month with a rotating cast of friends, clear time in my calendar to be present for my loved ones' birthday celebrations and stay up-to-date in five-plus group chats with friends and family. In a sense, I was trained to do this: I have five siblings, and growing up in our household, showing up for each other was a non-negotiable. But there's more to it. Whenever a friend crosses my mind, I reach out to them , just to see how they're doing or ask when we can hang out in the near future. I host small get-togethers — one of my favorites was an October 2025 party themed around the movie "Coraline." I travel to visit my friends who live in different states at least once a year, or plan vacations together with them. Ayers says she approves of my practices. Even the simple act of sending a friend a quick note because you briefly thought about them is "a brilliant practice," she says, adding: "It is the best thing you can do." The first step: 'Just reach out' to your friends To keep your friendships healthy and strong, Ayers recommends three things: "Just reach out to them," she says. It doesn't have to be super frequent, but let your friends know you value them: "When they come to your mind, send them a text, 'Hey, thinking of you.'" Prioritize relationships built on intrinsic qualities over external ones, Ayers recommends. Friendships based on shared values like loyalty and honesty are often much more meaningful than connections built on more superficial qualities, she says. Bring something to the table in each friendship, and expend a reasonable amount of time, resources and energy to show up for your friends — even if, sometimes, you'd rather stay home. In other words, be the friend you'd want others to be to you. "Remembering that you are a valued person in this relationship is important," says Ayers. Ayers and her best friend live in different states — Idaho and California, respectively — she says. They send each other voice memos throughout the week, ranging from quick check-ins to 15-minute breakdowns of an important update, she says.

events.title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’
events.summary: Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up. Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England . But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story. Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset. The businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt. As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs. And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge. Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup. The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50. Bekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room. He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head. Hugh Thomas, a food writer from Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.” Some, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs. Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomed a cage of endangered red squirrels . But there, too, lay a problem. The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds. Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.” While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds. People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas. Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Writer Emma Craigie, who is not part of the group, but also lives nearby, is particularly concerned about flooding. She said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on.

events.title: How Supreme Court justices are leaning in major 401(k) case over private funds and underperformance
events.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court heard a case this week in which a former Intel employee alleged company retirement-plan fiduciaries breached their duty by investing in hedge funds and private equity, pointing in part to the funds' underperformance. Lower courts already rejected the claims, ruling underperformance alone is not enough without showing a "meaningful benchmark" for courts to assess performance. Several justices appeared receptive to Intel's position during oral arguments. A ruling for Intel could make some retirement plan sponsors more comfortable adding alternative investments to 401(k) plans, though the largest employers may still move slowly. The Supreme Court heard a major case this week concerning an Intel retirement plan which could result in a decision that influences employers' appetite for private investments in 401(k)s. Many plan sponsors are in limbo, awaiting the Supreme Court decision and finalized Labor Department rules covering alternative investments before changing their 401(k) menu, even as the asset management industry is gearing up with new products. "I think companies want to know what's going to happen with the proposal and what's going to happen with the Supreme Court case before they go rushing in to change their investment strategies," said Elizabeth Hopkins, principal at Hopkins ERISA Law and a former senior trial attorney with the Labor Department, who filed an amicus brief in the Supreme Court case on behalf of former high-ranking DOL officials. Here's what employers and employees need to know about forces influencing the market for private investments in 401(k) plans. What Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch and Kagan said Employers have been whipsawed for the past several years by changing government policies on alternative investments in 401(k) plans and a high-profile lawsuit filed in 2019 by a former Intel employee. That case, Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee, which the Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Tuesday, Oct. 6, concerns private investments in a defined contribution plan like a 401(k) and the circumstances under which these investments are appropriate. The case is not challenging whether alternative assets like hedge funds and private equity can be used in a 401(k) plan alongside stocks and bonds. Rather, the question before the court is whether a retirement plan underperformance claim requires alleging a "meaningful benchmark." The heart of the dispute is how to handle claims by employees that plan sponsors have invested their retirement funds imprudently. Employees contend that the relatively low returns on Intel's plans reflect a breach of fiduciary duty. The lower courts disagreed. Their reasoning: claims of underperformance alone are not enough without showing a "meaningful benchmark" for courts to assess performance. During the arguments, Supreme Court justices seemed skeptical that plan sponsors' investment choices should provide easy fodder for litigious individuals. Justices frequently turned to a fruit metaphor, with Justice Clarence Thomas summing up his take on the Ninth Circuit's decision as: "you can't compare apples and oranges…if you have a fund…that is designed to produce high returns but riskier returns…you can't compare that to a fund that is to protect against losses." Several other justices, including from among the liberal side of the court, seemed to agree with his line of reasoning, Ronald Mann, co-director of the Charles Evans Gerber Transactional Studies Center at Columbia Law School, noted in an analysis on SCOTUSblog . Justice Elena Kagan, for instance, commented, "the thing that you need … is another apple." Justice Samuel Alito challenged the employees' attorney, Matthew Wessler, to clarify whether his position was that one could "state a claim by comparing apples and oranges but supplement that with the suggestion that the strategy was flawed." Justice Amy Coney Barrett opted for the same metaphor as well. Meanwhile, Justice Neil Gorsuch asked Wessler to "agree with the general principle that when we're limited to underperformance claims … a meaningful benchmark of some kind is required, apples, not oranges." Wessler did not respond to a request for comment for this article. The underlying problem for the court seemed to be the lack of a benchmark. Notably, justices explicitly asked Aimee Brown, assistant to the Solicitor General, how much guidance the court should provide in this case. Brown's view was that the court should suggest "some parameters" for what a "meaningful benchmark" needs to be. "Prudence is about process and not about performance," she told the justices. Legal experts say SCOTUS seems likely to side with Intel Attorneys who attended the arguments in person, listened to the recording or read the transcript took the justices' questions as a sign they were leaning toward siding with Intel and affirming the 9th Circuit.

events.title: The big unknown behind Democrats' polling leads
events.summary: Poll after poll spells trouble for GOP candidates — in purple states and deep-red ones alike — but while Democrats see a blue wave coming, some Republicans see a polling mirage. Why it matters: Pollsters worry they're flying partly blind. Even a modest polling error could mean the difference between Republicans retaining control of Congress and President Trump facing Democratic majorities in both chambers. The big picture: Polling Trump voters has long been notoriously difficult. The polls underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Midterm polling has been more accurate, though some still underestimated Republican support in 2022, notes Scott Keeter, senior survey adviser at Pew Research Center. Catch up quick: With less than a month until the midterms, the polls paint a bleak picture for Republicans. The House: Democrats lead Republicans 49.8%-41.9% in the RealClearPolling generic congressional ballot average. Cook Political Report projects Democrats will gain nine to 19 seats, enough to win a narrow majority. The Senate: Cook now sees a potential Democratic net gain of two to six seats. Democrats need four to take control, and Cook just moved the Kansas Senate race into its toss-up column. Trump: The president's approval rating stands at 37.6% in Cook's polling tracker . A recent Economist/YouGov poll found 35% approving and 60% disapproving of his performance. State of play: Research suggests Republicans have become somewhat less likely than Democrats to participate in telephone surveys, and response rates overall have plummeted since the late 1990s, per Pew . "We definitely have more people answering surveys who voted for [former Vice President Kamala] Harris than who voted for President Trump," says Brent Buchanan, a Republican pollster and founder of Cygnal. "But if you're a good pollster, you still get the other people." Pollsters can compensate by giving greater weight to Trump voters or adjusting samples to better reflect the Republican electorate, which skews male, white and working class. Advanced statistical modeling tools can also take a poor sample and make it look like the true electorate, though results may be inaccurate for subgroups like young people or Hispanic voters, Pew's Keeter says. But that has risks: "The adjustment assumes that the Republicans who respond to a poll are similar to the Republicans who don't respond to the poll," Rice University political science assistant professor Matthew Tyler tells Axios. Tyler said weighting GOP respondents more heavily can backfire if those willing to answer polls are also more willing to vote Democratic than the Republicans who never respond. That could inflate the apparent size of a Democratic wave. Between the lines: Predicting who will actually vote can dramatically change the results. YouGov chief scientist Douglas Rivers found Democratic leads ranging from six to 16 points depending on how likely voters were identified in a September survey — and called the 16-point margin "almost certainly an overstatement." The bottom line: Even with the questions about the accuracy of recent polls, most pollsters believe Democrats have the edge heading into Election Day. " I think it's telling that we're hanging our hopes on, 'The polls are wrong,'" Buchanan says. "That's not very strong."

events.title: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement that the Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences. Why it matters: The Trump administration has made a show of flexing American power, sometimes with grisly footage. Now, it's preparing to make the government's ultimate punishment available for all to see. The big picture: Americans are increasingly encountering shocking images on their phones, often without warning. Graphic footage of Charlie Kirk's assassination spread widely across social media, searing in the brains of social media users — often young ones. Since Oct. 7, 2023, footage from the Hamas attacks and Israel's military campaign in Gaza has circulated online. Some videos have spread from Telegram to social platforms like X , where clips are easy to find. Footage of the August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte train went viral across X, stirring debate about crime and public safety. President Trump later said he had watched the video and wished he hadn't. A livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts interviewed by Reuters. Public executions are increasingly rare worldwide. In recent years, most have taken place in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. Friction point: Tech companies are now facing the question of whether they would allow the Pentagon to livestream the execution on their platforms. Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009 at the Fort Hood Army base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3. TikTok and Kick said that livestreaming the event would violate their policies, The Verge reported. YouTube, Meta, X and Twitch did not respond to The Verge's requests for comment. Yes, but: Elon Musk has positioned X, in particular, as a bulwark against internet censorship in the name of free speech. Hegseth's plan is putting the limits of that free-speech philosophy to a new test. The platform defended its decision to keep graphic content of the Kirk shooting on the platform, saying: "We will continue to stand against violence and censorship, ensuring this platform amplifies truth and open dialogue for everyone." After a bishop was stabbed during a livestreamed church service in Australia in 2024, X defied government demands to remove footage of the attack worldwide. Zoom out: Hegseth's announcement raises the prospect of reversing America's nearly century-long retreat from public executions. He justified making the execution public, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky, which drew 20,000 spectators, is widely considered America's last public execution. A modern-day livestreamed execution could reach billions. The intrigue: Vice President JD Vance questioned Friday whether the execution would actually be livestreamed and said he wouldn't watch if it were. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) posted : "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. ... Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." Trump told reporters he had approved the decision to livestream the execution. The bottom line: America spent nearly a century moving away from public executions. Now, with real-world violence just a click away, the U.S. government is preparing to show one to the world.

events.title: Buffett's 'trips down YouTube rabbit hole' revealed
events.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Portfolio Tracker (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.) Buffett's 'nightly trips down the YouTube rabbit hole' revealed Warren Buffett watches CNBC in the morning, but nearly every evening he "can't get enough" of watching YouTube clips while sitting on a recliner in front of an "enormous" television in his Omaha home. A Wall Street Journal article this week quotes friends as saying he's "hardly ever" looking at anything related to investing or finance, although he is a "fan of Berkshire Hathaway's own content" and "proud of how it performs on the video platform." Instead, it's things like "Glenn Close clips ... commercials from the 1950s ... Paul Anka videos ... speeches by complete unknowns ... show tunes, railroads, the big-band era, Nebraska and early Frank Sinatra performances from the 1930s." He will also go down some "random rabbit holes." For example, Buffett might "come into his office, gushing about a moving amateur rendition of 'My Way.'" Sharon Osberg, the three-time world bridge champion who has taught Buffett and Bill Gates the finer points of the game , is also Buffett's "frequent viewing companion," says the WSJ. She reports "Warren's range is broad. It can be the silliest things," like a "really good documentary on Roy Cohn" or "the Uzbekistan version of America's got talent ." Osberg says Buffett has also been watching clips featuring his late friend and business partner, Charlie Munger, including a 2017 appearance at the University of Michigan. "You feel the bond between the two of them as he watches Charlie. It's really quite something." The WSJ knocks down the idea Buffett's YouTube habit had anything to do with Berkshire's big investment in Alphabet , the platform's corporate parent. "He just really likes watching the clips, friends say." The article notes that while Buffett, now 96 years old, is notoriously slow to adopt new technologies, in this instance his move to YouTube is in line with an ongoing shift from streaming to video clips that has made the platform the most-watched video provider on TVs in the U.S. Berkshire Hathaway added another $192.6 million to its bet on homebuilder Lennar late last week. In an SEC filing Monday, Berkshire reports buying 2.4 million shares of Lennar Class A at an average price of $79.65 and 15 thousand shares of Lennar Class B at an average price of $78.33 on Thursday, October 1 and Friday, October 2. Since Berkshire's stake topped 10% in mid-September, it's been required by an SEC rule to disclose additional purchases within two business days. There's been no filing so far this week, so it appears there wasn't any new buying through at least Tuesday. In total, Berkshire has added $595.3 million of Lennar shares on 11 trading days since September 17. At today's closing prices, its disclosed 12.2% stake of 29 million shares is valued at $2.2 billion . At the end of last year, it owned just 7.2 million shares, then worth $742 million. Over that period, LEN has dropped more than 25% as rising interest rates have made homes less affordable. Now, virtually every person on the globe — maybe, well, let's get it down to 75 percent of the people on the globe — have some notion in their mind about Coca-Cola. events.title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review. Experts are alarmed
events.summary: Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review. The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb). But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage . The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing. The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “ promises kept ” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken , injure or kill people. But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception. Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science. “The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues. “I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added. The FDA did not respond to a request for comment. The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”. Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts. Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”. Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity. Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical. “They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.” How TOR led to children eating rocket fuel chemicals The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats. Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample.

events.title: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
events.summary: Dollar General, BJ's Wholesale Club, Lululemon and Under Armour have said in earnings calls that they have already cut or plan to cut assortments. Analysts said that after trimming product lines, brands may focus on raising prices to get back to healthy growth. Box retailers can offer thousands of individual brands, so product cuts can help streamline assortments and stabilize their businesses. Trimming assortments comes with challenges, as retailers risk losing customers and have to answer to investors as their revenue base shrinks in the short term. Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets. As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs. In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%. Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make. When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems. "If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly." Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns. Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue. "Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price." Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power. Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years. "Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer." Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand. Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level. "It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel. He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026. Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June. For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices. Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business. "When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel. BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.

events.title: Squeezy olive oil bottles, Meghan’s pot filler tap and the rise of ‘cheffy’ kit in home kitchens
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Social media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buying T he Duchess of Sussex is no ordinary home cook, but when Meghan appeared on Instagram this week at a hob presided over by a special pot filler tap , it spoke to a shift in the everyday kitchen – the rise of “cheffy” kit. While the pot filler is now most often found in luxury residential kitchens, it was reportedly invented in the early 20th century as a functional fixture for commercial kitchens. It joins a wealth of other restaurant equipment to have infiltrated our homes, from squeezy olive oil bottles to stainless steel mixing bowl sets. At Sous Chef, a UK-based independent speciality food brand, sales of chef presses are up 26%, while sales of chef’s trays are booming, according to Holly Thomson, the company’s food editor. For Ella Risbridger, author of The Kitchen Book: Good Food for Every Day : “It’s an amazing thing, the blurring of lines between restaurant and home kitchens.” A byproduct of the increasing visibility we have of professional chefs at work, whether via open kitchens in restaurants or “chefluencers” on social media, the utilitarianism and gadgets of restaurant kitchens are increasingly aspirational. This week, in a home tour with Architectural Digest, Julianne Moore showed off her Ikea industrial shelves. “People now can see what is happening in professional kitchens,” says Risbridger, “and likely, if they are watching The Bear or a lot of cheffy Instagrams, the algorithm knows that and knows what you might, might, want to buy for yourself.” From the white T-shirt to the Japanese Hasegawa chopping board , people want to channel Carmy and Syd as they make dinner midweek. Thomson suspects it might have something to do with the economic climate – people are thinking: “‘I’m not going to spend 90 quid on a meal, but I might invest in these products that are going to help me take eating at home a bit more seriously.’” According to James Lawless, a spokesperson at David Mellor, this shift links back to the pandemic, which “reignited interest in home cooking”. “Professional chefs’ equipment may have specialist functions, but it isn’t special,” says Lawless. “They are first and foremost tools to perform a particular function.” For Thomson, they are “an extra piece of kit that adds a bit of ease, finesse, or streamlines the process”. Coming from a professional kitchen, where “you don’t have anything that takes up space that isn’t fully useful, used every day and has multiple purposes,” they’d have to be. Of course, one person’s useful can be another’s waste of space. In the case of the pot filler tap, in an ordinary small kitchen that might be unnecessary, but, according to Helen Parker, the creative director of deVOL Kitchens, it “has become the must-have addition to a larger kitchen”. Sometimes, you don’t know what you don’t know. As Thomson says of the squeezy olive oil bottle, which, at a few quid, is proof that this isn’t all about expensive equipment: “Precision squirting is just so useful, and once you’ve done it once, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is so much better than glugging oil out of a bottle.’” For Risbridger, “the trick is that it’s nice to buy something fancy for a hobby – it’s often a shortcut to taking yourself more seriously … you can now access a reasonably cheap version of something professionals use, and that makes you feel more like a professional. Which increases confidence. Which makes the thing you make better, whether or not you could have achieved it without the gadget.”

events.title: S&P lifts UK GDP growth view on resilient consumer spending and services sector
events.summary: S&P Global Ratings has upgraded its growth outlook for the UK, citing “reasonably resilient” consumer spending and services that have helped shield the economy from the conflict in the Middle East. Real gross domestic product in Europe's second-biggest economy is now expected to climb by 1.3 per cent, from a previous lowered prediction of 1.1 per cent , the New York-based agency said on Friday. S&P analysts noted that hospitality and professional services underpinned economic growth in the second quarter. GDP growth is seen to average 1.4 per cent from 2027 to 2029, expecting the economy to improve if the situation in the Middle East is “contained”. The agency also maintained the UK's long and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at AA, two notches below the top prime grade. An investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises. “The stable outlook reflects our view that the UK economy has remained, and will remain, resilient in the face of the energy shock emanating from the Middle East conflict, with growth remaining reasonably robust,” analysts at S&P wrote. “This is balanced against risks from the UK's constrained fiscal position, elevated public debt levels, and high government spending, including on debt servicing.” S&P also noted the UK's policy direction under Andy Burnham, the UK's sixth prime minister in the past decade. The start of his tenure in July was marked by questions about how he would handle the economy, including how to ensure fiscal discipline. Mr Burnham's government has “focused on devolution, industrial renewal, social care and closer ties with the EU, with simultaneous pledges to respect fiscal prudence”, S&P said. UK inflation was pegged at 3.1 per cent in August, the highest in five months, according to the Office of National Statistics, and well above the Bank of England's 2 per cent threshold. S&P said this has risen on domestic price pressures and energy and transport costs, underpinned by higher hydrocarbon costs. The agency expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 0.25 basis points at its November meeting after maintaining them last month, “then hold that level until the second half of 2027 because the current policy rate level of 3.75 per cent and soft labour market conditions suggest the UK may require less additional policy tightening than the eurozone”. Egypt's growth accelerates Meanwhile, S&P said Egypt's economy accelerated at its fastest pace in three years, but cautioned the North African nation remains vulnerable to shocks stemming from the conflicts in the Middle East. Real GDP in the Arab world's most populous nation jumped by 5.1 per cent in fiscal 2026, buoyed by non-oil sectors including manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, information and communication technology, and tourism, it said in a separate report. That compares to a 4.7 per cent reading in its previous estimate . Household consumption emerged as a primary factor, boosted by record remittances, easing inflation and stable labour market conditions, it added. S&P, however, projects this growth to ease to 4.5 per cent in the fiscal year 2027, as shipping disruptions related to the war are expected to further pressure trade, logistics and import prices. Consumption and investment activities are also predicted to soften amid persistent uncertainty and rising inflation. Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, according to Capmas data. S&P expects inflation to average 12.9 per cent in fiscal 2027. This might result in a policy reversal from the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates. S&P also kept its B sovereign credit rating on Egypt, which is six levels below investment grade, with a stable outlook. “Nevertheless, we expect the continued implementation of the reform agenda, including the commitment to exchange rate liberalisation, to enhance structural economic competitiveness over the medium term,” the S&P analysts said.

events.title: Tourism expansion v turtle nests: the dispute dividing communities in one Tobago resort
events.summary: Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat V isitors to Rocky Point in south-west Tobago are drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest. But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best. As elsewhere in the Caribbean, the need for economic growth has led to growing interest in tourism development. Rene Seepersadsingh, the first vice-president of the Tobago Hotel and Tourism Association , says: “Tobago is very focused on attracting private partnership investment because our tourism product is now in that evolution stage, where we’re looking to upgrade the offering that we have. “There are great opportunities for participation and development within the sector,” he adds. With that goal in mind, the 12 hectares (30 acres) of Rocky Point became the subject of a request for expressions of interest in 2021 from the government agency Eteck , which manages and develops economic zones. Eteck invited proposals from qualified firms to design and manage a premier hotel and property development on the site. Superior Hotels, a locally owned company, ultimately won. It received a 99-year lease to develop a $500m (£378m), 200-room property on the site, which also includes plans for a number of privately owned villas. Since then, the project has sparked a struggle that has been going on for the past four years, led by environmentalists, Tobagonians and others who believe the development will ruin Rocky Point. Duane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation – one of several entities that submitted an expression of interest to Eteck – is now advocating for increased accountability. A former hotel manager, he is an avid surfer at Back Bay and owns tourism-related businesses in Tobago. “Our focus is to make sure that whatever is done on that site is done in an environmentally sound way, in a way that preserves it for Tobago and for future generations,” he says. He says he and his associates replied to the expression of interest with a proposal for a small eco-resort featuring nature trails, turtle watching and a wax museum showcasing Amerindian artefacts discovered at Rocky Point. He also highlighted the remains of Fort Monck, a distinctive fort with well-preserved masonry. Kenny says the winning project’s initial design raised concerns about it seemingly ignoring many archaeological and ecological features at Rocky Point, and that the subsequent amendments still do not adequately address many of the issues raised. “The amount of concrete development on this site, at least in the current model, makes us worry that the impact on the environment will be significant,” he says, adding that in his view a 200-room hotel has little chance of success in Tobago, where most large hotels struggle to achieve sustainable occupancy levels. Michelle Cazabon-Mannette, an environmental biologist and director at the NGO SpeSeas , says more than 100 people submitted written objections to the Environmental Management Authority (EMA) as part of the environmental impact assessment, which the project needs to obtain a certificate of environmental clearance (CEC). She says that after widespread objections at town hall meetings and in written submissions, the project holder made only minor design adjustments. After the adjustments, the EMA granted Superior Hotels a CEC , with about 20 pages of mitigation measures attached that the project must follow. Kirkland Brathwaite, principal at Katalyst Solutions, an environmental and project management firm, says a CEC often includes several environmental impact mitigation measures, adding that a quality assurance project plan is mandatory to ensure proper monitoring. Cazabon-Mannette says the mitigation measures listed in the CEC are insufficient, though she acknowledges that “the project designs provided – on which the CEC is based – were conceptual and (Superior Hotels) made it clear these were not final designs”. Whatever form the final designs take, Cazabon-Mannette and Kenny say a 200-room hotel and numerous villas will probably mean removing many of the trees on Rocky Point. “A major concern is having an appropriate scale of development that would minimise the footprint in terms of the coastal vegetation that would need to be cleared,” Cazabon-Mannette says.

events.title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales
events.summary: In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales. Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely. When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere. Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople. Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16. “I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape. In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer. When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”. As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival , held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan. Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim. The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week. The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs. “The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.” Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way. Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge. Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders. Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company. One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies. “We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.

events.title: ‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staff
events.summary: Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale U nion officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints. “People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth. TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”. Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs. “People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.” “Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.” Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturers recommend sitting while operating the machines. Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations. Following the policy change, TSA workers were also required to sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union. “They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones. He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US. Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents. US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy. “A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.” AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees, launched a letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”. Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.” The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facing possible pay freezes and significant increases to their health insurance premium costs. Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judge ruling in January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction. TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year. The Trump administration has also been expanding privatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airport abandoned its plan to join the program.

events.title: Trump rages over Nobel Peace Prize loss
events.summary: President Trump lashed out late Friday night after he once again did not win the Nobel Peace Prize he has openly coveted . Why it matters: The award is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about frequently and believes he deserves. This year's prize went instead to a former judge of a court Trump has sanctioned and called "rogue" and "evil." Navi Pillay, the winner, reacted to the award by saying world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war," according to the AP . What he's saying: " I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel. I don't know what the woman has done," Trump said in a Truth Social post of nearly 600 words that went up just before midnight on Friday. "I settled 8 Wars, with letters being sent from every President and Prime Minister from the countries that I helped to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I'm about to settle, or win, two more, Iran and, Russia/Ukraine," Trump wrote. "They're both happening at breakneck speed but, forget them, it's the 8 that I've already settled, any one of which, in particular, Pakistan and India, would be far more than necessary to win the Nobel Prize. In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1." Between the lines: Pillay, this year's winner, is a former judge of the International Criminal Court and also the former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Nobel officials said she received the honor "for her efforts to promote peace and international law." Originally from South Africa, Pillay, 85, also served as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Zoom in: Trump took aim at that UN association as well. "In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help. The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said. The intrigue: Trump also blasted Norway, as he's previously done over Nobel snubs, though the country doesn't award the prize. "This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten. The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!" The bottom line: The president didn't hold back making his case for why he should have won — and why his loss was a personal snub.

events.title: Telegraph owner poised to make newsroom job cuts in investment promise U-turn
events.summary: Exclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundancies The new owner of the Telegraph is preparing to make significant job cuts to its newsroom, just months after stating it would invest in the title to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”. Axel Springer, the German media company overseen by its billionaire chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to be examining proposals that would make between 50 and 100 journalists redundant. A source familiar with the plans said a forthcoming consultation was likely to propose cutting a “significant proportion” of editorial staff, possibly before Christmas. They said such proposals called into question Axel Springer’s promise to “back an investment programme in [the Telegraph Media Group] to grow and expand the business”. A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group declined to comment. No redundancies have been announced to staff so far. It would mark the first big intervention by Axel Springer since its £575m purchase of the Telegraph earlier this year. The sale ended three tortuous years for the Telegraph and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition. The proposed cuts have confused some Telegraph figures, who are struggling to understand how it aligns with Döpfner’s pledge to “bring that uncertainty to an end”. At a recent Axel Springer leadership summit held in London, Döpfner is also said to have stated that the company could not cut its way to growth. Axel Springer, which also owns Politico and the German titles Bild and Die Welt, recently brought in consultants to examine the financial health of the Telegraph titles, which include the Daily Telegraph, the Sunday Telegraph and its online news operation. Döpfner has made no secret of his desire to boost the Telegraph’s US operation , with senior editors already deployed to the US to develop those plans. However, consultants are understood to have drawn up potential cuts to the existing news operation at the 171-year-old titles. Sources said consultants had also recommended that the Telegraph set up side projects to support its journalism, such as price comparison sites and healthcare. Some insiders were said to be baffled by some of the suggestions. A source familiar with the proposals said they would anger Telegraph staff, who had hoped Axel Springer’s ownership would mark the arrival of “sunny uplands” after three years of being “starved of any form of investment, pay rises or management changes that could move us on”. “The path to growth is not to cut jobs,” they said. “They’re still going to need to hire people in the States if they’re going to make any sort of push there, but staff haven’t been told where that money is going to come from.” The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed that it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m. However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.
