AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Chap who took the job left a trail of wreckage – and invaluable case studies – in his incompetent wake Techie was stung by a wasp, held overnight by Chinese police, then trapped in a 13-hour meeting 9 days ago Techie assumed boss knew what they were talking about and killed Exchange by deleting data 13 days ago Project leader thought his team understood the plan, ended up fixing their 'interpretation' of it 16 days ago Your cloud survived everything except the real world 20 days ago Techie fixed Wi-Fi dead zone with a drill 23 days ago Welcome to another installment of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed Friday column which often shares your stories of what happens when incompetent people climb the greasy pole and send their failures straight back down into the lap of tech support. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Preston," who wrote to share his story of working as a field service tech in the late 1990s. "I'd risen to the rank of senior field service engineer and was offered a position in consultancy," Preston told The Register . He turned it down because he liked working at the coal face, and the people he worked with there appreciated his skills. "As soon as I arrived at clients, someone was making me a coffee just as I liked it," Preston explained, "so I turned down the consultancy position." One of Preston's colleagues took the promotion and was soon working on projects such as reconfiguring Windows NT 4.0 and the servers it ran on to handle two CPUs, configuring backup systems, and ensuring uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) were in place to keep things alive. Preston kept doing his own thing, but the character of his job soon changed. "Within weeks, I was getting assigned calls where upgrades had gone wrong, UPSes were failing, and backups were not working." Preston realized the chap who took the promotion was making basic mistakes on almost every job – some of them so bad that one customer refused to work with the newly minted consultant. One of the jobs that eventually landed on Preston's to-fix list saw the consultant wipe a customer database that his backup regime did not protect. At another site, he created a system that pointlessly powered down every day and botched the installation of the UPS that would have saved his bacon. Preston covered as best he could to protect his company rather than the incompetent "consultant." He eventually quit the IT services caper and became a trainer. "I used these incidents as examples of what to look out for when installing and fault finding on customer sites, and also as a lesson on why you should never rely on the person who does a job before you getting things perfectly right." events.title: Oil posts weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf coast
events.summary: Oil prices settled higher on Friday to post weekly gains as Hurricane Isaias hit the US Gulf coast, forcing oil companies to significantly taper down their operations. Crude was trading lower earlier in the session after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.42 per cent to settle at $104.72 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 0.39 per cent to close at $91.85 a barrel. From last week's close Brent, which settled more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday amid continuing tensions in the Middle East, jumped 2.41 per cent, while WTI added 0.81 per cent. “Brent crude rose ... as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD. “Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.” The US Gulf coast is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods. About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said. The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns. In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Impact on oil prices Oil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia. The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Gold, meanwhile, ended higher on Friday on bargain hunting and as investors weigh the possibility of further interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve. The precious metal, widely regarded as a safe-haven asset, added 1.52 per cent to a one-week high of $4,194.40 an ounce. Silver jumped 2.82 per cent to $60.82 an ounce.

events.title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
events.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings. The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests. Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn). One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not to take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said. Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta. It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region. The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street. Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment. The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear. A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres Published 26 October 2025 AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? Published 3 September UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors. He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans. "It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC. This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research. Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said. "It's more like a bet on a dream", he added. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment , thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to. There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more. That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create . In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public. The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each. AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought. events.title: Sale rescues landmark WA dairy brands from collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mundella yoghurt returns to shelves as deal revives collapsed WA dairy brands Mundella yoghurt was established in Western Australia in 1974. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Emerging processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets of collapsed Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company. The companies were put into liquidation in August, leaving creditors owed millions of dollars. Yoghurt production is expected to start near Margaret River before the Christmas period. A late rescue deal and sale is set to keep two landmark West Australian dairy brands on supermarket shelves. Mundella Foods and the Margaret River Dairy Company went into liquidation in August, with creditors owed millions of dollars. Local processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets, including processing facilities in Perth and Margaret River, for an undisclosed sum. Mundella Foods' operations near Mundigjong will not be used for processing by the new owners. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Artisanal Market managing director Kevin Sorgiovanni founded another well-known WA dairy and juice brand, Harvey Fresh. He said he had been interested in buying the companies back in 2023, when they were sold by Chinese-owned Manassen Foods to The Cheeky Cow, which has since collapsed. "We saw the Mundella and Margaret River business as a great opportunity for the South West and also to add some value back to the WA dairy market." Mr Sorgiovanni said both brands of yoghurt would be manufactured at the export-approved Metricup processing facility near Margaret River. Artisanal Markets will mothball Mundella's original manufacturing facility at Mundijong, near Perth, because of its poor condition. Artisanal Markets is jointly owned by PenAgri Group and Research Corporation. Mr Sorgiovanni told the ABC the new ownership had plans to target the Asian market for broader sales. There are hopes to export Mundella yoghurt to Asia. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) "We want to do more than just the WA market," he said. Mr Sorgiovanni said production at the Metricup facility would start at 2 million litres a year, but it had the capacity for 10 million litres. The revival is welcome news for dairy farmers across southern WA, but challenges remain. WA Farmers Dairy Council president Ian Noakes said he was keen to see how Artisanal Market would secure milk supply. Ian Noakes has welcomed the sale. ( ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia ) "Most of the milk in WA is contracted, and the main companies are not very good at letting a bit of milk go to somebody else," he said. "So it would be a matter of waiting probably until somebody comes out of contract to get a milk supply." Mr Noakes hoped the additional competition would improve the price points for local dairy farmers. events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Top of the Week TSMC and GF inked a $2B manufacturing agreement , under which GF will manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem at its Malta, New York fab. Volume production is expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. Applied Materials and Intel are expanding their R&D collaboration to develop next-gen transistors, interconnects, and advanced packaging technologies, combining work at Applied’s EPIC Center in Silicon Valley with Intel’s R&D operations in Hillsboro, Oregon. Rapidus launched Rapidus CORE , a global ecosystem framework intended to support customers from chip design through manufacturing for its planned 2nm foundry business. The first phase includes 17 design-service partners. Xanadu and GF formed a multi-year manufacturing partnership to move ultra-low-loss silicon nitride photonics and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors onto GF’s 300mm production line in Malta, New York. Big hauls Wolfspeed received a conditional commitment for up to $1.5B in 30-year U.S. government financing to expand domestic SiC materials and wide-bandgap power-device production. Vinci raised $250M in Series B funding at a $1.5B valuation to expand its AI-powered physics simulation platform . The platform models thermal, thermo-mechanical, and fluid behavior during design, with simulations reportedly running in minutes rather than hours or days. Oratomic raised $475M for its neutral-atom quantum computing hardware. VEIR raised $110M for superconducting power delivery technology for AI data centers. Atomic Machines launched with $250M for its Matter Compiler system that builds micro-machines from code , including an electromechanical micro-relay to cut power in 800VDC data centers during a fault. Financials TSMC (Sept. revenue) and Samsung (Q3 guidance). Analysis Global semiconductor sales reached $159.7B in August, up 8% from July, with year-to-date sales topping $1T , reports SIA/WSTS . McKinsey expects inference to account for about 60% of AI compute by 2030, driving demand for custom accelerators, HBM, chiplets, advanced packaging, and silicon photonics. Silicon photonics, CPO, and optical networking are emerging as the next U.S.–China semiconductor battleground as AI data centers outgrow electrical interconnects, says Wilson Center , which estimates China accounts for 56% of global optical-transceiver manufacturing capacity. Brookings estimates the U.S. AI buildout could require $10.3T through 2032 for data centers, power, networking and specialized chips, but it warned that increasingly complex financing could obscure financial risks. Lithography ASML and Carl Zeiss researchers outlined a hyper-NA EUV lithography architecture with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75, potentially enabling features as small as 5nm, more than one-third smaller than current high-NA systems. The technology could be ready in about a decade, although commercial production remains uncommitted. Canon says its nanoimprint lithography technology is entering the final stage toward full-scale mass production. DUV immersion lithography is the strongest remaining chokepoint on China’s AI-chip production, contends think tank Center for Technology & Statecraft . It estimates Chinese-owned fabs had accumulated more than 330 DUVi systems by 1Q26 and says continued imports could significantly narrow the U.S.-allied AI-chip manufacturing advantage. The report calls for a China-wide ban on DUVi exports, servicing restrictions and tighter controls on critical components. Memory Samsung is reportedly planning ~$3.9B in investment in memory-chip testing facilities in Vietnam . Netlist and Micron entered into patent license and settlement agreements covering Netlist’s portfolio for server DIMMs and high-bandwidth memory, ending all pending legal proceedings between the companies. Micron faces a potential walkout at its Taiwan facilities after workers voted overwhelmingly to authorize a strike over profit sharing. Toshiba plans to invest approximately $380M to double HDD production capacity for AI data centers by fiscal 2027, compared with 2025 levels, reports Nikkei Asia. Security and export controls Arteris won an additional $3.3M through the U.S. government’s Trusted and Assured Microelectronics initiative to expand its third-party IP (3PIP) security assurance program in collaboration with BAE and SiFive . The U.S. DOJ charged the owner of California-based Earthmade Computer with allegedly smuggling more than $300M in export-controlled computer servers to China . Prosecutors allege the servers contained high-end U.S.-manufactured GPUs and were routed through Malaysia and Singapore using false end-user and destination information to evade U.S. export controls. Meanwhile, CSET researchers modeled more than 10 million scenarios for detecting diverted AI chips and found ping-based location verification to be the most cost-effective approach. However, they cautioned that implementation costs and complexity could limit its usefulness, and said that combining PLV with targeted physical inspections could improve enforcement. Recognition Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines was inducted into the National Academy of Engineering for his co-invention of the blue-light-emitting diode and decades of leadership in the semiconductor/EDA industry. Asia Elephantech plans to open an advanced packaging center in Tokyo in March to support process development, prototyping, and scale-up for AI-server packaging and PCBs. AMD is working with 14 South Korean AI semiconductor and technology companies to develop heterogeneous computing systems that combine AMD CPUs and GPUs with Korean AI processors, reports SBS News. Cadence and Jilin University unveiled their CAE Multiphysics Joint Laboratory in China . The organizations also have a computational fluid dynamics joint lab. events.title: So long, Spokes: GitHub rewrites storage to restore reliability, just in time for agentic hordes
events.summary: Responding to unprecedented demand from AI agents, GitHub is rebuilding its Git storage architecture from scratch. Early tests with the new architecture show a promising 35x write improvement in internal tests. GitHub will need a miracle of that proportion just to keep up with customer demand. The plan involves decoupling writes from reads, offloading maintenance, and letting object storage manage redundancy. Most impressive is that the redesign is happening under the hood, with the goal of a non-disruptive change that won't alter developer workflows, review processes, or security controls. Running an enterprise-grade code repository means supporting “large engineering teams running busy CI pipelines alongside growing fleets of agents. Supporting these teams means building Git infrastructure for sustained, concurrent reads and writes at a scale few repositories reach today,” wrote Brian Celenza, GitHub principal software engineer, in a blog post describing the updates. Celenza did not offer a timeline for this ambitious migration. When GitHub’s customers shifted their coding focus to AI agents, activity on the platform spiked significantly. Between September 2025 and August 2026, GitHub traffic doubled, from 218.2 billion events per month to 473.3 billion. In September alone, commits hit 7.38 billion, a 5x increase from September 2025. This shift in traffic is stressing the system. According to the GitHub Availability Report, the service suffered 10 incidents in April alone that degraded performance. Another nine incidents landed in May, with each generating more bad publicity than the previous one. So long, Spokes GitHub's current storage architecture, nicknamed Spokes, uses a three-phase commit protocol, storing full repo copies across multiple local disks and requiring a quorum of replicas to acknowledge each write. While this approach ensures strong reliability, it bottlenecks write speed, as every push is bounded by the slowest replica required for quorum. The new architecture writes a commit only once, to Azure Blob Storage, an object store service that automatically handles replication (and hence redundancy) on its own, eliminating the quorum bottleneck. GitHub also gooses performance by separating read requests into their own channel, a job handled by lightweight compute workers. The only coordination between reads and writes is over the reference branch pointers. Maintenance duties – such as compaction and garbage collection — are moved from the serving path to operate as background processes, further reducing system lag. Git in the age of agents GitHub seems to be on the same page with others in rethinking Git for the agentic age. Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a Git-hosting service called Entire, which offloads agent traffic to mirror repositories, allowing a customer’s core GitHub repos to just serve the core development traffic. SpaceX subsidiary Cursor, which uses Git to back its agent-support service, also refined the storage layer for better performance. Cursor engineers also rejected Spokes’ three-phase commit in favor of uploading pushes into an object storage write-ahead log (WAL), which captured all changes as immutable objects, caching at least one copy on super-speedy solid-state disks. Respect for the Octocats While it's cathartic to hate on a service that often goes down, you have to feel empathy for the GitHub engineers who, when they created the service, couldn’t have guessed what they signed up for. “I've worked at extreme scale before and seen companies spend three months just preparing for events that will increase their traffic by 10% or 20% [...], which is nothing compared to what GitHub's facing now,” wrote PlanetScale CEO Sam Lambert in an X message. We can all hope the new storage architecture will give GitHub's engineers some well-earned rest. ®

events.title: JD Vance’s comments about immigrants 'unwarranted' and ‘deeply offensive’, India's Foreign Ministry says
events.summary: India's Ministry of External Affairs on Friday called comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Indian immigrants "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive". A day earlier, Mr Vance announced that Microsoft and some of India ’s biggest IT services were suspended from a programme allowing workers on H-1B visas to apply for green cards. He accused the companies of abusing the system, comparing foreign workers to “indentured servants”. "The history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," the ministry said in a statement. It added that Mr Vance's comments were "unwarranted" and ignore the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy. Roughly 70 per cent of the H-1B visas approved in 2025 went to people from India. "Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said, appearing to refer to Mr Vance's use of the term "indentured servants", which carries a heavy historical burden for Indians. During the colonial period in India, more than 1.6 million people were transported as indentured servants to serve on British, French and Dutch plantations around the world following the abolition of slavery. Many workers, who typically signed five-year contracts for unpaid labour, were tricked or coerced into service. The indenture system is also a painful feature of American history. During the American colonial period, poor workers and convicts were bound to an employer for up to seven years, receiving no wages for their labour, in return for food, shelter and transport to the colonies. Similar to the Indian system, abuse was rampant. "When I say indentured servants, here's what I mean: When somebody comes in on an H-1B, they are completely subordinate to that company," Mr Vance said at the Department of Labour on Thursday. "If they lose that job, they have to leave the country." The Vice President accused Microsoft, Adobe and six other companies of fraudulently utilising the H-1B visa programme, which he said is meant to allow firms to bring in "the best of the best" from outside the US to fill jobs that are impossible to fill with American workers. This "pernicious system" is a "fundamental insult to the American way of life", he said, as it lets companies lower wages and block Americans from jobs, while also allowing for the abuse of foreign workers. As a result of the alleged fraudulent use of the system, the companies have been removed from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, which allows firms to hire foreign workers permanently and offers the workers the chance to apply for green cards. The tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecoms companies have come to rely heavily on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies, which have developed a lucrative business in recruiting professionals from abroad for US clients. In the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, Microsoft was the fifth-highest user of H-1B visas, with 3,688, according to Bloomberg. In a statement, Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work”, that its wages are among the highest of all visa filings and that the vast majority of its employees in the US are Americans. Mr Vance’s comments came hours before US President Donald Trump gave Microsoft chief executive, Satya Nadella , the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. And last week, Mr Nadella, alongside other tech industry leaders, visited the White House for a discussion on safeguards for AI. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company," Mr Vance said. "It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.” Washington has been engaged in an across-the-board immigration crackdown since Mr Trump returned to office last year. The State Department said earlier this month that more than 250,000 visas have been revoked under the Trump administration. Along with companies with high issuance of H-1B visas, Mr Vance also took aim at universities he said had engaged in J-1 visa fraud. He accused nine institutions, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford universities, of bringing "in foreigners to undercut the wages" of American researchers and graduate students. J-1 visas are granted to people approved to participate in work and study programmes in the US. "They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," he said.

events.title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
events.summary: Mary O'Keeffe was one of several business people who said high value residents contribute positively to the island's economy More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy. Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals. One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island. However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling". About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme. O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes. "They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals. "So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy." High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external . They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external . O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way. "First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income. "And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand. "High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off." Industry leaders from law, finance, business and real estate met at a Chamber of Commerce lunch to discuss the role of high value residents in Jersey Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them. He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy. Former economic advisor to the government of Jersey John Christensen said the amount of tax paid by high value residents was "piffling" "If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said. "So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%. "We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax. "We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions." John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme. He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly". "I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community. "As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all. "I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally. "And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work. "They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
events.summary: Longbow's co-founders and CEOs Daniel Davey (left) and Mark Tapscott show Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds (left in car) and mayor Richard Parker the Speedster A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire. Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year. West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs. Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said. Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it. "So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight." The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car. At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise. Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars. "Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added. People around the world are waiting to buy the limited edition car for around £85,000 The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund , external , which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry. West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year. Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow. "They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car." Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car. "So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing." events.title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
events.summary: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 The coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies? While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home to four of the world’s top 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, the UK produces 6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research. events.title: Firmus wobbles have opponents relieved, critics questioning deals
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus wobbles have data centre opponents relieved, critics questioning Tasmanian sports deals Firmus has abandoned its ASX float after lacklustre demand, with the news welcomed by Tasmanian opponents of its plans. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) The news of data centre builder Firmus' share market float being pulled after lacklustre demand has been met with a mixed reaction. While there has been disappointment from some investors, for the opponents of Firmus' data centre plans in northern Tasmania, the response has been relief. The news of data centre operator Firmus's share market float being pulled has been met with disappointment from some investors. But in one community where Firmus had big plans, the response was relief. Firmus was attempting to raise cash from investors to fund its data centre plans until this week's development . A group based in northern Tasmania, called the Environmental Awareness Association, has been campaigning against the company's three projects in the region. Anti-data centre protesters pictured in August outside George Town Council building, ahead of the vote on whether to approve Firmus' proposed data centre. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Nicholla Thompson from the association lives at Rowella, across the Tamar River from Firmus' proposed Bell Bay site, and said community backlash had contributed to investor concerns. Nicholla Thompson believes community opposition to Firmus contributed to investor hesitancy. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) "The dominoes are starting to fall," she said. "They wanted it to sneak through and not be seen by people; it was thanks to the little group that we've got that really highlighted what was happening over here." The opponents' group was relieved by the news, but was not yet celebrating it as a win for their campaign. "A big company shouldn't be able to come in and change substantially how we choose to live in a beautiful community like this and put an AI factory up in the middle of it and have us have to endure the sound, the diesel fumes and the total destruction of our properties in value and in peace and how we live," Ms Thompson said. Firmus 'well-positioned' to continue plans, company says When asked about any impact on its Tasmanian projects, a Firmus spokesperson said nothing had "fundamentally changed" about the business. Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors. Sam Baker, from Shadforth Financial Group, said it was hard to tell if the community opposition had contributed to the IPO failing, but it would have been considered by investors. He said it would be important to watch what Firmus did over the coming weeks and months to see if it could raise the capital. "Firmus not being able to get this ASX listing off the ground has cast some doubt over the funding of their potential rollout of data centres in northern Tasmania," he said. Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said the IPO was a matter for Firmus, but the Tasmanian government had been supportive "all the way through" the company's plans in the state. "That relationship is positive and we look forward to it continuing in a collaborative, positive way," he said. Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder. The Tasmanian Greens said the state government should be embarrassed by its support of Firmus, saying investors, academics and communities had been raising concerns for months. "The big question for Tasmania is why our government was so easily pulled into uncritically supporting this company despite the furiously waving red flags surrounding it," Tabatha Badger, the Greens' information and technology spokeswoman, said. Ms Badger said the government should pause any planning decisions on Firmus's three proposals in Tasmania. Firmus was also named a sponsor for Tasmania's NBL team, the JackJumpers. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The Tasmanian-founded company had recently announced sponsorships with the Tasmania Devils AFL club, several cricket teams, including the Hobart Hurricanes, and the JackJumpers and Tasmania Jewels basketball teams. Dr Andrew Hughes, a political marketing specialist at ANU's College of Business and Economics, said the Firmus IPO falling over was a golden opportunity for the Devils to walk away from the deal. He said he was surprised the Devils had signed with Firmus, given the club was already exposed to community backlash over the proposed AFL stadium in Hobart .

events.title: India’s tech giants shrug off changes to USA’s skilled visa program
events.summary: India’s peak technology industry body, NASSCOM, has shrugged off changes to the USA’s skilled visa regime, and Microsoft has denied it abuses the program. The changes, announced on Thursday by US vice president JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, mean that Microsoft and Adobe can no longer use the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) program to convert holders of the H-1B visa for skilled workers to permanent residents. Sonderling also revoked access to PERM for Indian companies Infosys, Tata, Wipro, and HCL, plus Capgemini. The secretary said the change followed criminal investigations and alleged “fraud and abuse.” “Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers,” he said. “They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers.” Vice President Vance weighed in with what he called a “message to Microsoft.” “You’re a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.” Critics of the H-1B visa have often alleged that US companies use it to bring in foreign workers who are prepared to work for less than Americans. The theory even extends to an allegation that India’s outsourcers use H-1B visas to bring in workers whose main agenda is offshoring more work to India. Some observers suggest skilled workers have a secondary motivation of using their time in the US to seek visas for family members. Microsoft, whose CEO Satya Nadella once held an H-1B visa, and which has fired over 20,000 staff since early 2025, took issue with the administration’s decision in a strongly worded post. “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” “Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce,” the company’s post continues. “We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world.” That’s essentially the same argument used by NASSCOM, and Indian politicians such as minister of state Vardhan Singh, who last year said that “skilled talent mobility has long played a significant role in promoting technology advancement, innovation, economic growth, and wealth creation in both India and the United States.” NASSCOM, which has never found a reason to doubt that Indian tech companies are anything other than excellent corporate citizens, took to X to share its view that “immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues and should not be viewed through the same lens.” The lobby group also argued “Over a number of years, Indian technology companies have significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas, while steadily expanding local hiring and building a strong domestic workforce in the U.S.” “They work with majority of the US fortune 500 companies, enable them to innovate and grow, and generate more local jobs. Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited.” Microsoft vowed to provide the Trump administration with more information about its migration initiatives. ®

events.title: Hollard insurance fined $2m for handling of claim that destroyed home
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance giant Hollard fined $2 million after claim delays leave house uninhabitable The Federal Court has ordered Hollard insurance to pay $2 million. ( Supplied ) Insurance giant Hollard has been fined $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable. The corporate watchdog ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof. The Federal Court ordered Hollard to pay $2 million for failing to promptly assess the damage, delaying rectification work and for failing to properly protect the property from further damage. It was also found to have taken too long to find temporary accommodation for the couple, failed to consider expert reports, and not clearly communicate with the couple throughout the claims process. Hollard has also been ordered to pay ASIC's legal costs. In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for Hollard said the insurer acknowledges the Federal Court's findings initiated by ASIC. "We extend our deepest apologies and sincerely regret the impact of this experience on the customer," the spokesperson said. ASIC says delays caused unnecessary and prolonged harm Hollard is a privately owned insurance company and one of the largest in Australia, underwriting insurance for motor, home, contents, bicycle, pet, and business products. It is the company behind brands including CBA's insurance product, Everyday Insurance, Real Insurance, Australian Seniors and Steadfast. In 2024, the company had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion. Hollard initially accepted the couples' claim, before repeatedly delaying inspections, reports and repair work, only to then reject the claim in April 2023. ASIC said the rejection was based on a non-expert opinion, despite prior expert reports outlining the damage. ASIC alleged the combination of delays in decision-making, poor communication and ignoring expert advice exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm. Sarah Court says Hollard's delays mean the home in regional Victoria needs to be demolished. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Its chair Sarah Court said the outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith. She said it was a warning to insurers about the devastating impact poor claim-handling and prolonged delays can have on consumers. "Hollard's serious claim handling failures left a family in limbo for years and living in a home that was uninhabitable," Ms Court said. "When Australians make an insurance claim they are often facing some of the most difficult times in their lives. "This decision confirms that insurers must act fairly, communicate clearly and make decisions without unnecessary delay, and must put their customers first." ASIC says decision sends clear message The family was initially offered $1,000 from Hollard as a goodwill payment in late 2022 to settle their claim. Once Hollard denied the claim, the couple then lodged a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which determined the storm caused structural damage to the roof. Hollard had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion in 2024. ( Supplied ) Hollard then agreed to pay the couple a cash settlement of more than $1.5 million for the total loss of the building, as well as temporary accommodation. ASIC sued Hollard after the cash settlement. The penalty Hollard has been ordered to pay goes to the Commonwealth of Australia, to be paid within 28 days. In delivering the judgment the judge said: "The saga experienced by the insureds was extended and must have been stressful and traumatic." "They were given the run-around in more ways than one and lived in their ever-deteriorating home as the saga wore on.

events.title: Judge issues arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro, brother of presidential candidate
events.summary: A Brazilian Supreme Court justice issued a warrant on Thursday for the arrest of Eduardo Bolsonaro SAO PAULO -- A Brazilian Supreme Court justice issued a warrant on Thursday for the arrest of Eduardo Bolsonaro, one of the brothers of presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Eduardo Bolsonaro was sentenced in June to four years in prison for lobbying the Trump administration. Bolsonaro, a 42-year-old former lawmaker who lives in Texas and is a green card holder, was sentenced for lobbying to impose sanctions against members of the Brazilian government and implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, for a coup attempt. His lawyer didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. Members of the Trump administration have never made comments about Eduardo Bolsonaro's conviction. Justice Alexandre de Moraes' decision came less than three weeks before a runoff for the country’s presidency between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, who won the most votes in the first round on Sunday. Eduardo Bolsonaro has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration. De Moraes, who the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, also canceled Eduardo Bolsonaro's Brazilian passport. The judge chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced last year to 27 years in prison for a coup attempt, but has since been involved in corruption accusations. The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his sentence immediately and warned the country's federal police that he should be arrested if he returns to Brazil. “The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” the judge said. Eduardo Bolsonaro has lived in the U.S. since 2025, which has caused him to lose his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator because of his long absence. The U.S. and Brazil signed an extradition agreement in 1961, but the Trump administration would have to approve an extradition request for Bolsonaro, which is unlikely, said Raphael Vieira da Fonseca Rocha, a law professor at the Federal University of Juiz de Fora. Due to the unlikeliness of an extradition being granted, “requesting it through the existing diplomatic channels of international legal cooperation would weaken the Supreme Court,” Fonseca Rocha said. He said the Supreme Court probably won’t even try and instead appeared to be applying pressure by cancelling his passport. As a consequence, “the United States would have no legal basis to extradite Eduardo Bolsonaro,” he said, adding that there was also a territorial question since Eduardo Bolsonaro was in the U.S. when he committed the crimes which led to his conviction in Brazil. The former lawmaker gave his brother's presidential bid a boost on May 26 by taking him to the White House to meet Trump. At the time, Flávio Bolsonaro was under fire for his confessed links to a disgraced banker , which analysts believed could derail his candidacy. AP journalist Eléonore Hughes contributed to this report from Rio de Janeiro. events.title: Ukrainian drone attack takes out Russian datacenter
events.summary: Russian web giant Yandex says one of its cloud availability zones is unavailable due to a drone attack. Yandex is Russia’s rough equivalent of Google, and dominates the local market for search, email, and mapping services. The company also operates a cloud computing service whose status page says its ru-central1-b availability zone is down. “The incident was caused by a fire caused by a drone attack on Yandex's data center in Sasovo, which affected part of the Yandex Cloud infrastructure. Data center operations have been completely halted.” Sasovo is a town around 300 kilometers southeast of Moscow. Yandex later recommended users employ unspecified “alternative service restoration plans,” including its own bare metal servers, but advised users “it will not be possible to restore service in the near future.” The Russian company hasn’t commented on the source of the drone attack, but Ukrainian press report that President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Russia has attacked Ukrainian datacenters and that his government always responds in kind. Reuters reports that Yandex is uncertain if it is possible to restore operations at the datacenter. If Yandex must write off the datacenter, it will be the second cloud provider to lose facilities to drone attacks this year after AWS decided its Bahrain facility could not be recovered after an Iranian drone attack. Iran hit AWS facilities because it believed the cloud giant hosts workloads for the US military and its suppliers, and that an attack could therefore disrupt hostilities. For years, industry execs have told The Register that datacenters are critical infrastructure and will therefore likely become a target for kinetic attacks during conflict – either directly or by attacking their connections to energy grids and communications services. Clouds and pundits alike advise using multiple geographically dispersed availability zones, and cloud suppliers, to improve resilience. That advice is a little less potent in Russia, where sanctions mean local businesses aren’t welcome in clouds across the border. Russia also has a smaller pool of cloud operators to choose from. ® Updated to add at 1230 UTC: Yandex has just confirmed a second datacenter has been struck. Looks like Ukraine is going after more critical infrastructure.

events.title: AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI
events.summary: Anthropic has launched an effort to help people patch the software vulnerabilities exposed by its own Project Glasswing. If that sounds like a careless camper starting a wildfire and later funding a fire department, well, that's one way of looking at it. Anthropic insists it wants to give defenders access to the tools attackers are already using. Under a program name that sounds like a forthcoming Tom Cruise film – "Anthropic Cyber Mission" – the Claudefather is directing its effort into two areas. The first is a Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, because no one wants AI models showing miscreants how to shut down public utilities with newly discovered zero-day SCADA vulnerabilities. The program combines the company's priciest models with on-site engineers – sometimes now referred to as forward deployed engineers – because despite the sophistication of AI coding agents, human security experts are still useful and many organizations lack in-house talent tutored in the ways of machine learning. Anthropic aims to tackle this challenge with the help of a stable of partners: Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation. These organizations have ties to critical infrastructure organizations and are already working to safeguard the fragile technical framework being probed constantly by AI agents. The second area of focus for the Anthropic Cyber Mission involves a service called OSS Scanner, "which offers open-source projects regular security scans from our strongest models, for free." The offer does not extend to all open-source projects, nor is it entirely free. Anthropic has borrowed the eligibility criteria used by Google for its OS-FUZZ project and will therefore work on "established projects that have a critical impact on infrastructure and user security." So if you just have a public web app repo languishing on GitHub, you can instead turn to existing tools like Socket, Dependabot, OSV-Scanner, Trivy, Renovate, or something similar. And maybe you'll be able to get your AI coding agent of choice to audit your site without balking when faced with a security audit. But for those involved in influential and widely used open-source projects, reinforcements are at hand, so long as project maintainers don't mind having their "materials" – inputs and outputs – used for model training, per the consumer terms of service Anthropic applied to OSS Scanner. Really though, most established open-source projects have already been captured in training data sets. Projects allowed to enroll can expect periodic automated scans that provide details about how identified bugs may be exploitable. These reports go out without human review, but Anthropic has assembled a set of quotes from participating OSS maintainers who believe the robo-reporting is worthwhile. At the beginning of the year, according to Anthropic, automated AI bug reports were considered mostly slop but are now considered high-quality bug reports. LLMs, the company said, now find more than 85 percent of vulnerabilities, up from 20 percent at the start of 2025. The AI biz predicts that in two years, defenders will have the advantage because AI will catch bugs before they ship. But until then, attackers have the upper hand. "Defenders of critical infrastructure and the OSS community have decades of security experience but have faced severe resource shortages that are exacerbated by this moment," Anthropic said in a blog post. Anthropic's moment of generosity comes after recent incidents that saw frontier models break into at least 20 organizations (and maybe over 100), most notably HuggingFace. After months of Anthropic and OpenAI allowing their AI agents to operate without the sort of oversight that would catch unlawful or undesirable network activity, public concern, government backlash [PDF], and perhaps plans to tap public markets for further financing, appear to have created a more urgent sense of civic responsibility. ®

events.title: California threatens to worsen House Democrats' 2027 headaches
events.summary: More than half a dozen U.S. House districts in California will send a Democrat to Capitol Hill next year no matter what. Party leadership still has a lot riding on the outcome. Why it matters: Most of these Democrat vs. Democrat runoffs — a quirk of California's election system — are between an establishment candidate and an outsider vowing to make leadership's life hell. Democratic Reps. Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui and Jimmy Gomez are all facing well-funded challenges from younger, less establishment-aligned Democrats. There are also several Northern California races that feature a pro-leadership Democrat facing off against a more left-leaning rival. Sought for comment on this story, Justin Chermol, a spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios: "Stop wasting our time with your irrelevant stories that have nothing to do with taking back control of the House of Representatives." 4th District: Rep. Mike Thompson vs. Eric Jones Thompson , a 75-year-old first elected in 1998, faces a challenge from 35-year-old former venture capitalist Eric Jones. "I don't think anyone in Democratic leadership today is really doing their job well," Jones said in an interview with Axios. Asked if he would vote for Jeffries as speaker, Jones replied: "As of today, I wouldn't vote for any member." Jones is trying to cobble together a populist, anti-establishment coalition consisting of both progressives and Republicans. He said he does not identify as progressive, telling Axios he prefers "no labels." He said that, if elected, he will "have the benefit of independence ... of not taking party money, and I'm not going to vote a party line." 7th District: Rep. Doris Matsui vs. Mai Vang Matsui, 82, is seen as particularly vulnerable after finishing second to Mai Vang in the jungle primary election in June. Vang, a progressive Sacramento City Councilmember in her 40s, has positioned herself alongside a new bloc of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb and Melat Kiros. She previously signaled to Axios she won't vote for Jeffries as speaker, saying she "cannot support this kind of leadership" and that "we need new leadership and a new direction." 11th District: Scott Wiener vs. Connie Chan The fight between state Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been particularly bitter. Chan has positioned herself to the left of Wiener, a longtime progressive who has come under fire from the pro-Palestinian movement for being insufficiently critical of Israel. Wiener told Mission Local he looks "forward to electing Hakeem Jeffries speaker." Chan told the outlet that "any candidate for speaker, including Hakeem Jeffries, will have to earn my vote." 14th District: Rep. Aisha Wahab vs. Melissa Hernandez Wahab , a progressive former state senator, defeated Hernandez, the more moderate former mayor of Dublin, California, in an August special election to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell . The two are now duking it out for a full term. Wahab has already shown her willingness to buck leadership: She defied Pelosi and Jeffries by running in the special election instead of allowing a "caretaker" to run unopposed, according to The Sunday Times . The Wahab and Hernandez campaigns did not respond to questions about whether their candidates would vote for Jeffries as speaker. 34th District: Rep. Jimmy Gomez vs. Angela Gonzales-Torres Gomez has come under fire after the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into him in August over allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies. He has been a longtime target of the left, having survived three consecutive primary challenges from Democrat David Kim since 2020 by 2 to 11 percentage points. This time he faces a challenge from Angela Gonzales-Torres, a progressive local neighborhood councilor backed by many of the same left-wing groups that support Vang and Wahab. Gonzales-Torres , asked in an interview with Axios if she would vote for Jeffries as speaker, said she looks forward to "supporting leaders who are not nearly funded by corporate super PACs." Gonzales-Torres, pointing to her support from DSA, said she considers herself part of the "national slate" of progressive insurgents such as Avila Chevalier, Rabb and Kiros. "Right now [what] we are focusing on is winning this election and hopefully getting to be part of utilizing our bargaining power as this incoming class in Congress," she said. The bottom line: The larger the bloc of Jeffries skeptics that arrives on Capitol Hill in January, the worse a time Democratic leadership will have. That could be tempered to a large degree by the size of Democrats' potential majority, but, as Axios previously reported , many red-seat candidates are also maintaining their independence from leadership. Still, few Democrats think Jeffries will ultimately be denied the speakership. The fights that come after are more uncertain. Editor's note: This article has been corrected to note Rep. Matsui is 82 (not 85).

events.title: 'Fed a lie': Locals frustrated as construction site remains at famous WA beach
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cable Beach development limbo leaves sceptical Broome locals unsurprised Topic: Urban Development and Planning The foreshore redevelopment at Cable Beach in WA's Kimberley continues to remain a construction site as its opening date approaches. Originally slated for completion mid-to-late this year, it's unclear whether work will be finished in 2026. Broome locals remain frustrated but not surprised by delays. One of Australia's most-famous beachfronts continues to remain a construction site with a timeline for the multimillion-dollar redevelopment of Cable Beach blowing out. The landmark beach in Broome, 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, is a major state and national tourists drawcard with its famous camel rides and sunsets a feature of West Australian tourist campaigns. But the long-term redevelopment of the precinct, which will see a water park, amphitheatre, new beach access and other features added, has left access to some of the area restricted since 2023. Keen tourists and locals were promised the final stage of the project would be complete by the mid to late-2026. Camel rides are a staple of Cable Beach tourism. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) But as that deadline approaches the Shire of Broome says the project's official opening will not occur until 2027. They were unable to confirm whether construction work would be complete by the end of this year. The development has drawn a mixed reception from locals, with many frustrated by the ongoing restrictions to parking and beach access. Jemma Vincent and Giles Fresher grew up in Broome, enjoying everything Cable Beach has to offer. Ms Vincent said she was not surprised to hear about delays to the opening. "Sounds about right, everything takes a long time to do here," she said. Jemma Vincent and Giles Fresher grew up in Broome and say the redevelopment delays impact the lifestyle. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) Among Ms Vincent's circle of friends, being denied car access via ramp to the northern side of Cable Beach was the biggest concern. "People didn't really care about [the construction] as long as you could get down onto the beach and have car access," she said. But fellow Broome local Grant Garrett said he believed the redeveloped foreshore would be great for tourism. Grant Garrett has lived in Broome for two decades and is supportive of the project. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) "Any kind of progress for Broome is good, but I think it's come along very slowly, unfortunately," he said. "Overall, when it's all done, it will be a great improvement for the community and tourism industry." While supportive of the redevelopment overall, Spinifex Brewing chief executive Leanne Andrews said the road closures had reduced foot traffic and spontaneous visits to its Cable Beach venue. "Probably the biggest thing is not knowing when it's going to finish and the prolonged staffing impacts," she said. "I've no doubt it will be positive in the end but it would be good to know when it's actually going to finish."' The chief executive of Broome's Spinifex Brewing said road closures had impacted their Cable Beach business. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) Ms Andrews said a lack of communication around progress and timelines had proven disruptive for Cable Beach businesses. "It's still on the website as mid to late-2026. It's been one of those developments that's just kept on keeping on," she said. "We're one community and I guess we all just want to see each other succeed." Cable Beach is known for its four-wheel drive access. ( ABC News ) A Shire of Broome spokesperson said it was committed to providing updates as key milestones were confirmed. "We know there is strong community interest in the redevelopment," they said. "The shire is working closely with the contractor and reviewing the latest project information to ensure the information we provide to the community is accurate and up to date. "Planning is also underway for an official launch event which is expected to take place next year." events.title: Data centre operator Firmus pulls blockbuster ASX float after lacklustre demand
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) The mega float of data centre operator Firmus has been pulled. It follows poor interest from investors amid concerns about the company's debt and a lack of detail. The company says it will pursue private funding. AI data centre company Firmus has withdrawn its application to list on the ASX, scrapping what was set to be one of Australia's biggest share market floats. The company cited recent market volatility and conditions, saying the offer would not appropriately reflect its long-term growth prospects. Firmus said it would now pursue private market funding while considering other options. "We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said in a statement. Firmus, the AI factory builder backed by chip-making giant Nvidia, was set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997. The company's founders, co-chief executives Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield, targeted a $44 billion valuation, but prospective investors pulled back based on the high sale price of $11 a share and concerns over an AI bubble. Yesterday, reports emerged that Firmus and its advisors were considering reducing the size of the initial public offering (IPO) and lowering the per-share price from $11 to $8.25. Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield at Firmus's St Leonards, Launceston site. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Many investors were also focused on Mr Curtis's criminal background — he is a former investment banker who served one year in prison a decade ago for insider trading. With AI infrastructure demand accelerating across the Asia-Pacific, Firmus's website says its broader portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries: Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia. It said two sites were operational in Australia and Singapore and five were "under development, targeting ready-for-service over the next 24 months". Its website also spruiks its relationship with US chip giant Nvidia, which has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus. Institutional investors raise doubts Today, after Firmus announced the IPO had been pulled, UniSuper chief investment officer John Pearce said it was disappointing. "The ASX needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," he said. Firmus tries to save mega share market float The company is reportedly having to price its shares lower as it closed its books to potential investors abruptly overnight. Ahead of the announcement, he had released an investment update detailing potential investors' doubts about the AI company and why the super fund would not directly invest in it. "Firmus is a neo-cloud company, and that means it provides cloud services, in very simple terms, to AI companies," he said. "The capital raise will be about $7 billion and that will give Firmus a total market value of around $44 billion." Mr Pearce said even though UniSuper was not directly investing in Firmus, UniSuper would own some shares if the float proceeded "because we have index strategies in our portfolios and Firmus will ultimately be a part of the major indices". He said the reason UniSuper was doubtful about investing was the high valuation. "At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation. "Furthermore, we're quite concerned that Firmus will have to keep coming back to the market for a lot more debt and more equity to fund its expansion plans." Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway yesterday raised concerns over the company's debt levels. Lochlan Holloway is not convinced by the Firmus float. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "The neo-clouds are heavily geared," he wrote in an economic note. "The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans." Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about $US30 billion ($43 billion) of debt, about six times the $US5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028. "Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," Mr Holloway said. CDC was set to build data centres with Firmus but scrapped the deal.

events.title: US disrupts Chinese hacking tools as 7 govts warn of PRC spies stealing sensitive data worldwide
events.summary: The FBI announced that it has seized seven web domains linked to hacking tools allegedly operated by a Chinese security firm called Integrity Technology Group and used by Beijing-backed cyber operatives to scan a South Carolina power company's network and other critical infrastructure systems for vulnerabilities. In a subsequent advisory, the FBI and other government agencies in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Spain warned that Chinese government-linked attackers, enabled by Integrity Tech, are using botnets, malware, and other intrusion tools to target organizations worldwide and steal sensitive data, including from US critical infrastructure networks. “These actors exploit vulnerabilities by using scanning tools, cross-site scripting attacks, and password spraying on Microsoft Exchange servers, while establishing persistence through VPN software and exfiltrating emails and credentials using scripts,” according to the security alert. Based on this activity, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog: CVE-2015-3306 CVE-2015-5477 CVE-2016-3081 CVE-2021-3199 CVE-2023-22894 The court-authorized seizures are the latest in a long series of US law-enforcement attempts to disrupt a Beijing-backed cybercrew called Flax Typhoon and shut down its botnet. From 2021 until its disruption, Flax Typhoon allegedly used a version of this Mirai-based botnet to infect internet-connected devices with malware, scan networks for vulnerabilities, and launch additional cyberattacks, all while hiding the PRC government hackers’ true IP addresses and physical location. The feds allege Integrity Tech developed the botnet and a vulnerability scanner called Microscan, and operated a post-compromise tool called FishHub. The latter allegedly downloaded additional malware to the phishing victims’ networks and stole sensitive data. Court documents, unsealed on Thursday, allege Integrity Tech has contracts with the PRC government, and the feds have long linked Flax Typhoon to the private firm. “Flax Typhoon actors conducted successful computer intrusions against multiple victim entities which had been scanned using the Microscan tool,” according to the court documents. Victims include a university in Hsinchu, Taiwan, that Flax Typhoon compromised in March 2023, and a second university in Puli Township, Taiwan breached in August 2022. “On or about April 26, 2022, and on or about December 29, 2022, Flax Typhoon actors also used the Microscan tool to scan for vulnerabilities on the networks of a U.S. power company based in South Carolina, a multi-national Non-Governmental Organization, Japanese and Polish airports, and at least two Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies in the natural gas and power sectors,” the documents allege. Integrity Tech accessed Microscan through one of the seized domains, c0cc[.]cc. Meanwhile, five of the seized domains, 98aicai[.]com, 98aicode[.]com, outlook3650[.]com, youtubecard[.]com, and linkedinns[.]net, delivered the FishHub malware as recently as March, and infected about 20 Taiwanese universities. “Based on my training and experience I believe the tool was named FishHub because it facilitated phishing activity,” FBI special agent Adam James said in a seizure warrant affidavit. After FishHub downloaded a file onto victims' computers, that file used the five domains to retrieve additional malicious programs and code. The malware created a file listing, searched for specific files, compressed documents, and then exfiltrated the selected files to an attacker-controlled server. This gave Flax Typhoon remote access to compromised networks. In September 2024, the FBI said Integrity Tech and Flax Typhoon tore down their 260,000-device botnet after the FBI and its international pals went after them. As recently as this year, however, both private sector security researchers and Western governments warned that Chinese hackers continue to turn compromised routers and IoT devices into botnets and break into critical networks. In February, operational technology (OT) security provider Dragos said China’s state-sponsored spies haven't let up on their attempts to compromise America's critical infrastructure, and this includes a group whose activity overlaps with Flax Typhoon. This group focuses on gaining long-term access to OT engineering workstations and exfiltrating operational files, and it targets manufacturing, defense, automotive, electric power, oil and gas, and government organizations across the US, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. In April, a 10-country joint advisory warned that basically every Chinese “Typhoon” group is using botnets “strategically, and at scale.” Some of these covert networks are built and maintained by Chinese infosec companies including Integrity Tech, which also controlled and managed the so-called Raptor Train network, the alert said. In late August, the FBI said that it had disrupted a different botnet and seized domains associated with two platforms that Chinese government-backed operatives allegedly used to target NASA, the US Senate, the Department of Energy, and several other government agencies and critical networks. The DOJ subsequently clarified that not all the named organizations had been compromised.®
